#1. Bitcoin rally could revive treasury buying, but easy-money days over

“A return to last year’s indiscriminate capital raising looks unlikely,” said Bitfinex head of derivatives Jag Kooner.

Corporate Bitcoin purchases could accelerate toward the end of 2026 and into 2027 if the cryptocurrency rallies, but investors are likely to be more selective about which treasury companies they finance, according to analysts.

Speaking to Cointelegraph, Bitwise head of research Ryan Rasmussen said there was a broad slowdown in Bitcoin treasury buying in Q3. Strategy’s Bitcoin holdings increased by a net 1,666 BTC in Q3, down from 83,901 BTC in Q2, according to company filings. Other public companies added a net 5,617 BTC, compared with 45,725 BTC in the previous quarter, according to figures supplied by Rasmussen.

Rasmussen said he expects a re-acceleration of corporate Bitcoin purchases to begin as early as this year. Bitfinex head of derivatives Jag Kooner said renewed buying could follow if treasury companies regain premiums to the value of their Bitcoin holdings, allowing them to issue shares and acquire more Bitcoin without diluting existing shareholders’ Bitcoin exposure per share.

The model became popular during the 2025 treasury boom, when companies could raise capital by issuing shares at a premium to the value of their Bitcoin holdings. But as those premiums narrowed or disappeared, issuing new shares became less attractive, limiting companies’ ability to finance additional purchases.

“Shareholders have seen premiums collapse and some companies sell into weakness. Investors are now pricing these businesses on funding costs, balance-sheet discipline and bitcoin per share,” said Kooner.

Bitwise’s October market report also showed a decline in the number of Bitcoin treasuries in Q3, driven by smaller companies abandoning their Bitcoin treasury strategies. A dozen companies that entered during the 2025 treasury boom sold their entire holdings mostly to repay debt or return cash to shareholders after their stock premiums evaporated, said Rasmussen.

Kooner expects established players to attract capital first if buying resumes.

“Initially, capital would likely gravitate towards established players, which have the scale, the liquidity in their own securities and the track record investors now demand,” he said.

Related: Bitcoin is rejected at $83K as US bond yields reverse higher with equities

Rasmussen said most of the largest corporate buyers outside Strategy were operating businesses adding Bitcoin from cash flow rather than issuing stock to fund purchases. That represents “a smaller source of demand but a healthier one,” he said.

Meanwhile, Kooner cautioned that a broader resurgence of new treasury-companies could emerge only after a rally is well underway.

“A broad wave of new listings would most likely arrive late in a rally, once premiums have widened and that timing is itself a warning sign.”

Even without another corporate Bitcoin buying boom, Rasmussen said there will be other drivers for a Bitcoin recovery, pointing to $6.4 billion in spot Bitcoin net inflow in Q3.

“Corporate purchases are one source of demand for bitcoin, but not the only source,” he said.

Kooner agreed ETF demand could sustain the recovery for a period, but cautioned that some activity reflects basis trades that can unwind quickly.

“Without corporate buying, the market loses a price-insensitive bid and becomes more dependent on allocators who rebalance with macro conditions,” he said.

Recent flows show that ETF demand can reverse. US spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded around $229 million in net outflows last week, their second consecutive week of net withdrawals, according to SoSoValue data.

#2. BlackRock files for bitcoin ETF offering downside protection and upside exposure to IBIT

Get The Block’s latest crypto news and price alerts for the coins you follow, right in Chrome. Add our free extension here.

BlackRock filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission for the iShares Bitcoin Managed Protect ETF on Monday.

BlackRock, the world's largest investment manager, has filed for another bitcoin fund, this time one that would give investors both downside protection and upside exposure to its flagship bitcoin exchange-traded fund.

On Monday, the firm filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission for the iShares Bitcoin Managed Protect ETF. That fund will follow BlackRock's multi-billion-dollar iShares Bitcoin Trust ETF, the firm said.

"The Fund seeks to provide upside exposure to the iShares Bitcoin Trust ETF iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) and/or similar bitcoin exposure up to an approximate limit, while seeking to provide a level of downside protection," BlackRock said in the filing.

BlackRock's iShares Bitcoin Trust holds more than $65 billion in assets under management, making it the largest of its kind, according to The Block's bitcoin ETF tracker. BlackRock launched IBIT in January 2024. In June, the firm launched its iShares Bitcoin Premium Income ETF, which is designed to provide investors with exposure to bitcoin while generating monthly option premium income.

In a post on X, Bloomberg Intelligence's James Seyffart noted that BlackRock still just has bitcoin and Ethereum products. Over the past couple of years, other companies have launched ETFs tracking assets from XRP to SOL to DOGE.

"Notably, this is the third Bitcoin ETF filing from them," Seyffart said on Monday. "Still only have Bitcoin and Ethereum products -- no other cryptos."

#4. AnchorWatch Launches Nevada Trust Company, Caps Bitcoin Custody Fees at $10,000 a Month

AnchorWatch’s AnchorWatch Trust Company has now opened its custody service.

Bitcoin custody and insurance firm AnchorWatch has said that its Nevada state-chartered trust company opened for business, offering qualified custody for fiduciaries, public companies, trusts and high-net-worth individuals.

AnchorWatch Trust Company, authorized by the Nevada Financial Institutions Division to act as a custodian, opened on Monday, according to AnchorWatch.

The service is aimed at public companies holding BTC, a category that has expanded sharply as more corporations have added the asset to their balance sheets.

JUST IN: AnchorWatch Trust Company launches a Bitcoin custody service with up to $370 million in insurance per client 🚀"Its clients include fiduciaries, public companies, trusts, and high-net-worth individuals requiring qualified bitcoin custody." — The Block pic.twitter.com/sxGL36ee7I

The company’s flagship differentiator is pricing: fixed-dollar annual fees tiered by vault size, capped at $10,000 per month, rather than the percentage-of-assets charges typical among qualified custodians. Once a client hits the cap, additional bitcoin purchases or price appreciation do not increase the annual fee.

“For large enterprises, the pricing cap will translate to potential six- or seven-figure annual savings for qualified custody,” the company said in its announcement.

ATC offers clients two qualified-custody models. Flagship Custody, where ATC holds the keys required for qualified custody while the client’s trustees or executives hold additional keys, and multi-institution custody, where key control is distributed across three institutions — AnchorWatch Trust Company, BitGo in the United States, and CoinCorner in the Isle of Man.

The multi-institution model addresses a growing concern among institutional bitcoin holders: concentration risk at a single custodian, an anxiety sharpened by past industry failures.

Clients may also apply for insurance issued in the covered client’s or entity’s name — a structure AnchorWatch contrasts with policies held in the custodian’s name, where coverage terms may leave ambiguity about the client’s position in a claim. The insurance is provided by AnchorWatch and backed by A+ rated Lloyd’s of London syndicates.

As a Lloyd’s of London Coverholder, AnchorWatch says it has authority to write up to $370 million in limits per ATC client, covering loss of Bitcoin from perils including violent coercion and kidnapping, as well as losses arising from fraudulent acts by AnchorWatch itself. Coverage is subject to underwriting approval and policy terms.

Insurance is available to U.S.-domiciled companies and subsidiaries and U.S.-resident individuals. Custody without insurance may be available across a broader range of jurisdictions, subject to KYC and AML requirements.

AnchorWatch’s underlying custody platform, Trident Vault, has secured customer Bitcoin for 20 months, according to the company. It has been audited or reviewed by security firms Halborn and Doyensec, and by the technical underwriters at the Lloyd’s syndicates backing the policies.

AnchorWatch describes itself as a Bitcoin-native insurance and custody company; ATC is its Nevada state-chartered trust company arm.

#5. Strive Buys $335 Million in Bitcoin After Investors Pour In $369 Million

Strive Buys $335 Million in Bitcoin After Investors Pour In $369 Million

Strive, a Nasdaq-listed company that holds Bitcoin as a treasury asset, bought 4,045 BTC between October 12 and 16, according to a regulatory filing published Monday.

The average price was about $82,803 per coin, meaning the stash was worth about $335 million, and the purchase lifts its holdings to 36,818 BTC, up from 32,773 a week earlier. That’s a total just north of $3 billion worth of Bitcoin at today’s prices.

The money comes from a Wall Street machine that has become a steady source of Bitcoin buying: public companies sell shares to investors, then put the cash into Bitcoin. Their stock gives investors exposure to Bitcoin’s price through an ordinary brokerage account.

This week’s cash came from warrants, contracts that let holders buy new shares at a fixed price. On October 12 and 13, investors exercised 273,493,909 of them for 13,674,703 new Class A shares, raising about $369.2 million. The leftovers expired unexercised on October 13, and the filing says no traditional warrants remain.

Class A shares outstanding rose from 101.2 million to 114.8 million in a week, about 13.5%. That shrinks each existing shareholder’s slice of the company unless the new cash earns it back. Strive ended the week with $317.5 million in cash, up $7.2 million.

Strive began in 2022 as an anti-ESG asset manager co-founded by former presidential candidate Vivek Ramaswamy. It adopted Bitcoin as a treasury reserve in May 2025 as it moved to merge with a listed company called Asset Entities, then agreed that September to buy Semler Scientific, a medical device maker holding about 5,000 BTC, in an all-stock deal valued at about $1.3 billion.

When Semler shareholders approved the deal in January, the combined company held roughly 12,800 BTC, so holdings are up almost 3X since. Strive’s previous purchase was 3,311 BTC, about $280 million, at roughly $84,500 per coin, a week before this one. The last 1,223 coins in this week’s batch, bought October 14 to 16, averaged about $81,734.

Strategy, the largest corporate bitcoin holder, also bought last week: 267 BTC for about $22.1 million at roughly $82,900 each, bringing its total to 848,517 BTC. It also spent $193.1 million repurchasing its own STRC preferred stock, a security of which Strive holds 505,000 shares, and it increased its preferred-stock buyback program from $2 billion to $3 billion.

MSCI, the index provider whose benchmarks many funds are built to track, finalized a rule on October 15 targeting “non-operating companies.” Companies that fail a screen for substantial operating assets and a follow-up financial test would be dropped from its indexes as of the close of November 30.

Strategy’s Michael Saylor had called the proposal discriminatory in a September letter, and MSCI will publish the final list of affected companies on November 11.

Across the digital asset treasury space, Tom Lee’s Bitmine added 12,535 ETH, about $30 million, and now holds 6,041,481 ETH, or 4.9% of Ethereum’s roughly 122.1 million tokens. Lee has said buying will stop once the firm hits 5%, and he cited a broad risk-off shift (investors pulling back from risky assets), AI funding worries, U.S.-Iran tensions, midterm election jitters, and rising bond yields.

Strive meanwhile priced an upsized offering on October 15 of 7 million shares of a new 15% Series A Perpetual preferred stock, called SATS, at $90 each, for expected gross proceeds of about $630 million.

Preferred stock pays a set dividend when the board declares it, similar to a bond’s interest but not guaranteed, and “perpetual” means it has no maturity date. The dividend here is 15% of the $100 stated amount, or $15 a year, about 16.7% for buyers paying $90.

The dividends are cumulative, meaning any that go unpaid keep accruing. Strive plans to park $22.50 per share in a reserve for the first 18 months of dividends. The offering is scheduled to settle on October 20, and regular dividend dates start November 9.

#6. Tether: Senator's investigation misses positive work that's led to lower Iran volumes

Tether is answering back against a report issued last month by Democrats on the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations that had accused the stablecoin firm of providing "a significant financial lifeline within Iran's shadow banking network," with Tether CEO Paulo Ardoino saying Monday that the probe missed the positive work it's doing to observe sanctions.

Senator Richard Blumenthal, the subcommittee's top Democrat, led the effort, which further highlighted Democratic lawmakers' concerns that crypto is used to support illicit finance. But Ardoino contends that Tether freezes suspicious transactions well before entities such as the U.S. Treasury Department's Office of Foreign Assets Control and Israel's National Bureau for Counter Terror Financing formally flag them.

"Senator Blumenthal's 'analysis' of Tether's sanctions report misses that, since 2023, Tether froze on average 4 weeks prior to OFAC & NBCTF official sanction designation and for 99% of the times Tether froze the reported addresses before Chainalysis labelled them," Ardoino wrote in a post on social media site X.

Ardoino went on to argue that the company's actions "led to Iran-linked stablecoin volumes declining by 94%."

Tether's CEO also spoke remotely at a Washington event, DC Fintech Week, and addressed the senator's report there, as well, last Tuesday. He criticized how it was released to the media before his company could review it.

"I believe it's important for the public also to hear our side of the story," he said.

"Our aim is to push out the bad actors from USDT," Ardoino said. "Those bad actors are moving to other means that are outside of the control of the United States, and now outside of our control."

He added that the work "is not finished," but he said he's happy with Tether's role.

"I wake up in the morning and I look at myself in the mirror, and I know that we're doing the right thing," he said.

The Senate report went back a number of years, focusing in part on the period before 2024 in which it said Tether didn't comprehensively freeze flagged wallets. "This absence of deterrence invited abuse: Terrorist organizations such as Hamas shifted from transacting in bitcoin and a mix of cryptocurrencies to promoting USDT," it said.

Since the report, Blumenthal has additionally been probing the relationship between Tether and its U.S. financial partner, Cantor Fitzgerald, which has close ties to the administration of President Donald Trump. Tether also named Bo Hines, Trump's former White House crypto adviser, as the CEO of its U.S. division last fall.

In recent weeks, the odds that Democrats — including Blumenthal — may return to the majority in the Senate have been climbing, according to prediction market Kalshi. If that happens, Blumenthal could have significantly increased powers to investigate crypto matters.

#7. Solana treasury firm SkyAI sells all SOL holdings, launches $201M buyback

The former medical device maker has liquidated its Solana treasury and is offering to repurchase shares and warrants using its $223.8 million cash holdings.

SkyAI, formerly Sharps Technology, has sold its entire Solana (SOL) treasury and launched a tender offer to repurchase up to $201.3 million in shares and warrants, reversing its cryptocurrency accumulation strategy.

The company held approximately $223.8 million in cash as of Oct. 16 after liquidating its SOL holdings, according to a filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission on Monday.

The tender offer allows shareholders and warrant holders to sell their securities directly back to SkyAI at a fixed price. It covers up to 95% of each class of the company’s outstanding shares and warrants, funded entirely by cash on hand.

The company said the tender offer is no longer tied to SOL’s price, a condition it had initially planned to include when announcing the buyback on Oct. 11. SkyAI intends to continue developing a financial platform combining stablecoin infrastructure on Solana with artificial intelligence.

SkyAI shares closed Monday at $2.79, up 5.3% on the day, according to Yahoo Finance data. The stock has gained approximately 65% over the past month but remains down about 41% over the past year.

Related: Solana shows resilience, but some areas need continued observation, Fidelity says

SkyAI launched its Solana treasury strategy in August 2025 after raising more than $400 million through a private placement. The company acquired more than 2 million SOL the following month, establishing a position valued at more than $400 million at the time.

By the end of 2025, the company held approximately 2.08 million SOL with a cost basis of $403.1 million, or roughly $194 per token. Its holdings were valued at $250.1 million, representing approximately $153 million in unrealized losses, according to its annual financial disclosures.

The losses reflected broader pressure on companies that accumulated SOL as a treasury asset. By February 2026, publicly traded Solana treasury companies faced more than $1.5 billion in combined unrealized losses as falling token prices weighed on their holdings and share valuations.

SOL fell to around $62 in June but has since recovered, trading near $104 as of Monday, according to CoinGecko data.

#9. Mesh taps Visa to let users spend crypto without a separate card

Get The Block’s latest crypto news and price alerts for the coins you follow, right in Chrome. Add our free extension here.

Initial availability, supported devices and participating platforms for the Mesh-Visa linkup have yet to be announced.

Mesh has partnered with Visa to let users spend cryptocurrency and stablecoin balances held in participating wallet apps at more than 175 million merchant locations worldwide.

The integration will enable in-store and online payments through a Visa credential provisioned behind the scenes, with Mesh handling transaction funding and conversion without requiring users to sell or transfer assets beforehand.

"Crypto never had a spending problem — it has a last-mile problem, and until now, closing it meant getting a separate card," Bam Azizi, CEO and co-founder of Mesh, said in a release. "Mesh handles the funding and conversion, so a balance becomes purchasing power at the moment of payment, with nothing for the user to move and nothing for the merchant to change."

Initial availability, supported devices and participating platforms for the Mesh-Visa linkup have yet to be announced.

Mesh is a crypto payments infrastructure firm behind PayPal's "Pay with Crypto" launch. In August 2025, PayPal Ventures, Coinbase Ventures and others lifted Mesh's total funding past $130 million. The company hit unicorn status after a $75 million Series C led by Dragonfly in January.

This is also the latest extension of Visa's continued push into connecting crypto holdings to its native merchant network.

In April, Visa and WeFi planned to let users spend digital assets through Visa while retaining control of their crypto in self-custody wallets. And last year, Visa and Bridge partnered to let developers issue Visa cards funded by stablecoin balances, with Bridge handling the backend and currency conversions.

#10. Circle targets 40 markets – Can USDC make cross-border payments cheaper?

Read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

Read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

Circle and Tether are the leading stablecoin issuers across the globe, providing USDC and USDT, respectively. However, it is Circle that has been making moves toward regulatory clarity faster than Tether.

For instance, USDC became the EU‘s first significant stablecoin under MiCA regulation. In fact, Circle’s revenue for the first half of the year, at $1.40 billion, confirmed its growing adoption.

Circle’s USDC has been dominated by agentic payments, which has contributed to such revenue. Even with that, the protocol is aiming for a larger global reach.

While stablecoin adoption has continued to grow, it has not reached greater levels. As such, CEO Jeremy Allaire of Circle announced they were targeting expansion into 40 developing markets across Latin America, Southeast Asia, Africa, and the Middle East.

In this context, Visa is now moving USDC funding for cross-border payouts from pilot to commercial use across 180 countries.

However, the cost of turning USDC back into local money is unknown. A cheap transfer can still have an expensive last step.

This could widen the gap between USDC and USDT in transaction volume. According to Bernstein reports, it now handles over 60% of adjusted transaction volume in 2026, despite USDT having a bigger cap.

That is, USDC was capped at $72.5 billion, while USDT was at $183 billion, which is more than double. Still, Circle continues to provide stablecoin liquidity, minting $3.75 billion in USDC on Solana over the past 7 days.

As Circle challenges Tether in stablecoin business dominance, it launched its chain in mid-September under the name Arc. However, the Arc blockchain is still underutilized, accounting for less than 1% of all USDC, equivalent to $661.4 million.

As per Token Terminal, 66.6% of the supply was on Ethereum [ETH], with Solana [SOL], HyperEVM, Base, and Arbitrum One [ARB] following, respectively. This indicates that Arc is yet to play a key role in challenging USDT’s dominance.

It is still worth noting that the DeFi TVL of USDC grew by 6% upon chain launch. Weekly asset senders also increased by 5.4%, reaching 5.5 million as of press time.

#11. Binance AI Pro Turns Plain-Text Prompts Into Automated Trading Strategies

Home » Crypto Market News » Binance AI Pro Turns Plain-Text Prompts Into Automated Trading Strategies

Binance’s new AI agent lets users build and test trading bots without code.

Binance has launched Binance AI Pro, a finance-focused AI agent that turns plain-language prompts into automated trading strategies, according to an official announcement.

The tool is available on Binance’s web and mobile apps and removes the need to write code or configure API bots. It lowers the technical barrier to algorithmic trading for retail users.

According to an official video, users describe their intended assets, entry conditions, and risk limits in plain English, and the agent builds the strategy.

On desktop, each strategy appears as a visual workflow called the Strategy Canvas, shown beside the chat interface. Users can review steps, modify parameters, add or remove components, and attach instructions to modules.On mobile, workflows are created and edited through chat.

The tool also supports daily reporting, market monitoring, subscription alerts, and signal generation. Binance AI Pro combines Binance’s market data and research with selected third-party sources.

The service uses a large language model and a finance-specific framework to analyze information and convert user instructions into trading strategy code. It also includes safeguards governing how the system operates.

Strategies can be tested using paper trading, which simulates market activity with virtual funds, before going live.

Live trading requires separate user approval and takes place in an AI Strategy Account, a virtual sub-account isolated from the user’s main Binance account.

Only the user can fund it through manual transfer. According to Binance, the agent cannot move funds on its own, and strategies can be paused, adjusted, or revoked at any time.

“Users describe the idea, review the workflow, test it with paper trading, and approve deployment themselves,” said Jeff Li, VP of Product at Binance.

Binance says AI Pro follows the “bounded autonomy” principles outlined in a policy paper by its Global Policy team. Under this approach, AI agents can analyze markets and make recommendations, while consequential actions require explicit human approval.

Binance AI Pro currently supports Spot and USDS-M Futures strategies, subject to regional restrictions. The company plans to expand the service to additional trading products.

All users start on the free Standard Plan, which includes 250,000 monthly credits. The Premium Plan costs 19.99 USDC per month and raises the allowance to 10 million monthly credits. It also adds frontier models such as ChatGPT Sol, ChatGPT Astra, and Claude Opus where available, and allows credit top-ups. Payment is made via Binance Pay.

Binance AI Pro shows a major exchange packaging AI-driven strategy building directly into its trading apps, with human approval kept in the loop. It may shape how other exchanges approach AI agents for retail users.

#14. The Architecture of Money: Mapping Financial Power in the Age of Bitcoin

Carlijn Kingma, Thomas Bollen, and Martijn Jeroen van der Linden on The Waterworks of Money, the hidden structures of finance, and bitcoin's place in Europe's monetary future.

Money determines where we live, what we can afford, and how wealth accumulates across generations. Yet the mechanisms that create and distribute it remain largely occluded, even as their consequences become harder to unsee. For Dutch artist Carlijn Kingma, investigative financial journalist Thomas Bollen, and monetary researcher Martijn Jeroen van der Linden, that disconnect became the impetus for The Waterworks of Money. This ambitious project maps the hidden architecture of the financial system through drawing and animation, rendering it understandable to the people living within it without flattening its complexity.

The Waterworks of Money depicts the financial system as a vast network of reservoirs, channels, and pumps, revealing how money moves through banks, governments, businesses, and households. Some areas receive an abundance of liquidity, while others remain perpetually dry. The resulting drawing operates simultaneously as an artwork, an educational tool, and an examination of financial power.

The project emerged from two years of research, including interviews with more than 100 experts across banking, government, academia, and monetary reform movements. Kingma spent more than 2,200 hours translating that research into an intricate architectural landscape. Bollen, whose investigative journalism examines the workings of the financial system, and van der Linden, whose academic research explores money and monetary reform, helped develop the economic research and narratives behind the work.

One of the project’s scenarios explores a monetary future shaped by bitcoin. As bitcoin enters traditional finance, an alternative monetary system either challenges existing structures of financial power or eventually becomes part of them, and the project’s collaborators have watched both happen.

Ahead of Bitcoin Amsterdam, November 5-6, where Bollen joins two panels, I sat down with all three of the project’s collaborators to discuss making money visible, the relationship between monetary systems and inequality, and bitcoin’s place in Europe’s financial future.

BMAG: The Waterworks of Money illustrates the financial system as a network of reservoirs, pumps, and channels, with some parts of society receiving abundant liquidity while others remain dry. After two years of research and interviews with financial experts, what surprised you most about how money actually works? What do you think the public most fundamentally misunderstands about it?

Thomas Bollen: What surprised me most is that many people inside the system know a great deal about their own corner of it: interest rate derivatives, asset management or mortgage lending. Very few of them can oversee the larger system in which they operate.

What is clearly not well understood is that banks create new money when they make a loan. They are not just intermediaries that pass on the savings of their depositors.

But can you blame ordinary people for that? During the research phase we spoke to many bankers and even a CEO of a major bank who did not know they were working for a money creating institution.

If we want to improve understanding we should start at our schools and universities. Many textbooks still get it wrong, and economics education hardly pays any attention to it. In 2022 even the Riksbank’s prize in economics (the Nobel prize that is not really a Nobel prize) was awarded for research that presents banks as mere intermediaries.

BMAG: One of the central ideas in The Waterworks of Money is that money doesn’t flow evenly through society. Housing affordability has become a major issue in Europe and the United States, while asset prices and financial wealth have increasingly outpaced wages. How much of this inequality results from the design of our monetary system, rather than broader economic forces?

Thomas Bollen: It is impossible to capture that in a precise number, because so many factors play a role. But it is quite clear that the money system exacerbated inequality enormously during all those years when credit was extremely cheap.

Ray Dalio, founder of the hedge fund Bridgewater Associates, summed it up in 2019: “Money is free for those who are creditworthy.” For everyone without money or creditworthiness, it was out of reach.

Cheap credit for rich people and large multinationals (who used it for share buybacks and M&A deals) drove up the price of shares, and of houses. Bank money creation produced a specific kind of inflation: asset inflation. Wealthy households and large multinationals, who already owned those assets, profited far more from it than people without them or small businesses that did not have the same kind of access to cheap credit as their larger competitors.

BMAG: The Waterworks of Money is filled with details that help explain how the financial system works. What was the most difficult part of the monetary system to illustrate? Did anything you learned during the research change how you approached the drawing?

Carlijn Kingma: The biggest challenge was the way all the parts are connected. How do you show that clearly?

Water is the obvious metaphor for money, and it takes you a long way. Liquidity, cash flows, money drying up: they are already in the language of finance. It was also great for connecting the different parts of the system, because I could draw the pipes and canals that run between them.

But in some places you need more than that if you want to be completely accurate. Money comes in many forms: commodity money, public money, private credit money, and further out short-term debt and repo contracts can also serve as money or near-money. It was not possible to draw that many different kinds of water running through the system.

BMAG: The Waterworks of Money has been shown to both art audiences and people interested in economics, including at Bitcoin Amsterdam last year. Have you noticed differences in how these audiences respond to the work? Has their feedback influenced how you think about the role of art in explaining complex ideas?

Carlijn Kingma: The response depends on what people already know. Visitors with more financial knowledge usually laugh more, because they catch all the small jokes. We renamed Basel III to “Babel III”, for instance, because the bank rules written after the crisis add up to about three bibles.

In our bitcoin future scenario, The Republic of a Thousand Coins, we put in a lot of jokes about central bankers. You can see Alan Greenspan there as an inflatable doll. That works best if you know who he is, and the bitcoin crowd knows far more about monetary history than the general public.

Above all, we noticed that art opens doors. The drawing gives people a visual starting point for a conversation. Even without any prior knowledge, the metaphor lets you see the social outcomes of how money flows.

BMAG: Your research has examined how financial crises can reinforce the influence of institutions considered too important to fail. More recently, you’ve explored the growing power of asset managers such as BlackRock and Vanguard. Are we witnessing a genuine transformation in how financial power operates, or have the same underlying problems simply taken new forms since 2008?

Martijn Jeroen van der Linden: Following the crisis of 2008, there was a general consensus among mainstream policymakers, think tanks and many economists that the banking sector needed to be repaired. In Europe, the influential de Larosière Group concluded that the causes of the crisis were excessive leverage, opaque securitisation, shadow banking risks, and fragmented supervision in the EU, and argued that “repair is necessary and urgent.” The banking repair consisted of new and stricter regulations, stronger coordinated supervision and new crisis management procedures. The underlying architecture remained unaltered, meaning that fundamental change never occurred.

But the architecture remained fragile. Take, for example, 2023. When Silicon Valley Bank and Credit Suisse got into trouble, the crisis playbooks developed after 2008 stayed in the drawer. The US authorities guaranteed all SVB deposits, including the more than 90 percent above the insured limit. In Switzerland, the state backed the rescue of Credit Suisse by UBS.

Advocates of banking repair often claim to have made the system safer. But the inherent fragility of funding long-term loans with runnable bank deposits is still there. Even with all the regulation, you cannot prevent a bank run, and that fragility is precisely what they refuse to solve. The banking system only survives because of massive public safety nets and privileges given to banks.

Large powerful non-banks have indeed emerged but they do not play a pivotal role in money and payments. This is a key distinction between the two sectors.

BMAG: Bitcoin began as an attempt to create money outside the control of governments and banks. Today, it’s increasingly held through investment funds and traditional financial institutions, including some of the same powerful asset managers examined in your recent work. Does this integration strengthen bitcoin’s ability to change the financial system, or risk reproducing the concentration of power it originally sought to challenge?

Martijn Jeroen van der Linden: As a financial asset, bitcoin has benefited from investments from traditional financial institutions. But the increasing use of bitcoin as an investment has compromised its promise of an alternative payment system.

At the same time, bitcoin and the rise of stablecoins have challenged the banks on their payment infrastructure. The banks are now innovating too: look at Wero, the payment wallet that a group of European banks launched in 2024. That is a change. But it is something different from the structural reform of money and banking.

BMAG: Your project imagines bitcoin as an alternative to the existing monetary system. Amsterdam also has a remarkable history of monetary experimentation, from the development of modern financial institutions to David Chaum’s pioneering work on private digital cash decades before bitcoin. Given that history, how do you see bitcoin’s role in Europe’s financial future? Has your perspective changed since you began working on the project?

Thomas Bollen: What I appreciate about bitcoin’s design is that it resembles full reserve banking. A bitcoin is not a claim on something else, so it carries no risk of a bank run. Bank deposits are: they are a promise that you can withdraw your money at any moment, while the bank can never keep that promise to all its customers at once.

We can learn a lot from our history. The Amsterdamsche Wisselbank, founded in 1609 and often seen as the world’s first central bank, started out as a full reserve bank: every bank guilder was backed by coins in its vault. It went under only after it secretly began lending more and more to the Dutch East India Company.

That is the risk of every monetary experiment: it can go in the wrong direction. In the crypto world, all kinds of companies started copying the banks. They lent out their customers’ bitcoins, while those customers still saw their coin-balances in their accounts. Sam Bankman-Fried’s FTX shows how this practice can go horribly wrong.

Thomas Bollen will participate in two panel discussions at Bitcoin Amsterdam on November 6, 2026, on the Treasury Stage. Europe’s Monetary History & Future: Austrian Economics, Banks & Bitcoin (11:00–11:30 AM), alongside Rahim Taghizadegan and Willem Middelkoop, and Staat vs. de Markt: Hoeveel Overheid Hebben We Nodig in Geld? (1:55–2:25 PM), alongside Paul Buitink and Simon Lelieveldt.

#16. Solana Achieves 104% Transaction Growth

Solana (SOL), one of the leading layer-1 blockchains, has recorded a massive increase in transaction activity, with its non-vote transaction count more than doubling compared to late 2025.

According to a recent announcement by the official Solana account on X, the network processed a staggering 8.92 billion non-vote transactions in the third quarter of 2026.

Solana co-founder Anatoly Yakovenko, better known as Toly, responded to the milestone with a characteristically brief comment.

"Put the cryptography into the computer," he wrote on X, apparently celebrating the blockchain's growing adoption and activity.

The 104% growth represents a significant increase from approximately 4.38 billion transactions recorded in the fourth quarter of 2025.

Notably, Solana also recorded 7.54 billion transactions in the first quarter of 2026, followed by 7.19 billion in the second quarter.

This means that transaction activity increased by approximately 24% on a quarter-over-quarter basis in Q3, reversing the decline observed during the preceding quarter.

Non-vote transactions are particularly important for evaluating blockchain activity because they exclude the routine voting transactions that validators use to maintain network consensus.

Instead, they capture activity involving token transfers, decentralized applications, trading, and other interactions with the blockchain.

The latest figures suggest that Solana continues to experience substantial demand for its network infrastructure.

According to data compiled by Solana Compass, the blockchain processed approximately 3.18 billion completed non-vote transactions in September alone, marking its third consecutive monthly record.

However, the growing transaction count does not necessarily translate into an equivalent increase in individual users, since automated trading bots can account for significant on-chain activity.

Meanwhile, Solana's native SOL token was trading near the $104 level on Oct. 19, with a market capitalization of approximately $61 billion.

Cardano founder Charles Hoskinson says he is personally developing a new programming language for the blockchain. In an October 18 post on X, he said he was working with a developer to build it.

According to him, the proposed tool would help applications carry out users’ requests and provide evidence that the required conditions were followed. That could give Cardano developers another way to build applications, although Hoskinson’s post offered no release date.

Hoskinson described the language as supporting “intents and PCD via Groth16 proofs,” calling it the first of its kind.

So, for example, someone swapping tokens could specify the minimum amount they want to receive. Software would handle the steps needed to complete the request while making sure the conditions are met.

The proof component would provide mathematical evidence that the relevant rules were satisfied.

Cardano already has programming tools, including Aiken, which developers use to create smart contracts. Aiken’s official documentation describes an existing language and toolkit, so what this means is that Hoskinson’s project would add another development option.

The announcement leaves important questions open

Hoskinson did not include a name, technical specification, or code link in his reply. So, it is not yet known how his proposal would work or fit alongside existing tools.

His earlier October 17 post described a Midnight concept as the “magnum opus” of his career. He announced the Cardano language in a subsequent reply, but did not explicitly say that the two were the same project.

ADA traded around $0.2173 at the time of this writing, down 1.76% in the ongoing session.

It had fallen from the high $0.28 price level it hit earlier in the month. The recent rebounds it experienced have not been able to reverse that decline, which leaves the price close to its latest lows.

The $0.21 area was the nearest zone to watch for buyers who want to get some of it. If it is able to remain above $0.23, it would mean a stronger sign of recovery.

#18. Crypto PAC pours $362K into California race voters essentially decided in August

A Fairshake affiliate is supporting incumbent Aisha Wahab through ads in November, but the congresswoman already won a special election in the district.

Protect Progress, an affiliate of the cryptocurrency-aligned Fairshake super political action committee (PAC), reported spending $362,000 on ads to support a Democrat in California’s 14th congressional district, just weeks after she won a special election against the same opponent.

According to a Sunday filing with the US Federal Election Commission (FEC), Protect Progress reported spending $362,000 on media supporting incumbent Democrat Aisha Wahab in the Bay Area district against her fellow party member, Melissa Hernandez.

Wahab defeated Hernandez in an Aug. 18 special election with more than 53% of the vote, raising questions about why the cryptocurrency industry-aligned PAC is supporting her in the 2026 midterms.

Notably, both Wahab and Hernandez were ranked as “strongly supports crypto” after they went on the record with the digital asset organization Stand With Crypto to complete questionnaires ahead of the August special election. That election was used to determine who would replace Democrat Eric Swalwell for the remainder of his term, ending January 2027. Swalwell resigned in April amid sexual assault allegations.

Fairshake launched in 2023, backed largely by contributions from Coinbase, Ripple Labs and Andreessen Horowitz. Since the 2024 US elections, the Super PAC has spent tens of millions of dollars on candidates the group considers “pro-crypto” in efforts to fill Congress with lawmakers more likely to support policies favorable to the digital asset industry.

Related: Ex-Trump crypto adviser profited after helping pass stablecoin bill: WSJ

In an Oct. 7 debate, Wahab signaled that she opposed Hernandez for not denouncing expenditures from corporate PACs aligned with the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC), adding that the spending “really deteriorated our democracy.” Cointelegraph reached out to both the Hernandez and Wahab campaigns, and Fairshake for comment on the spending but did not receive immediate responses.

One notable change between the August special election and the November midterms will be the boundaries of California’s 14th district. The current boundaries, which include parts of San Francisco’s East Bay, will be expanded in accordance with the 2025 passage of the state’s Proposition 50, requiring new maps for the midterm elections.

The crypto PAC reported in January that it had $193 million in cash on hand ahead of the elections, and it had already used tens of millions of dollars to support Democratic and Republican candidates in primaries and special elections.

With just over two weeks until the 2026 election, Fairshake reported additional spending on media for Senate races in Ohio and Nebraska.

Defend American Jobs, a Fairshake affiliate largely supporting Republican candidates, reported spending more than $6.7 million to oppose Independent candidate Dan Osborn in Nebraska’s Senate race. The PAC also reported $8 million on media in Ohio, supporting incumbent Republican Jon Husted against Democrat Sherrod Brown in a race where it has spent more than $46 million so far.

Brown’s race could be another bellwether for how the crypto industry potentially impacts the 2026 midterms. The Democrat lost his seat to Republican Bernie Moreno in 2024 after Fairshake and other interest groups spent a combined hundreds of millions of dollars on ads opposing Brown.

#19. Mastercard unveils Stablecoin Security tool to screen payments for fraud and sanctions risks

Get The Block’s latest crypto news and price alerts for the coins you follow, right in Chrome. Add our free extension here.

The service will give banks a risk score before stablecoin payments are completed, with Borderless.xyz and Keyrails among its first partners.

Mastercard said Monday that it is introducing Stablecoin Security, a risk intelligence service that will let financial institutions assess the risks of stablecoin payments before funds move onchain.

Borderless.xyz and Keyrails are the first partners announced for the product, which Mastercard unveiled at Money20/20 USA.

Stablecoin Security checks where money came from and looks for possible links to fraud, scams, sanctions violations, and other financial crime risks throughout the stablecoin payment lifecycle. It also looks at the transaction context before assigning a risk score, with Mastercard providing the information through an API, so banks can use it with the existing fraud and compliance systems they already have.

"Stablecoins are creating new possibilities for value exchange, but financial institutions need the right intelligence and controls to participate with confidence," Ann Johnson, Mastercard's executive vice president of Security Solutions, said in a statement shared with The Block.

Mastercard cited a BIS study that looked at 593 million stablecoin transfer events across 141 million Ethereum transactions in 2025. Nearly 60% of stablecoin transfer events occurred within complex, multi-step transactions, rather than simple one-to-one payments, the study found.

The launch adds to Mastercard's growing stablecoin-related initiatives.

In August, Mastercard and Borderless.xyz announced a Crypto Credential pilot, involving Infinia, Walapay, and Koywe to add trust signals to cross-border stablecoin payments. Both Borderless.xyz and Keyrails have also participated in Mastercard's Start Path Blockchain and Digital Assets program.

Borderless.xyz connects financial institutions with licensed stablecoin providers across more than 113 countries and 72 currencies, while Keyrails works on high-value cross-border trade payments, particularly in emerging markets, according to Mastercard.

Mastercard also acquired stablecoin infrastructure provider BVNK in August, after announcing an agreement worth up to $1.8 billion in March. Last week, Mastercard launched its Global Money Platform, combining fiat and stablecoin accounts, real-time conversion, card spending, and local bank payouts through a single API in its first major integration of BVNK. The company expects to bring BVNK into its Stablecoin Security plans next year.

Mastercard said the new service will launch first in North America, with commercial availability expected worldwide in 2027.

#21. Anthropic Gives 5% of Itself to the Public. Musk Answers by Giving Away SpaceX Shares

Anthropic Gives 5% of Itself to the Public. Musk Answers by Giving Away SpaceX Shares

Anthropic, the company behind the Claude chatbot, said Sunday it will commit 5% of its shares to a new Public Benefit Fund. On Monday, Elon Musk answered by promising one SpaceX share to every child in the United States next year.

“The Anthropic Public Benefit Fund will have increased flexibility and scale, enabling us to pursue our mission in new ways: for example, we might explore large donations to traditional nonprofits or direct distributions to specific populations,” Anthropic said. The company has already committed $200 million to studying that.

Americans are uneasy about how fast AI is moving: an AP-NORC poll in late September found that 64% of U.S. adults say the technology is developing too fast, and 8% say too slow.

Anthropic is preparing an IPO, meaning it would sell its shares to the public on the stock market, as soon as November at a reported valuation of around $2 trillion. At that price, 5% of the company would be worth about $100 billion on paper, though that is the value of the shares, not cash sitting in an account.

The fund is set up as a wholly owned LLC rather than a nonprofit, which Anthropic says gives it room to switch between types of giving. The board can add another 2% of shares each time the company's value rises 50% above a baseline that has not been disclosed, and none of the fund's equity can be used for lobbying or political donations.

The co-founders' pledge to donate 80% of their equity and a matching program for employee donations, and Anthropic says roughly 20% of its shares will be dedicated to the public good. The company has not said how the fund will be taxed or what it will disclose publicly, as a traditional charity must.

Musk, never one to leave the spotlight to someone else, pushed for Universal High Income (as opposed to Universal Basic Income) writing on X that he will give one of his SpaceX shares to every kid in America. "This will be the first of many," he added.

His first reply to Anthropic, recommending "giving the shares directly to the public" instead of routing them through a fund, came Sunday night, and the pledge for kids followed early Monday, less than a day after Anthropic's announcement.

Next year, I will give one of my SpaceX shares to every kid in America.

With roughly 72 million children in the country, the pledge comes to about $10.5 billion at SpaceX's price of roughly $147 a share. That is just over 1% of the 6.42 billion shares Musk held as of June 30, per an SEC filing, and about the same slice of a fortune estimated at $908.5 billion that has crossed $1 trillion several times this year.

The Treasury Department recently let companies and charities donate individual company shares to Trump Accounts, tax-advantaged savings accounts for children, with donated stock generally held for five years. This is likely the option Musk is going for instead of Anthropic’s path of creating a fund, which he more or less confirmed in a reply post on X.

The Anthropic giveaway comes from a company whose CEO wrote in January that "we are considerably closer to real danger in 2026" and which is known to preach the gospel of AI doomerism while maxing out accelerationism, releasing the most powerful AI models on the market.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman accused Anthropic in April of using fear-based marketing to promote Claude Mythos, and Anthropic is now giving away a slice of itself ahead of a stock market debut.

Two days before the fund, Anthropic had quietly presented lawmakers with its own draft AI safety bill. It would let the government block the release of a model posing a foreseeable, imminent risk of killing or seriously injuring more than 50 people or causing over $1 billion in damage, through a bioweapon, an AI slipping beyond human control, or a cyberattack.

A block would have to run through the Commerce Department and a federal court order, and developers would publish safety frameworks and transparency reports for new models. Anthropic says the bill reflects its Advanced AI Framework, promoted to lawmakers since June, the month CEO Dario Amodei called for binding rules on frontier models, meaning the most powerful AI systems.

Anthropic critics include investor and former White House AI czar David Sacks, who responded to the company’s pledge with his own post on X: “You’ve put 20% of your equity in an LCC. Whether it serves the public good remains to be seen.”

Anthropic says it will release the fund's governance structure and valuation thresholds in the coming months, and its IPO could come as early as November.

A proposed SEC custody framework could make it easier for investment advisors to hold XRP directly for clients, wealth commentator Kamilah Stevenson says in her latest YouTube episode.

Her key argument: custody restrictions, not simply skepticism about crypto, have kept some advisory firms from offering digital assets.

Stevenson describes an October 1 proposal that would clarify custody arrangements for advisors and regulated funds. The transcript does not specify the year, and the changes she discusses remain a proposal rather than a final rule.

According to Dr. Stevenson, the framework would clarify that state trust companies can serve as crypto custodians, permit limited advisor self-custody when no qualified custodian can hold an asset, and allow regulated funds to use brokerage firms for crypto custody. It would also update audit requirements.

That could matter for firms whose compliance teams have resisted direct crypto holdings. Stevenson says SEC-registered advisors manage more than $100 trillion, though that figure describes their overall business—not money expected to enter XRP or other digital assets.

“An ETF gives a client the price of XRP and holding the asset gives a client the asset,” she says. The distinction matters for separately managed accounts and strategies requiring direct ownership, although custody permission alone would not establish that those strategies are suitable for a client.

Dr. Kamilah Stevenson also cites a 60-day public comment period. Final requirements could differ, and firms would still need their own operational reviews and investment approvals.

The YouTube video connects the proposed changes to Ripple’s custody software business, arguing that providers already serving financial institutions could benefit from clearer rules. That is a potential business opportunity, not evidence of automatic demand for XRP.

Dr. Stevenson also points to Ripple’s litigation history.

Her description of the July 2023 ruling is broad: the court distinguished between categories of XRP sales, rather than granting every XRP transaction an unconditional exemption from securities law.

A clearer custody route could expand access, but neither adoption nor fresh buying would follow on a fixed timetable.

#23. U.S. CFTC rebuffs CME legal stance in consequential fight over perpetual futures

The U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission threw open the doors for perpetual futures in the U.S. in May, approving the first bitcoin perp from Kalshi and suggesting that it was open for business on ensuring a domestic surge in such contracts. But the CME Group objected in court, and the CFTC has responded in court that the derivatives giant has no right to get in the way.

"Allegations of increased competition, without any plausible inference of an imminent financial injury," don't give CME the legal standing to challenge the CFTC's actions, the agency said in a brief filed on Friday, noting that volume in crypto futures at the CME has actually risen since its policy shift.

Perp contracts had soared overseas, becoming a major form of transaction in crypto derivatives, and the CFTC's move sought to clarify how the market could get rolling in the U.S. The agency — in response to President Donald Trump's aggressive crypto agenda that included bringing perps into domestic trading — said it'll regulate the products on a case-by-case basis as futures.

Perps allow traders to speculate on the future price of an asset with a typically leveraged position, and the contracts don't come with a built-in expiration.

But CME, which operates the leading global venues for derivatives trading, has insisted the contracts are not futures, because they have no end date. They're really swaps, the company's argument would have it, which would come with an entirely different regulatory approach. Spokespeople for CME didn't immediately respond to a request for comment on the CFTC's latest filing.

The CFTC first asked a federal judge to dismiss CME's case last month, and this latest filing details its argument against the company's legal standing.

"CME must plausibly allege an actual or imminent increase in competition," the CFTC argued. "CME has not even done that."

The agency argued that CME has been telling investors that it hasn't heard of a demand for perps and that they aren't substitutes for the futures it's offering.

"CME cannot have it one way with the court and another way with the investing public on earnings calls," the CFTC contended in its brief.

Jaret Seiberg, a policy analyst at TD Cowen, argued in a Monday client note that CME may still have the edge, in both its standing as a competitor and its argument that perps may be appropriately treated as swaps. However, the clock is ticking on the new market.

"What increasingly concerns us is the growth in perps while the litigation is playing out," Seiberg wrote. "If this growth continues, it could create complications in trying to unwind this market if the CME prevails in the lawsuit."

#24. Super League Stockholders Approve Metaplanet’s 2,100 BTC Investment, Paving Way for ‘Superplanet’

Japanese bitcoin giant Metaplanet is acquiring around 96% of Nasdaq-listed Super League.

Super League stockholders have approved all proposals tied to Metaplanet‘s 2,100 BTC investment, clearing the way for the Nasdaq-listed company to be renamed Superplanet and become the Japanese firm’s U.S. Bitcoin treasury vehicle.

The proposals passed at Super League Enterprise, Inc.’s 2026 annual meeting of stockholders, held Friday and were disclosed Monday morning. The transaction itself was first announced in August.

Under the definitive agreement, Metaplanet, Inc. will contribute 2,100 Bitcoin and $2.5 million in cash through its wholly owned U.S. subsidiary, Metaplanet Holdings, Inc.

JUST IN: 🇯🇵 Japan's Metaplanet to buy Super League for 2,100 BTC and $2.5 million 👀This will give the 2nd-largest corporate BTC holder a U.S. listed Bitcoin treasury platform! 🚀 pic.twitter.com/0gucAALjAX

In exchange, Metaplanet receives 44,859,400 shares of common stock at $3.00 per share, along with preferred stock and warrants.

At closing, Super League will be renamed “Superplanet, Inc.” and trade on Nasdaq under the ticker symbol “SUPA.” Its advertising and media activation business will continue as a distinct operating segment, and Matt Edelman will remain chief executive officer.

Among the measures stockholders approved were the issuance of common stock and warrants to Metaplanet and the corporate name change. The proposals also included an increase in authorized preferred shares from 10 million to 100 million, according to a summary of the meeting posted on X.

“Super League stockholders have voted to approve the proposed Metaplanet transaction, an important step in our transformation from a Bitcoin treasury company into a global Bitcoin-native financial platform,” Metaplanet CEO Simon Gerovich wrote on X.

“Upon close, Superplanet will be our U.S.-listed Bitcoin treasury platform, providing direct access to U.S. capital markets and greater flexibility to opportunistically raise capital.”

Edelman framed the vote similarly in the company’s announcement: “Their approval brings us one step closer to redefining what this company can become.”

Closing is anticipated in the fourth quarter of 2026, subject to customary closing conditions, including required filings with the Nasdaq Capital Market. The shareholder approvals represent a required step but not the final one.

Super League said the arrangement is intended to establish conditions governing Metaplanet’s ability to dispose of its equity holdings following the transaction. The company did not provide details of exceptions to those restrictions in its announcement.

Metaplanet held 43,000 BTC as of August 18, describing itself as the third-largest corporate Bitcoin treasury among publicly traded companies. The combined structure is intended to give the group two listed Bitcoin treasury platforms — one on the Tokyo Stock Exchange, one on Nasdaq — each with its own investor base and reporting currency.

Super League connects brands with what it describes as a 3.3 billion-person global gaming population through advertising and branded content programs across gaming and digital media platforms. Metaplanet is a Tokyo-listed company building Bitcoin-based financial products and infrastructure.

Shares of Super League moved higher on the news.

#27. Hyperliquid Demands Five Critical Fixes to SEC Crypto Proposal

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. We believe that all content is accurate as of the date of publication, but certain offers mentioned may no longer be available.

The Hyperliquid Policy Center (HPC) has submitted an official comment to the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) on the draft of the new Regulation Crypto Assets. The organization supported the regulator’s general initiative but stated that, in its current form, the document contains systemic legal traps.

For the proposed draft to work, the crypto industry demands five fundamental changes.

In August, the SEC first presented this compromise plan: startups will be allowed to raise up to $75 million a year under a simplified scheme and will also be granted “Safe Harbor” status, which protects matured tokens from prosecution by regulators.

Before that, the agency assessed the crypto market using the 1946 Howey test, created for trading shares in Florida citrus plantations. Because of the legal impasse, American Web3 startups have spent years moving offshore or blocking U.S. users.

Hyperliquid’s lawyers point out that the SEC’s new compromise is still detached from reality. The policy center’s main objections boil down to five key categories:

The regulation must clearly state that a free distribution of tokens for on-chain activity is not an investment contract, since users do not invest money and bear no financial risks. Moreover, completing verification (KYC) or connecting a wallet to receive an airdrop cannot be legally interpreted as “payment” for the asset.

The other three changes concern the long-term survival of projects. Currently, to enter the Safe Harbor, a project must acknowledge that, at the development stage, the token depended on management, which automatically exposes startups to lawsuits for past years.

HPC demands that companies be given the right to declare that their tokens have never been securities. In addition, the proposed rules do not describe the status of decentralized protocols (DEX) at all, although without the right to legally trade tokens on on-chain platforms from day one, the entire regulation loses its economic meaning.

Finally, the regulation currently exempts approved projects from oversight by the authorities of individual states, but this immunity expires upon exit from the Safe Harbor. The industry demands that this protection be made indefinite, to relieve businesses of oversight from more than 50 jurisdictions at once.

By defending the market, Hyperliquid is acting preemptively. The platform is the leader in the on-chain futures sector, but because of strict U.S. laws, it is forced to fully block American residents. At present, there are no official lawsuits or fines against the platform from the SEC or the CFTC.

Nevertheless, the project is under pressure from traditional exchanges (CME) and the U.S. Congress. In September, the House Oversight Committee demanded internal data from Hyperliquid co-founder Jeff Yan as part of an investigation into possible insider trading ahead of tariff announcements.

Shareholders of Nasdaq-listed Super League have approved a transaction that would give Japanese Bitcoin treasury company Metaplanet a 93.7% ownership stake in exchange for 2,100 BTC and $2.5 million in cash.

Under the agreement, Metaplanet will receive nearly 45 million common shares, preferred stock carrying governance rights and warrants to purchase additional shares. The deal would give Metaplanet control of Super League’s board and major corporate decisions.

Super League plans to rebrand as Superplanet and trade under the ticker SUPA, shifting its business toward accumulating Bitcoin. The company intends to fund future purchases primarily through preferred stock offerings rather than conventional debt.

World Liberty Financial’s USD1 stablecoin has shed over $400 million in market capitalization over the past two weeks, driven by large redemptions on Ethereum and BNB Chain.

The decline extends a period of concentrated redemptions on Ethereum and BNB Chain, according to blockchain research firm Onchain Benchmark. The research platform found that nearly $200 million in BNB Chain redemptions originated from a single unidentified address, although it could not establish who controlled the funds or why they were redeemed.

Despite the redemptions, USD1 maintained its dollar peg throughout the period examined by Onchain Benchmark, trading between $0.998 and $1.000.

The researchers found no evidence of a sustained depegging event, indicating that the decline in circulating supply was not accompanied by a significant loss of the token’s dollar value.

Layer-1 blockchain network Qubic halted operations Sunday after an attacker reportedly exploited weakly generated wallet seeds to drain approximately $1.4 million from more than 1,400 accounts, according to the project.

In a statement on X, Qubic said the network was halted at tick 85,371,949, where it remains paused at the time of writing. Qubic said the vulnerability affected wallet seeds generated using any browser on an iPhone or iPad, Safari on a Mac until Oct. 18, 2026, or the Qubic iOS app before July 2025, leading to 2.94 trillion Qubit (QU) stolen.

“87.1% of the drained funds never left the Qubic network and remain frozen in place,” said Qubic. “The remaining 12.9% was sent to MEXC, whose team froze the receiving account within about an hour.”

The Qubic theft is the latest in a series of attacks tied to weak wallet seeds. In July, Coldcard disclosed that attackers had stolen funds from wallets whose seeds were weakened by a firmware bug. Similar flaws affected Trust Wallet’s browser extension and the Libbitcoin Explorer tool in 2023.

#31. XRP Ledger Repairs Its Lending Protocol Before It Goes Live

XRP Ledger Repairs Its Lending Protocol Before It Goes Live

The XRP Ledger is patching its new lending feature before a single loan has been written on it, adding a second code amendment to repair the system while it waits in the network’s approval queue.

The ledger’s lending protocol, a DeFi building block that enables on-chain, fixed-term, uncollateralized loans drawn from pooled funds, was introduced through an amendment called LendingProtocol that is still open for validator voting.

Rather than wait for that version to go live and then fix it, developers have published a follow-up, LendingProtocolV1_1, that corrects issues in the original before it ever takes effect. The documentation now lists both amendments as requirements for the feature, meaning the network would adopt the repaired version from the start.

The approach reflects how changes reach the XRP Ledger. New features and fixes ship as amendments that must earn support from at least 80% of trusted validators over a two-week period before activating.

Because the original lending code hasn’t cleared that bar yet, patching it with a second amendment avoids launching a known-flawed system onto the live network, then scrambling to repair it afterward.

The protocol itself is built for institutional-style credit rather than the collateral-and-liquidation model common in DeFi. It relies on off-chain underwriting to vet borrowers and uses “first-loss capital,” a buffer a loan broker puts up to absorb the initial hit from defaults, in place of automated on-chain collateral. Issuers retain compliance tools, including the ability to freeze accounts or claw back funds.

The caution follows a close call elsewhere in the ledger’s code. Developers recently disclosed and fixed a critical bug in the XRP Ledger’s payment engine that could have let an attacker mint counterfeit XRP, a flaw that sat dormant for roughly a decade before a researcher flagged it. Fixing the lending code pre-launch fits a more cautious posture around new functionality.

The lending feature is part of a broader buildout of credit and DeFi capabilities on the XRP Ledger, which has been adding the financial-market plumbing Ripple and others have long said it lacked.

#34. Zerohash rolls out a new tool to move crypto without copying wallet addresses

Zerohash launched AUTH, a service that lets users move crypto between linked accounts without copying wallet addresses or choosing a blockchain network, simplifying digital asset transactions.

The crypto services firm announced the tool, which lets users link exchange accounts or self-custody wallets at the Money20/20 conference in Las Vegas.

“Onchain rails scale when users stop thinking about the underlying technology. Usability, trust and control is the inflection point for mass adoption,” said Ryan Beaudry, general manager of AUTH. Beaudry, who was previously executive vice president of global product and operations for open finance at Mastercard, will be the general manager of AUTH, according to a statement.

AUTH supports crypto, stablecoins and blockchain-based securities like stock tokens. Zerohash said the service supports more than 600 connections, including Coinbase, Robinhood, Gemini, MetaMask and Phantom. Zerohash’s developer documentation listed support for 639 wallets and four exchange or brokerage accounts. Coinbase, Robinhood and Gemini are live, while Kraken is in beta.

The launch comes as Zerohash seeks to expand its regulatory standing. In July, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency returned the firm’s application for a national trust bank charter, a step the agency takes when it considers a filing materially deficient. The firm called the return an administrative process and refiled a narrower application on Aug. 18. The application is still pending.

The goal of this new product is to reduce the steps required to move funds, the firm said.

To make a transaction, users pick an account or wallet inside an app that offers AUTH, sign in and approve the move. The service handles routing and settlement, while each app sets which assets, accounts and transfer types it allows.

Alex LaPrade, CEO of a popular non-custodial Ethereum and multi-chain crypto wallet, said that transfers to wallets have previously involved repeated address checks and test payments, which were “one of the biggest points of friction” that AUTH is aiming to simplify.

Zerohash, founded in 2017, has a global regulatory footprint across the EU, Latin America, Bermuda, and the U.S., and operates regulated entities in 51 U.S. jurisdictions, according to its website. The Chicago-based company was in acquisition talks with Mastercard, which fell through earlier this year. At the time, Zerohash was reportedly in talks to raise $250 million at a $1.5 billion valuation.

Companies connect to zerohash through APIs and developer tools, and the firm handles custody, compliance, liquidity, settlement, and blockchain connectivity. The firm already provides crypto infrastructure for firms, including Morgan Stanley’s E*Trade.

#37. Market participants weigh in on SEC’s proposed crypto regulations

The financial agency is scheduled to close public comments on its ‘Regulation Crypto Assets’ proposed in August.

The US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) is set to move forward with digital asset policies after Congress failed to pass legislation that would have established a framework for regulating cryptocurrency at the agency and across other parts of government.

On Tuesday, the SEC will close to public comments on its ‘Regulation Crypto Assets,’ a set of rules proposed in August intended to create what the agency called a “clear and fit-for-purpose framework for certain investment contracts involving crypto assets.” Over the 60-day period, the agency gathered about 140 comments from interest groups and individuals on rules and regulations related to a proposed safe harbor that would prevent token issuers from being considered “investment contracts,” as well as exemptions for companies permitting offerings up to a certain amount.

The Markets in Crypto Assets (MiCA) Crypto Alliance, a group established to help organizations looking to implement the EU framework on digital assets, largely supported the SEC’s proposed changes to disclosure requirements. The alliance recommended specific amendments to have the SEC better define “concepts and data structures specific to crypto assets and the disclosure requirements.”

Others, including SkyBridge Capital founder Anthony Scaramucci, said they would support the SEC’s proposed crypto rules. Scaramucci said the digital asset regulations responded to “organic adoption” and “represent a return to the Commission’s proper role” without citing inaction from Congress on the Digital Asset Market Clarity (CLARITY) Act. Six people submitted comments anonymously.

While many public comments praised the SEC’s efforts to advance crypto regulation or said they would be open to further discussion, some legal experts suggest the rules could be more easily overturned than an act of Congress. Both financial agencies overseeing aspects of the crypto industry, the SEC and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, are also still understaffed at the leadership level.

#40. Long-Awaited XRP Twitter Account Finally Goes Live

The XRP cryptocurrency has finally made its official debut on X (formerly Twitter) under the coveted @XRP handle, drawing enthusiastic reactions from Ripple executives and the broader XRP community.

The account announced its arrival with a brief message: "hello, world. It’s about time."

#41. Hackers Are Running Apple's iOS on Android Phones for the First Time

Hackers Are Running Apple's iOS on Android Phones for the First Time

Hobbyists are booting Apple’s iOS, the software that runs iPhones, on Android phones just to prove that they can, and video demonstrations are going viral on social media.

One clip of iOS 16 on a Redmi Note 12 has passed 2 million views on X, and another developer posted a build running on a Nothing 3a.

iOS, the operating system that runs everything on an iPhone from the touchscreen to the apps, is built to run only on Apple’s own hardware. Choosing a phone has meant choosing its software, and the reverse. If that wall cracks, cheap and old phones could one day run software they were never sold with.

Android has run on iPhones before: a project called iDroid let early iPhones boot it in April 2010. A decade later, security firm Corellium launched Project Sandcastle, which put Android 10 on iPhones with Apple’s A10 chip.

Nobody has been able to make it the other way around—until now.

WTf, Running real iOS on Android hardware.

HackiOS is attempting a full code rewrite to run actual iOS on Android hardware.

They’re in the final polishing stage. If it works, the project will be completely free and open no paywalls, no premium tiers. pic.twitter.com/oQywSdi9Y5

— Md Ismail Šojal 🕷️ (@0x0SojalSec) October 16, 2026

Users are achieving good results with a combination of tools. The closest public code is an open-source project on GitHub, the site where developers share code, called ios-sweet, built for the Redmi Note 10 Pro.

It takes XNU, the kernel Apple publishes openly (the core of an operating system, which talks to the chip, memory and storage), and patches it to run on that phone’s Qualcomm Snapdragon 732G chip. Unmodified iOS 16.7.16 files from an iPhone X then sit on top.

The “readme” file from its developers calls the project an “experimental bring-up, not a usable phone OS,” and says the Redmi Note 10 Pro reaches the lock screen, home screen, Control Center and Settings, with touch and the buttons responding. Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, mobile data, audio and the camera do not work, the gesture to leave an app does nothing, and with no graphics driver the processor draws the screen at roughly 20 to 30 frames per second.

A separate group calling itself OOSexGang says its HackiOS project runs iOS 16.5 on a Poco X5 Pro, using a custom UEFI (the firmware that starts a device) and the XNU kernel. The researcher sharing the demo notes there is no public source code or independent verification. In a newer clip, Safari downloads an Android app file from APKMirror and then fails to open it, which, to be fair, is what iOS has always done with Android apps.

iOS 16.5 just Running on an Android phone hardware.

and it can’t open Apk because of iOS,Safari pulls an APK from APKMirror, then fails to run it.

New HackiOs/OOSexGang demo it can be soon public release https://t.co/Iv3FDwuXyK pic.twitter.com/TGclBWllxp

— Md Ismail Šojal 🕷️ (@0x0SojalSec) October 19, 2026

The idea of running things where they shouldn’t has been gaining enthusiasts with the advent of AI and the ability to ship code—and improve it—extremely fast. Just days ago. the security firm Calif.io jailbroke an iPhone 18 Pro on stage at the Hexacon conference in Paris, and the root access survived a reboot. Jailbreaking removes Apple’s restrictions to give a user deep control of the phone.

Another major tool that sparked the movement is REA, short for Reverse Engineer Anything, a free toolkit that lets AI coding assistants pick software apart, with examples that included a developer’s demo of GTA V running on iOS.

For now, the practical ceiling of a Redmi Note 10 Pro running iOS is looking at the iOS home screen. Wi-Fi, mobile data, and audio don't work, the screen is drawn by the processor at roughly 20 to 30 frames per second, and the first boot takes four to five minutes on the Apple logo.

Anyone tempted to try it should know the install wipes the phone's Android user data, leaves security protections mostly switched off, and that the devs themselves say not to keep anything personal on the device.
