#154. Binance Founder CZ Takes Swipe at Peter Schiff

Changpeng Zhao (CZ) of Binance recently took a sarcastic jab at well-known gold bull Peter Schiff for his notorious track record of Bitcoin (BTC) bear market predictions.

"He will be right one day... after he changes his mind :)" Zhao wrote on X.

Zhao responded to a post from Bitcoin historian Pete Rizzo that compiled Schiff's numerous pessimistic predictions over the years.

The exchange brought Schiff's long-running skepticism of the world's number one cryptocurrency back into the spotlight. The skepticism can be traced back at least as far as 2011.

Schiff has been very vocal in his criticism of Bitcoin dating back to 2011, when he dismissed the cryptocurrency as a fad.

In November 2013, when Bitcoin was trading around $350, Schiff drew a parallel between the cryptocurrency's meteoric growth and the notorious Dutch tulip mania.

He said during an interview with CNBC that he believed the speculative run of Bitcoin would eventually collapse. Bitcoin experienced a massive correction at that point, but later recovered and set new all-time highs.

In December 2017, when Bitcoin was nearing $20K for the first time, Schiff reiterated his negative view of the cryptocurrency and called it the biggest speculative bubble he had ever seen.

Schiff also declared Bitcoin's demise during the March 2020 market crash.

Schiff admitted in 2021 that his previous prediction that BTC would never reach $50K was wrong. BTC soared above $50K at the time.

However, he remained steadfast in his belief that Bitcoin would end up worthless.

"While possible for there to be a temporary rise to $100K, it's inevitable there will be a permanent fall to zero," Schiff wrote back in February 2021.

Bitcoin ultimately climbed above $100K in December 2024. This proved multiple of Schiff's past price predictions wrong.

But the bearish forecasts from the economist did not stop there.

In April 2025, he predicted that the next financial crisis would be the end of Bitcoin.

"Bitcoin was created as a result of the financial crisis in 2008. But the irony of it is that the financial crisis in 2025 will be the death of Bitcoin," Schiff wrote.

Interestingly, Schiff seemingly changed his mind on one of his most controversial predictions earlier this year.

Schiff, in a debate with Bitcoin bull Anthony Pompliano in June 2026, admitted that the chances of Bitcoin falling to zero were probably slim.

"It's not going to go to zero. Maybe," he said when prompted to bet on Bitcoin's survival.

However, he later explained that he still believed Bitcoin would see a 99%+ drop in market capitalization, but that even if Bitcoin survives to trade at a positive value, most people would lose most of their investment as a result of such a crash.

The European Banking Authority has designated USDC as the EU’s first significant e-money token under MiCA, setting up an additional layer of supervision for Circle’s euro-area issuing entity.

TL;DR: The classification was announced on October 14. From November 12, the EBA takes direct responsibility for specified prudential areas of USDC supervision, while French regulators retain other oversight functions.

Circle Internet Financial Europe SAS issues the token within the bloc. The EBA said 45 e-money tokens had been notified under MiCA and that USDC was the first to cross the threshold for significant classification. It is a milestone in the operation of Europe’s crypto rulebook rather than a new stablecoin launch.

The supervisory division is more nuanced than one agency taking over everything. The EBA will assume responsibilities covering own funds, reserves, liquidity and recovery or redemption planning. France’s ACPR will continue overseeing matters including governance, outsourcing and the suitability of key personnel.

That matters because stablecoin risk is not confined to whether a dollar token tracks its peg on a quiet trading day. Redemption pressure, the liquidity of backing assets and operational failures can become important when demand for withdrawals surges. Significant-token designation puts extra scrutiny on those areas.

For European banks and payment companies evaluating USDC, a clearer line of supervision may help with due diligence. It does not remove market, custody or operational risk, and it should not be taken as a guarantee of redemption under every conceivable scenario. MiCA is meant to establish a framework for managing such risks, not make them disappear.

#156. XRP Ledger is set to fix its lending code before anyone can use it

A batch of bug fixes is set to go live on the XRP Ledger on Friday, and some of them patch the lending system Ripple has pitched to banks and payment companies since June — a system that hasn’t been switched on yet and is still 10 votes short of approval.

Validators are the independent servers that agree on which transactions count. A change to the network’s rules needs backing from more than 80% of the 35 validators the network trusts by default, which works out to 29, and that backing has to hold for two straight weeks.

Under the plan, a lender deposits XRP or another token into a vault, and a loan broker lends that money out for a fixed term. The ledger records the loan and tracks repayments, and the broker decides offchain whether a borrowe

Borrowers don’t post collateral, so the broker’s judgment is all that stands between lenders and a default. Ripple has pitched the setup to payment companies that need cash while a cross-border settlement clears.

The bug-fix package, called fixCleanup3_4_0, had exactly 29 votes as of Monday, according to the XRPL Dashboard. It’s nine days into its two-week countdown and on course to go live around 09:34 UTC on Oct. 23. It has no votes to spare, so one validator pulling support would restart the clock.

The lending system has 19 votes. The vaults that would hold lenders’ money are a separate change and have 21. Neither has started a countdown, so even if both hit 29 votes today, lending couldn’t go live before early November.

Separately, the patch also closes a loophole that could let an account allowed only to burn, or destroy, tokens on an issuer’s behalf create new ones under certain conditions, according to the xrpld 3.4.0 release notes.

It will further changes how vaults round amounts and how the lending code decides when a loan is late or in default.

#157. Stocks rebound into key tech earnings: Three things to know in Bitcoin this week

Analysts expect Bitcoin to retest $80,000 support again as stock markets attempt to recover last week’s losses.

Bitcoin (BTC) starts the third week of October at $82,000 as crypto and stock markets begin a tentative rebound.

A lighter week of US macro data prints will shift the market’s attention to corporate earnings as stocks rebound from last week’s sell-off. Some 15% of S&P 500 companies are due to report third-quarter earnings figures this week, including SpaceX on Tuesday and Tesla and Meta on Wednesday.

Tech-stock performance remains in focus after a major drawdown last week that began with South Korean markets. The KOSPI Composite Index lost 2.8% on Oct. 12 before dropping to the week’s low of 5,455 on Thursday, bringing the week-to-date losses temporarily to 17%.

KOSPI Composite Index one-day chart. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView

Contagion spread to neighboring Asian markets before US equities began to weaken later in the week. The S&P 500 index finished Friday down 2% for the week.

As in early August, tech stocks saw considerable sell-side pressure amid concerns over AI expenditure plans and the associated debt obligations. In Korea, the threat of competition in semiconductor manufacturing from China exacerbated the downturn.

Warnings of a “Black Monday” event on global stock markets spread through social media over the weekend. The panic, which coincided with the 39th anniversary of the 1987 Black Monday crash, appeared misplaced, with KOSPI gaining 1.8% on Monday and S&P 500 futures 0.7% higher at the time of writing.

S&P 500 futures one-day chart. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView

Commenting on the disconnect between public sentiment and market performance, market commentator The Kobeissi Letter suggested that stocks should outperform based on investor demand. Persistent high US inflation and a global energy crisis have positioned equities for a surge on any potential signs of conditions improving.

“All while the AI Revolution continues to accelerate and many large-cap technology stocks become cheaper on a forward earnings basis, even as their stock prices rise. And in the background, the demand for asset ownership is historically robust,” it summarized in analysis last week.

Kobeissi noted that while tech giants led S&P 500 strength, 80% of index stocks are trading at least 10% below all-time highs.

Ahead of the Federal Reserve’s next decision on interest-rate changes on Oct. 28, markets have tempered their expectations on policy tightening.

Data from CME Group’s FedWatch Tool shows 85% odds of rates staying within their current 3.75-4.00% range in October. The Fed’s December meeting, meanwhile, carries just 11% odds of a further pause. Instead, markets see a 75% chance of a 25-basis-point hike, with a 50-basis-point move attracting 13% odds.

Fed target-rate probabilities (screenshot). Source: CME Group

In a discussion with International Monetary Fund Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva last week, Fed chair Kevin Warsh avoided any hints of forward guidance on policy, reinforcing a pledge made at the Jackson Hole economic symposium in August.

“I don’t prejudge meetings. I don’t believe in saying now what I might do at the meetings that we have in the balance of this year,” he said.

Markets, however, interpreted the lack of information as a dovish signal, doubling down on the Fed hiking rates just once more before 2027.

Adopting a cautionary tone, meanwhile, market commentator Mosaic Asset Company saw inflation trends forcing the Fed to avoid easing off, keeping a crypto and risk-asset headwind in place.

“While investors expect the Federal Reserve to hold rates steady at its next meeting later this month, a growing inflation problem will keep favoring tighter monetary policy,” it wrote in analysis on Sunday.

The September print of the US Producer Price Index (PPI) released last week showed the ongoing impact of the Middle East crisis on fuel prices. PPI delivered its largest month-on-month increase since March 2022 at 1.7%.

“Half of the September increase in the index for final demand goods can be traced to prices for gasoline, which jumped 20.3%,” the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported.

Fuel also accounted for more than half of the September increase in the Consumer Price Index (CPI), which beat expectations by 0.1% to hit 3.7% year-on-year.

#158. UK Trio Jailed Over Home Invasion in Failed Crypto Theft Attempt

UK Trio Jailed Over Home Invasion in Failed Crypto Theft Attempt

Three men who forced their way into a man's home in Bristol, England, and assaulted him in a failed attempt to steal cryptocurrency have been jailed, Avon and Somerset Police said on Friday.

Terroll Paul, 31, Mohamed Samagassi, 37, and Pierre Madzou, 30, broke into the victim's home in the early hours of May 15, assaulted him and demanded he hand over a large amount of digital currency. He was hit over the head, suffering a substantial injury that required hospital treatment.

Three men who broke into a man's home in Bristol and threatened him in a failed attempt to steal cryptocurrency have been jailed.

Terroll Paul, 31, Mohamed Samagassi, 37, and Pierre Madzou, 30, were sentenced yesterday (15 October).https://t.co/gQf1FuZiY6

— Avon and Somerset Police (@ASPolice) October 16, 2026

The victim's teenage sister alerted police, and all three men were arrested at the scene.

They pleaded guilty to aggravated burglary in August, and were sentenced at Bristol Crown Court on Thursday. Paul, of Barking in London, received six years in prison, Madzou, also of Barking, five and a half years, and Samagassi, of no fixed address, five years.

The victim's sister showed "extreme bravery," said PC Gemma Childs, the investigating officer, adding that her actions led directly to "the apprehension of the offenders and preventing her brother from further harm."

In a statement read in court, the victim said the break-in had changed him. "Before, I was bubbly, talkative and outgoing but now I would describe myself as tense and apprehensive," he said.

The police did not say how much cryptocurrency the men demanded.

The case is the latest in a run of so-called "wrench attacks" in the UK, in which criminals target crypto holders in person. In February, three teenagers were jailed over a $4.3 million wrench attack robbery caught on police video in London, while last month a $10,000 reward was offered after a West Midlands couple was attacked in a crypto home invasion.

Wrench attacks cost victims $124 million globally in the first six months of 2026, a twelvefold increase year-on-year, according to blockchain security firm CertiK.

#160. Satoshi-Era Bitcoin Holders Move $33.85M in BTC After 12 Years, Record 638x Gains

Two Bitcoin (BTC) wallets that had remained dormant for more than 12 years have become active, transferring a combined 417 BTC worth approximately $33.85 million.

According to a Sunday tweet from blockchain analytics platform Lookonchain, the wallets returned 638 and 229 times their original value, respectively, after accumulating Bitcoin when the cryptocurrency traded at about $127 and $355.

Notably, while the transfers highlight the substantial gains made by early Bitcoin investors, it remains unclear whether the owners intend to sell their holdings or have simply moved the funds to new addresses.

The reactivation adds to a series of movements involving older Bitcoin wallets. Another wallet that had remained untouched for more than a decade transferred 411.45 BTC a day earlier, worth approximately $34 million at the time. Blockchain data attributed to Arkham Intelligence shows the coins were largely accumulated in September 2013, when Bitcoin traded near $131.

Beyond these early-holder movements, data from CryptoQuant points to declining selling pressure from more recent Bitcoin investors.

According to analyst IT Tech, only 4.4% of Bitcoin aged 6 to 12 months that moved over the 30-day period ending October 15 went to exchanges.

This represents about 9,100 BTC of the 205,400 BTC moved during the period. By comparison, 40.4% of the coins moved during the 30-day window ending June 17, equivalent to 63,800 BTC, went to exchanges.

The proportion then fell to 30.9% in July, 9.8% in August, and 3.7% in September before slightly recovering in October.

Despite the substantial number of Bitcoin changing addresses, the data suggests that fewer of these coins are reaching exchanges, where holders could sell them.

IT Tech highlighted the difference between the volume of coins moving and their destinations, noting that 205,400 BTC moved during the latest 30-day period, compared with 157,700 BTC in the June window.

The analyst’s data points to reduced selling pressure from this group of holders, which could be pivotal to BTC price.

Meanwhile, CryptoQuant analyst Darkfost noted that Bitcoin fell below the 30th percentile of its Market Value to Realized Value (MVRV) metric after being rejected near $87,000.

He explained that the measure places Bitcoin’s valuation within its historical context rather than relying solely on the raw MVRV ratio.

“By falling back below the 30th percentile, Bitcoin is returning to a zone where it has spent only about 25% of its time at this valuation level,” the analyst stated.

Darkfost added that the level remained consistent with an accumulation zone, although Bitcoin had moved out of the extreme undervaluation range historically associated with market lows.

The analyst’s assessment suggests Bitcoin has returned to a historically less common valuation range, even as the market continues to seek stronger demand.

At press time, Bitcoin was trading at $82,146, up 1.02% in the past 24 hours.

The difference lies both in the size of the miss and in what each measure is telling you. Yesterday’s CPI came in 0.1 percentage points above forecast on the headline and core readings, close enough that economists would call it broadly in line. Coinbase will handle custody and currency conversion, while Marqeta manages card issuing and payment processing.

Payments technology company Marqeta is expanding a six-year partnership with Coinbase to let businesses offer payment cards funded by customers' stablecoin holdings.

A Friday release says Coinbase will hold the stablecoins and handle the conversions between digital and traditional currencies. That leaves Marqeta to handle issuing the cards and processing payments.

Coinbase's Base blockchain will provide the onchain settlement infrastructure.

The service is aimed at Marqeta's business customers, which include both crypto and traditional companies. Cardholders will be able to spend their stablecoins with the "millions of merchants" that accept cards, while businesses can fund their card programs 24/7, the companies said.

Coinbase and Marqeta have already worked together on Coinbase's own card. The crypto exchange named Marqeta as the processor powering its U.S. debit card offering in October 2020. That card allowed customers to spend crypto, including USDC, and earn crypto rewards.

The release did not specify fees, a rollout date, or what stablecoins would initially be supported.

#165. Stablecoin Payments Reach $482 Billion As Token Supply Barely Grows

Strict editorial policy that focuses on accuracy, relevance, and impartiality

Morbi pretium leo et nisl aliquam mollis. Quisque arcu lorem, ultricies quis pellentesque nec, ullamcorper eu odio.

A new payments dataset offers a useful correction to the idea that stablecoin growth must be measured by how many tokens are in circulation. The stock of digital dollars has barely moved this year, but the amount being used for payments has climbed sharply.

TL;DR: Allium estimates $482 billion in identifiable stablecoin payments through September 2026, up 45% from the comparable period. Stablecoin supply grew only 0.4% to roughly $305 billion.

The analytics firm’s October 15 research counted about 1.04 billion payment transactions across the first nine months, a 71% rise. That means the increase is not simply a handful of larger transfers distorting the total. More transactions are taking place, and the average payment has become smaller.

The figures are filtered to reflect payment activity rather than every on-chain movement. That matters when raw stablecoin transfer totals can be dominated by exchange arbitrage, transfers between a company’s own wallets or automated trading. The $482 billion estimate is not intended to represent all stablecoin transactions.

Payment companies have been connecting familiar card and banking systems to blockchain rails, reducing the need for businesses or customers to interact with crypto-specific tools. Allium’s report suggests this infrastructure is beginning to change usage patterns, even with supply essentially flat.

There are limits to what the numbers prove. Volume is not profit, nor does an active token necessarily reflect durable consumer adoption. But a market where existing coins turn over more often is different from one dependent on continuous new issuance. For payment providers, that distinction is becoming increasingly important.

#166. JPMorgan takes JPM Coin to Ethereum for institutional clients: Report

JPMorgan is reportedly expanding its JPM Coin deposit token to Ethereum, allowing institutional clients to make payments and settle tokenized asset transactions.

JPMorgan Chase, the world’s biggest bank by market capitalization, is expanding its JPM Coin deposit token to Ethereum, Bloomberg reported on Monday.

JPM Coin represents US dollar deposits held at JPMorgan and lets eligible clients transfer funds within seconds, around the clock.

Emma Landriault, global head of Kinexys Labs, said crypto companies could use the token for blockchain payments, while financial institutions could use it to settle trades and post collateral.

The expansion follows JPMorgan’s November 2025 rollout of JPM Coin on Base, an Ethereum layer-2 network built by cryptocurrency exchange Coinbase. At the time, JPMorgan said it planned to support additional public blockchains. In January, JPMorgan announced plans to bring JPM Coin to the Canton Network.

#169. Zcash Developer Zakura Proposes Fix to Stop Quantum Computers Linking Shielded Swaps

Zcash Developer Zakura Proposes Fix to Stop Quantum Computers Linking Shielded Swaps

Zakura, a developer of Zcash full node software, has proposed a way to stop a future quantum computer from linking users' private Zcash payments, in an engineering post by Zakura developer Adam Tucker announced on Sunday.

The approach needs no network upgrade, Zakura said in a tweet introducing what it called "post-quantum unlinkable swaps for Zcash."

Post-quantum unlinkable swaps for Zcash, no network upgrades required.https://t.co/hzBkdo1AHJ

Zcash's shielded transactions hide the sender, recipient and amount. Each shielded account has a single incoming viewing key behind all of its addresses, which its wallet uses to find and decrypt payments sent to any of them.

A classical computer cannot recover that key from an address. But a sufficiently powerful quantum computer running Shor's algorithm could, according to the post, and would then be able to see the value and memo of every payment the account has received and tie them together.

"Until Tachyon ships, there is a glaring hole: a single published shielded address lets a quantum attacker link every payment that address's key has ever received," Tucker wrote, referring to the proposed scalability upgrade for Zcash that its developers say would also deliver full post-quantum privacy.

The biggest risk comes from swaps through NEAR Intents, a cross-chain swap service, according to the post. Each swap out of ZEC writes one of the user's shielded addresses to NEAR's public chain as a refund address, whether or not a refund is ever made. The addresses look different, but they all belong to the same account, so breaking one would expose all of them.

Around $600 million to $700 million had flowed through Zcash's NEAR Intents route by May, Zcash Open Development Lab CEO Josh Swihart said at the time.

Zakura's fix derives a separate incoming viewing key for each address that has to be published, while leaving the account's spending key untouched. A quantum attacker who breaks one posted address would learn only about the payments to that address.

"If a quantum computer ever breaks a posted swap address, it will not be able to link this to any other transaction," Tucker wrote in a Twitter thread.

To stop the extra keys slowing down restores from a seed phrase, the wallet looks up NEAR's payouts using private information retrieval, a technique that lets it query a server without revealing which addresses it is asking about.

The proposal follows Zakura's plan for quantum-safe transparent addresses earlier this month, which also uses private information retrieval and said post-quantum signature opcodes were expected in Zcash in January. Swihart said in May that Zcash was aiming for full post-quantum status within 12 to 18 months.

Concern over the cryptography that secures crypto wallets is growing, with Ethereum Foundation researcher Justin Drake and Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin warning that AI could break it before quantum computers do.

Wallets using Zakura's open-source libraries, such as Vizor, will be able to integrate the one-time keys for software wallets in the coming weeks, and hardware wallets will follow once their firmware supports it, the post said.

ZEC was trading at $1,165 Monday morning, up 3.6% on the day per Decrypt data.

#175. Fidelity Pays $500,000 In California Crypto Withdrawal Settlement

Strict editorial policy that focuses on accuracy, relevance, and impartiality

Morbi pretium leo et nisl aliquam mollis. Quisque arcu lorem, ultricies quis pellentesque nec, ullamcorper eu odio.

California has secured a $500,000 settlement with Fidelity Digital Asset Services over restrictions that previously prevented some crypto customers from moving purchased coins to their own wallets.

TL;DR: Attorney General Rob Bonta announced the settlement on October 16. California challenged historical withdrawal restrictions; Fidelity disputes that its conduct breached state law, and transfers were enabled after a 2025 regulatory approval.

The issue is a straightforward one for anyone accustomed to self-custody: buying crypto through an app is not necessarily the same as being able to withdraw it. California’s commodity rules require certain transactions to involve physical delivery within a defined period. The state’s position is that delivery of cryptocurrency requires the buyer to be able to transfer the asset away from the dealer.

Fidelity told investigators that it had been waiting for permission from the New York Department of Financial Services before allowing external withdrawals. That permission arrived in April 2025, at which point the company enabled the functionality. The state says the earlier restrictions were unlawful; Fidelity disputes that conclusion.

The California Department of Justice linked its investigation to an earlier case concerning Robinhood Crypto. The announcement is therefore part of a wider regulatory argument over what rights buyers should receive when crypto is sold through a conventional financial services interface.

The dollar amount is relatively small for a company of Fidelity’s size. The principle is larger. Regulators are examining whether customers who pay for cryptocurrencies receive meaningful control over their holdings or only an internal account balance. Investors should still check withdrawal availability and the terms of their specific account rather than assume every Fidelity product works identically.

#176. Bitcoin, Ether ETFs shed $549M as October ETH outflows near $1B

US spot Ether ETFs recorded around $955 million in October net outflows so far, while Bitcoin funds extended their weekly withdrawal streak to two weeks.

US spot Bitcoin and Ether exchange-traded funds (ETFs) saw $549 million in net outflows last week as investors continued pulling money from two of the largest crypto funds.

Bitcoin ETFs recorded around $229 million in weekly net outflows, while Ether funds posted even higher withdrawals at $320 million, according to SoSoValue data.

The latest withdrawals marked a second consecutive week of losses for Bitcoin ETFs and a third for Ether funds. Outflows slowed from the previous week, when the two recorded $1.22 billion in net outflows.

Spot Ether ETFs have recorded roughly $955 million in net outflows so far in October, more than in any other month this year.

Monthly flows in spot Ether ETFs. Source: SoSoValue

Ether (ETH) fell 5% over the past seven days to around $2,433, while Bitcoin dipped 1.3% to $82,783 at the time of publication, according to CoinGecko data.

Despite the withdrawals, both Bitcoin and Ether ETFs remain in positive territory for 2026, with Bitcoin ETFs attracting roughly $259 million in net inflows year-to-date and Ether ETFs drawing about $610 million.

Solana (SOL) ETFs recorded around $26 million in net withdrawals during the week, followed by Zcash (ZEC) at $19 million and Hyperliquid (HYPE) at $18 million, according to SoSoValue data. XRP and BNB funds saw smaller outflows of $1.8 million and $285,000, respectively.

#178. Deutsche Bank targets Asia crypto custody expansion in 2027 as German launch nears

Deutsche Bank (DB) plans to bring its crypto custody service to Asia in 2027, extending its push into digital assets as it prepares to launch the service in Germany within weeks.

The German banking giant, Reuters reported citing the firm’s co-head, also plans to offer stablecoin conversion, tokenized deposits and services that help clients issue digital bonds and other blockchain-based securities.

The move could give institutional clients in Asia access to crypto services through an established global bank, without having to manage their own crypto wallets or private keys. It’s unclear which Asian financial services it will target first.

Deutsche Bank's custody service will allow corporate and institutional clients to hold and transfer cryptocurrencies, with the bank handling the technology needed to keep the assets secure.

The bank said in September that its initial offering would support bitcoin, ether and stablecoins including USDC, EURC and EURAU. The German launch remains subject to regulatory approval.

The bank received authorization from Germany’s financial regulator, BaFin, under the EU’s Markets in Crypto-Assets (MiCA) rules on October 12, according to the European Securities and Markets Authority’s interim register.

Podobnik said the expansion is part of Deutsche Bank’s broader plan to achieve roughly 8% compound annual revenue growth in its corporate bank from 2025 to 2028.

The Asia rollout would extend the custody service beyond Europe as banks seek a larger role in managing digital assets for institutional clients. Deutsche Bank has worked with Bitpanda and Taurus on its custody plans, and joins rivals such as Standard Chartered and BBVA in offering crypto custody.

#179. MapQuest Now Shows Drivers Where Flock Cameras Are Watching

MapQuest Now Shows Drivers Where Flock Cameras Are Watching

MapQuest, the mapping service many Americans last used to print driving directions, now wants to show drivers who’s watching the road.

The company announced on Bluesky that its app includes a “Surveillance Layer,” a toggle in Map Options that plots known automated license plate readers from Flock Safety.

The layer also covers cameras from Motorola Solutions’ Vigilant, Genetec, Axis Communications, Axon, Leonardo’s ELSAG, Neology, Rekor, PlateSmart, Ubicquia, Verkada and other outdoor surveillance systems. “The Roads Have Eyes!” the company wrote.

A demo video showed a dense cluster of eye-shaped icons around Los Angeles’ Marina del Rey neighborhood, each paired with a red cone marking the direction a camera faces. MapQuest didn’t say in its post where the location data comes from.

License plate readers photograph passing vehicles and convert their plates into searchable data. Flock’s AI-powered cameras go further, logging details like make, model, color and even bumper stickers.

These surveillance cameras can be networked so agencies across the country share access, and critics say that allows warrantless tracking of ordinary drivers. Flock is also developing an AI tool that helps police track drivers without the need for license plate data or even a name.

The new Mapquest feature lands amid a growing bipartisan backlash. Earlier this month lawmakers, including Sen. Bernie Sanders, introduced the Ban Flock Act, which seeks to prohibit federal agencies from using the technology. The move followed Sanders’ earlier call in late August to “stop Flock and AI mass surveillance.”

Also in late August, Texas Gov. Greg Abbott ordered state agencies to stop funding Flock cameras after the Texas Tribune found that a state agency had steered at least $30 million toward the network.

In response to the mounting public backlash, Flock CEO Garrett Langley asked Americans to compromise on privacy in exchange for safety. President Donald Trump, breaking his silence on the topic in mid-September, has praised the company’s cameras.

The cameras have also become a cultural target. A Grand Theft Auto mod lets players destroy Flock cameras in-game.

Drivers who switch on MapQuest’s layer can try to plan routes around known cameras. But the map only reflects devices that have been identified, and many destinations may be impossible to reach without passing one. Still, the feature puts a mainstream navigation brand squarely in the middle of the surveillance debate.

#180. Former Mt. Gox CEO Comes to Ledger's Rescue

Former Mt. Gox CEO Mark Karpelès has launched a project to create an inexpensive device for detecting whether spy implants are present in Ledger hardware wallets.

This may provide a much-needed alternative in the face of the current security crisis at the French crypto wallet maker.

Karpelès took to X to share the news. "Is my Ledger safe? Is there a spy implant in it?" Karpelès, the former Mt. Gox boss, suggests that it's possible to check for the presence of malicious hardware components without actually opening up the wallet.

He's working to create a cheap, accessible device for this purpose. What's more, Karpelès says he will make the printed circuit board (PCB) design and technical specifications available for anyone to build the detector themselves.

Karpelès' idea might allow Ledger users to perform a check on their hardware without taking it apart.

Of course, Karpelès hasn't yet shown us a fully functional, independently verified detector.

The idea behind this detector is to spot the presence of unauthorized antenna components within the wallet.

This is done using a low-power radio signal and resonance testing. The idea is that these antennas may have been planted in some wallets.

Hackers discovered them in wallets that had been altered to send out sensitive data to them.

Karpelès' project comes in the wake of a major security breach surrounding tampered Ledger wallets sold by a reseller in Southeast Asia.

It seems attackers managed to buy some genuine hardware wallets. Then, they injected secret electronic components into them. Finally, they managed to get the doctored hardware back out into the wild.

Ledger's security team claims these implants were able to capture the 24-word recovery phrase of users as they initialized their devices.

Then, these implants allegedly transmitted these phrases to the attackers via an LTE connection. This was made possible by an eSIM inside the wallet.

Independent researchers say the total amount of crypto lost is over $90 million.

On Oct. 15, Ledger issued an official statement regarding this issue. They stressed that their security chips, OS, and servers weren't hacked. In fact, they say the entire problem stems from criminals compromising their devices once Ledger no longer had control over them.

Ledger also said they were imposing stricter rules on their approved resellers. Among them, they said they would ban resellers from selling returns. Products would also have to be kept out of sight on public displays until they are bought.

#182. How Ethereum Works

Get The Block’s latest crypto news and price alerts for the coins you follow, right in Chrome. Add our free extension here.

State, Transactions, Gas, Smart Contracts, and Layer 1 Trade-offs

Ethereum is more than a network for sending ETH. It is a programmable Layer 1 blockchain where state, transactions, consensus, gas, smart contracts, token standards, and wallet design all work together to maintain a shared global system.

This guide explains how Ethereum works under the hood and how other Layer 1 networks approach similar design problems.

The focus is how it tracks and updates state, how transactions flow through the network, how computation is priced through gas, how smart contracts and token standards make Ethereum programmable, and how other Layer 1 blockchains approach the same problems in different ways.

Ethereum & Layer 1s 201 assumes readers already understand blockchain basics, wallets, private keys, ETH, and the general idea of smart contracts. It focuses on the mechanics that sit beneath the user experience.

By the end of this course, learners should be able to:

The lesson summaries below are a short overview of the full course content. Take the full interactive Ethereum & Layer 1s 201 course to explore each lesson in more depth through guided explanations, examples, and activities.

Compares Ethereum's account-based global state with Bitcoin's UTXO model and introduces EOAs, Contract Accounts, nonce, balance, code hash, and storage root.

Unpacks the Ethereum transaction envelope and follows chain ID, nonce, gas settings, destination, value, calldata, and signatures through the mempool or a private relay to validator inclusion.

Distinguishes inclusion, justification, and finalization through proof-of-stake slots, epochs, checkpoints, and validator attestations.

Explains how gas bounds computation and how EIP-1559 base fees, priority fees, gas limits, and block demand shape transaction cost and inclusion.

Follows Solidity or Vyper source code through Yul to EVM bytecode and introduces contract creation, variables, functions, events, and error handling.

Covers ERC-20, WETH, ERC-721, and ERC-1155, including approvals, allowances, transfers, events, and metadata that let applications support assets consistently.

Shows how ERC-4337 uses User Operations, bundlers, the Entry Point, aggregators, and paymasters to support smarter wallets, sponsored fees, social recovery, and flexible verification.

Compares Ethereum with other Layer 1 ecosystems through validator design, consensus, throughput, parallel execution, modularity, and interoperability.

A state model is the framework a blockchain uses to represent and update its global ledger. Bitcoin and Ethereum use different models because they optimize for different things.

Bitcoin uses a UTXO model. It tracks individual transaction outputs. There is no native concept of persistent accounts or balances. This design is simple and reliable for transferring value, but it is not built around running applications.

Ethereum uses an account-based state model. It tracks account balances and account data continuously. This design makes it possible to have smart contracts that store data, run logic, and interact with other accounts directly on-chain.

On Ethereum, every participant is an account, but not all accounts behave the same. Externally Owned Accounts, or EOAs, are controlled by private keys and can initiate transactions. Contract Accounts are controlled by deployed smart contract code. They cannot start transactions by themselves, but when triggered by an EOA, they can execute logic, update data, and interact with other accounts or contracts.

Every Ethereum account is defined by four fields: nonce, balance, code hash, and storage root. The nonce records transactions sent from the account and prevents replay. The balance records how much ETH the account owns. The code hash identifies smart contract code for Contract Accounts and is empty for EOAs. The storage root points to persistent contract data and is also empty for EOAs.

Together, these account records form Ethereum’s global state. Transactions are the mechanism that changes that state.

A transaction is the mechanism that updates Ethereum’s global state. It can send ETH, call a contract, deploy a contract, or trigger logic that causes other internal calls.

Ethereum transactions are packaged in a transaction envelope. The envelope carries the data, fee settings, destination, value, calldata, and signature the network needs to process the sender’s intent. EIP-1559 introduced Type-2 transactions, now the common Ethereum format.

A transaction envelope includes identity and replay-protection fields such as chain ID and nonce; economic fields such as gas limit, max fee per gas, and max priority fee per gas; action fields such as destination, value, and calldata; and authorization through the sender’s signature.

Once signed, a transaction can enter the public mempool or travel through a private relay. Validators and block builders evaluate pending transactions, include valid ones in blocks, and execute them against the current state. The result is recorded as a state transition: balances, nonces, contract storage, and gas accounting update together.

This is why state and transactions must be learned together. Ethereum’s state is the living ledger. Transactions are the instructions that modify it.

Ethereum uses proof of stake to coordinate block production and finality. A block can be included, justified, and finalized. These are not the same thing.

An included block has been proposed and added to the chain. A justified block has received enough validator support within Ethereum’s checkpoint system. A finalized block has reached strong consensus and cannot be reverted without a major consensus failure.

Ethereum organizes time into slots and epochs. A slot is the smallest proof-of-stake time unit where one validator may propose a block. An epoch is a group of 32 slots used for validator rotations and checkpoint voting. Validators provide attestations to support blocks and checkpoints, helping the network agree on the canonical chain.

Finality matters because applications, exchanges, bridges, and users need to know when a transaction is not just visible, but economically settled. Finality timelines show how inclusion, justification, and finalization fit together.

Gas is the unit Ethereum uses to measure computational work and bound execution. It prevents transactions and smart contracts from consuming unlimited network resources.

Each transaction has a gas limit: the maximum amount of work the sender is willing to pay for. If execution runs out of gas, the transaction can fail, but the gas used up to that point is still charged because validators still had to perform the work.

EIP-1559 changed Ethereum’s fee market by introducing a base fee and a priority fee. The base fee is determined by the protocol and adjusts with block demand. The priority fee is a user-selected tip that can help incentivize faster inclusion.

This structure means Ethereum fees are not simply “network charges.” They are part of a resource-pricing system. Gas prices reflect demand for blockspace, the amount of computation required, and the urgency of inclusion.

Smart contracts are programs deployed to Ethereum as Contract Accounts. They hold code and state, and they execute when called by a transaction or another contract.

A developer may write smart contract logic in Solidity or Vyper. That source code is compiled through intermediate representations such as Yul into EVM bytecode, the low-level code executed by the Ethereum Virtual Machine.

Smart contracts usually contain variables, functions, events, and error handling. Variables store data. Functions define what the contract can do. Events let applications track important state changes. Errors help contracts fail safely when conditions are not met.

This is the foundation of Ethereum’s programmable economy. Instead of only transferring value, Ethereum lets accounts run logic that can coordinate tokens, exchanges, lending markets, games, identity systems, governance, and other applications.

Token standards let wallets, exchanges, and dapps support many assets without building custom integrations for every project. They define common interfaces that contracts can follow.

ERC-20 is the standard for fungible tokens. These are interchangeable units, such as stablecoins or governance tokens. WETH, or Wrapped Ether, is an ERC-20 representation of ETH used across DeFi integrations.

ERC-721 is the standard for unique non-fungible assets. ERC-1155 is a more flexible standard that lets one contract manage many token types, including fungible and non-fungible assets.

Related topics include approvals, allowances, transferFrom, events, and metadata. These details matter because token standards do more than define assets. They define how applications can recognize, move, approve, and display those assets.

Traditional Ethereum wallets are based on EOAs. EOAs are simple and powerful, but they limit wallet flexibility. A private key controls the account, transactions must be signed in a specific way, and users usually need ETH to pay gas.

Account abstraction changes the wallet model by allowing smarter account logic. ERC-4337 enables account abstraction through User Operations without changing Ethereum consensus.

In this model, a user creates a User Operation. Bundlers collect these operations. The Entry Point contract coordinates validation and execution. Aggregators can support advanced signature schemes. Paymasters can sponsor fees, making gasless or sponsored transactions possible.

The result is a better wallet design space: social recovery, multi-signature verification, sponsored fees, batched actions, and more flexible security rules. Account abstraction does not remove Ethereum’s security assumptions, but it improves how users interact with them.

Ethereum is one Layer 1 design, not the only possible design. Alternative Layer 1 blockchains make different choices around throughput, decentralization, validator design, execution models, modularity, and interoperability.

Some networks prioritize high throughput and fast execution. Others use different validator sets, consensus designs, parallel execution models, or application-specific architectures. Examples include Solana, Avalanche, BNB Smart Chain, Tron, Hyperliquid, Sui, Aptos, and Polygon PoS.

The design space includes mechanisms such as Solana's Proof of History-based timing, Avalanche's subnet architecture, Move-based execution in Sui and Aptos, and sidechain models such as Polygon PoS. These systems should be compared by the assumptions they make, not by throughput alone.

The point is not to rank every Layer 1. The point is to compare trade-offs. Higher throughput may depend on different hardware assumptions. Faster execution may change decentralization requirements. Modular and monolithic designs distribute responsibilities differently.

Ethereum’s design choices emphasize security, decentralization, programmability, and a broad developer ecosystem. Other L1s approach the same core problems in different ways.

A user opens a wallet and signs a transaction. The transaction envelope includes the chain ID, nonce, gas settings, destination, value, calldata, and signature. If the user is calling a contract, the calldata tells the contract which function to run and which arguments to use.

The signed transaction enters the network. It may sit in the public mempool, or it may be sent through a private relay. A validator or builder includes it in a block. Ethereum executes the transaction against the current state. The sender’s nonce increases, gas is charged, balances may change, and contract storage may update.

The block is included first. Later, through attestations and checkpoints, the block can become justified and finalized. At that point, the transaction is not only visible. It is deeply settled in Ethereum’s proof-of-stake consensus.

Related topics include Bitcoin 201, Scaling & Layer 2s 201, DeFi 201, and Market Structure 201. Ethereum mechanics are especially useful before studying rollups, DeFi protocols, token markets, and account-abstraction-based wallet design.

This guide covers Ethereum and other Layer 1 networks beyond the basics. The full course goes deeper with guided visuals, interaction-based practice, transaction and finality walkthroughs, knowledge checks, feedback, completion tracking, and the full Campus learning experience.

Ethereum works by maintaining a shared global state. Transactions modify that state, validators include and finalize blocks, gas prices computation, and smart contracts let accounts run programmable logic on-chain.

Ethereum uses an account-based state model. It tracks persistent accounts with fields such as nonce, balance, code hash, and storage root, rather than tracking only spendable outputs like Bitcoin’s UTXO model.

An Ethereum transaction is a signed instruction that updates the global state. It includes fields such as chain ID, nonce, gas settings, destination, value, calldata, and signature. After propagation and validation, it can be included in a block and finalized.

Ethereum finality is the point at which a block has reached strong proof-of-stake consensus and cannot be reverted without major consensus failure. Finality follows inclusion and justification.

Gas measures computational work. EIP-1559 uses a protocol-determined base fee and a user-selected priority fee. Fees rise or fall based on demand for blockspace and the computation required by a transaction.

ERC-20 is the main standard for fungible tokens. ERC-721 is used for unique non-fungible assets. ERC-1155 lets one contract manage many token types, including fungible and non-fungible tokens.

Account abstraction makes wallet behavior more programmable. ERC-4337 supports User Operations, bundlers, Entry Point, aggregators, and paymasters, enabling features such as sponsored fees, social recovery, and flexible verification.

Ethereum emphasizes security, decentralization, programmability, and a broad developer ecosystem. Other Layer 1s may prioritize different trade-offs, such as throughput, parallel execution, validator design, or modular architecture.

#183. Latvia Changes Crypto Tax Treatment And Opens A 2027 Declaration Window

Latvia has passed a change to the way crypto investment-account gains are taxed, shifting attention from individual trades to what an investor ultimately withdraws from an eligible account. TL;DR: New Latvian legislation taxes qualifying account withdrawals above deposits and provides a one-time 2027 process for declaring older holdings. The country is also considering crypto tax payments, but that payment service is not yet established. The reform passed parliament on October 15. Under the investment-account approach described in reporting on the law, moving between crypto assets inside the account no longer automatically creates the same tax event as withdrawing more value than the amount contributed. Investors will still need records that establish their deposits and withdrawals. There is also an attempt to resolve a practical problem for people who bought digital assets years ago and cannot reconstruct their original cost basis. A declaration mechanism would let eligible holders regularize historical positions at a 10% charge based on their value at the end of 2026. Applications are scheduled for April 1 through May 31, 2027, with payment due by July 23. The proposed ability to pay taxes with cryptocurrency is a separate issue. Officials have discussed it as a potential step for 2027, but the currencies, provider and operational arrangements have not been announced. It should not be confused with the tax law parliament has already adopted. For the wider EU market, Latvia’s move illustrates how governments are adapting old tax concepts to assets that can be exchanged continuously. The details of account eligibility and recordkeeping will decide how helpful the change is in practice. Written by the News Desk and edited by Samuel Rae.

#185. Ethereum News: VanEck Withdraws Unlaunched Lido stETH ETF Application

VanEck withdrew its proposed stETH ETF registration, leaving the reason unknown and highlighting the custody, valuation and staking issues involved.

In Ethereum news today, VanEck Digital Assets asked the US SEC on October 14, 2026, to withdraw the registration for its proposed Lido Staked Ethereum ETF, nearly a year after filing it on October 16, 2025. The registration never became effective: VanEck said it issued or sold no shares or securities and distributed no preliminary prospectus.

The filing offers no detailed explanation for the withdrawal, leaving investors wondering whether institutional demand is waning. This is not simply an ETF filing removed from the regulatory pipeline. The proposed fund would have given brokerage investors exposure to Lido’s stETH through a conventional fund structure, but its withdrawal does not establish which obstacle, if any, drove VanEck’s decision.

Oct 16, 2025: VanEck files for a Lido staked ETH ETF.Oct 14, 2026: VanEck asks the SEC to withdraw it.

The fund would have held stETH directly, putting Lido's liquid-staking token inside a normal brokerage account. Its registration never became effective. VanEck's stated…

— Sun WU Kong (@wysndbb) October 15, 2026

Custody, valuation, liquidity, reward accounting, smart contracts and regulation are all additional considerations for a product built around liquid staking.

The distinction between standard Ethereum funds and staking-linked products is also relevant to efforts to incorporate Ethereum staking into U.S. ETFs. The filing describes an abandoned proposal, not a regulatory rejection or a blanket prohibition on staking-based funds.

VanEck requested withdrawal of the registration statement, its amendments and supporting exhibits under Rule 477 of the Securities Act of 1933.

The company stated in the filing that it no longer intended to offer shares in the proposed fund. The request asked the SEC to make the withdrawal effective on October 14 or as soon as practicable afterward.

The proposed ETF would have held Lido’s stETH and sought to track its price after operating expenses. It was designed as a passive product using a benchmark developed by MarketVector, a VanEck affiliate. The registration was still in progress: proposed operational details, including an exchange ticker and named custodians, had not been finalized.

Because the offering never proceeded, fund shareholders do not need to redeem their investments. The filing also does not identify a replacement product or say whether VanEck plans another fund linked to Lido.

This withdrawal came as spot Ethereum ETFs closed yesterday with $129.5M in outflows, potentially signaling waning interest in ETF products, although VanEck hasn’t confirmed that this is why it pulled its stETH ETF application.

Market Intelligence: Crypto Security Analyst Recommends Best Anonymous Crypto Exchanges

stETH is Lido’s liquid-staking token, representing Ethereum in its staking system and any associated rewards. Its rebasing mechanism increases stETH balances as rewards accrue, combining reward recognition, fund accounting, custody, and valuation.

VanEck’s prospectus highlighted risks such as validator penalties, smart-contract vulnerabilities, liquidity, and fluctuations in Ether’s market value, noting that staking rewards are not guaranteed. These risks would affect a registered fund holding stETH rather than ordinary ETH.

In August 2025, the SEC indicated that some liquid-staking arrangements might not require securities registration based on their structure, though this did not authorize ETFs holding staking tokens. VanEck’s prospectus asserted that its activities align with SEC interpretations while acknowledging potential legal risks.

The proposal is part of Lido’s broader involvement in Ethereum staking, offering exposure through a receipt token rather than direct custody of staked ETH. VanEck also filed for an ETF linked to the Solana liquid-staking token JitoSOL in August 2025; the October 14 request pertains specifically to the Lido fund, registration number 333-290918.

In other Ethereum news, the analytical question is not whether the SEC rejected this proposal; the filing says no such decision occurred. It is whether fund sponsors can translate token-level staking mechanics into workable custody, valuation, reward, and liquidity arrangements within a US ETF.

The filing leaves the reason for VanEck’s withdrawal unknown, but its proposed structure illustrates why stETH exposure is not identical to a plain spot-Ethereum wrapper.

Any future attempt to bring liquid-staking tokens into a U.S. ETF would still have to address those operational and regulatory questions. The SEC’s guidance remains conditional, and this withdrawal provides no indication of when, or whether, VanEck will make another Lido-linked filing.

#186. Zoom adds ‘proof of human’ badges to show you’re not a deepfake

Sam Altman-backed World has rolled out biometric verification badges for Zoom enterprise users, aiming to combat AI deepfake impersonation and fraud.

Zoom enterprise customers will now be able to see “proof of human” badges to verify that people appearing on video calls are real, after a global rollout of biometric identity technology from World.

On Sunday, the Sam Altman-backed project announced that World ID for Zoom is now available in the Zoom Marketplace. The system compares an image captured by the company’s iris-scanning Orb, a live selfie and the participant’s video feed before displaying a Human Badge visible to other meeting participants.

World first announced its Zoom integration in April, when it was undergoing limited beta testing with VanEck Funds. The feature is now available globally to Zoom enterprise customers. World also named Bain Capital, Pantera Capital and other financial firms as initial design partners for its broader identity verification technology.

The rollout follows incidents involving AI-generated impersonation. In 2024, an employee at engineering firm Arup transferred about $25 million after scammers impersonated executives during a video conference.

In February, suspected North Korea-linked hackers used fabricated video feeds in fake Zoom meetings to trick crypto and fintech companies into installing malware.

“World ID for Zoom is designed to protect sensitive, high-stakes conversations by proving that a real and unique human is present,” World said in a statement cited by Fortune.

#188. SEC tokenized stock framework faces issuer pushback as Broadcom, Verizon object to OKX-ICE listing

The SEC’s new framework for trading tokenized stocks is encountering resistance from some of the companies whose shares could trade, with Broadcom (AVGO), Verizon (VZ) and UnitedHealth (UNH) among the latest issuers to object.

Eight newly disclosed objections appeared in an October 15 public notice from OKXICE, the joint venture between crypto exchange OKX and New York Stock Exchange parent Intercontinental Exchange (ICE) preparing to offer tokenized stock trading.

Alongside Broadcom, Verizon and UnitedHealth, the notice names AppLovin (APP), Applied Digital (APLD), Rocket Lab (RKLB), CoreWeave (CRWV) and Applied Optoelectronics (AAOI).

It lists nine objecting issuers in total, including AI chipmaker Cerebras Systems (CBRS), which formally opted out of being listed earlier. The update did not disclose why the companies objected or when they submitted their notices.

Nasdaq (NDAQ) has separately said it would opt out of having its own shares tokenized under the framework, according to an FAQ on its website.

A Nasdaq spokesperson told the Wall Street Journal that the company does not want its shares trading on a venue that does not display best prices in real time or report to the consolidated tape, which aggregates stock-market trading data. Nasdaq is not among the nine issuers named in OKXICE’s notice.

OKXICE announced on October 5 that it had notified the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission of plans to launch the venue, initially targeting shares of 63 U.S.-listed companies. Former New York Gov. Andrew Cuomo, the venture’s co-chair, announced the move on X.

The venue would operate under the SEC’s five-year “Innovation Exemption,” issued September 17, which allows qualifying platforms to trade tokenized U.S. stocks using automated market makers and liquidity pools.

Tokenized stocks are blockchain-based representations of shares. OKXICE plans to operate around the clock using Uniswap v4 liquidity pools on OKX’s XLayer blockchain, with trades settled in stablecoins.

Under the model described in its notice, underlying shares would be held one-for-one against outstanding tokens through a registered broker-dealer. Token holders must receive equivalent rights, including dividends and voting rights.

The issuer pushback echoes findings from TD Securities analysts led by Reid Noch, vice president of U.S. equity market structure.

Conversations with dozens of issuers showed “little interest in tokenizing their shares outside a small group of crypto-adjacent companies,” the analysts wrote in a report shared with CoinDesk. Several issuers also approached the firm with significant concerns after discovering the framework, having been unaware of it when it was announced, the report said.

TD Securities named the framework’s reliance on temporary exemptive relief, rather than permanent rules, as its largest hurdle. A future commission could reverse the approach, complicating the case for investing in infrastructure and discouraging institutions from integrating with venues even after they launch, the analysts said.

That uncertainty is especially challenging when overseas platforms can continue offering synthetic stock products without assuming the operational requirements of the U.S. relief, they added.

#189. Bitcoin ETFs Shed Nearly $1 Billion in Two Weeks as Uptober Stays Red

Bitcoin ETFs Shed Nearly $1 Billion in Two Weeks as Uptober Stays Red

Bitcoin ETF investors spent another week heading for the exits.

U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs shed $82.4 million on Friday, according to Decrypt’s ETF tracker, capping a week in which outflows outweighed inflows on three of five trading days.

The funds lost a net $228.6 million for the week, according to SoSoValue, following a $681.1 million drain the week before. Over the two weeks, about $910 million has left the funds.

It was a choppy stretch. A $175.7 million inflow on Tuesday was wiped out a day later by $261.4 million in redemptions, the week’s worst session. Thursday brought a modest $5.1 million inflow before selling resumed Friday.

Wednesday’s selling coincided with a hot inflation print. The consumer price index showed prices up 3.7% year over year in September, above the 3.6% forecast. A hotter-than-expected producer price reading followed Thursday, reviving bets on another Federal Reserve interest rate hike.

Bitcoin briefly slipped below $80,000 on Thursday, and nearly $950 million in leveraged crypto positions were liquidated over 24 hours, about 90% of them bullish longs, according to CoinGlass. The drop also pushed Bitcoin below the average ETF holder’s estimated cost basis near $82,300, Nexo analyst Iliya Kalchev told Decrypt.

When inflation runs hot, the Fed tends to keep raising rates, pushing up Treasury yields and making a nearly risk-free return of around 5% a tough competitor for riskier bets like Bitcoin. Higher rates also make borrowing costlier and lift the dollar, squeezing the cheap credit that leveraged crypto traders depend on.

The back-to-back red weeks have dragged October deep into negative territory. After opening the month with roughly $293 million in inflows, the funds are now down about $615 million for October, based on Decrypt’s tracker. The slide began in earnest on Oct. 7, when a $484.9 million exit marked the funds’ worst day since June. Ethereum and Solana ETFs have also been in the red this month.

Spot Bitcoin ETFs are exchange-traded funds that hold actual Bitcoin. They trade on stock exchanges like ordinary shares, giving investors exposure through a regular brokerage account without buying or storing the asset themselves.

Since launching in January 2024, they’ve drawn $57.3 billion in cumulative net inflows, according to Decrypt’s tracker, making them a fixture of Wall Street’s crypto exposure. Because issuers report flows daily, and institutions and financial advisers account for much of the money, the figures have become a closely watched gauge of investor sentiment.

Total net assets stand at $104.29 billion, according to SoSoValue, while Decrypt’s tracker puts the figure at $100.2 billion. Bitcoin closed Friday near $81,590, down from about $82,337 a week earlier.

#193. South Korea to meet crypto exchanges amid calls for tax delay

Finance officials are reportedly set to meet major crypto exchanges on Tuesday, days after a lawmaker introduced legislation that could push the tax’s start date back two years.

South Korea’s senior finance officials are reportedly set to meet crypto exchanges on Tuesday as calls to postpone a planned cryptocurrency tax are heating up ahead of its scheduled implementation in January.

According to Yonhap, the government is planning to hold a consultation on crypto taxation, with representatives coming from Upbit, Bithumb, Coinone, DigitalX and Gopax, along with executives of the Digital Asset Exchange Alliance, known as DAXA.

Government officials attending include Kwon Dae-young, first vice minister of finance and economy, and Yoo Young-jun, director general for digital financial policy at the Financial Services Commission.

South Korean regulators have delayed the crypto tax three times, with the latest delay pushing the start date to 2027 amid political disagreement and industry pushback over exchange readiness and the threshold level.

An exchange official told Yonhap on Sunday that unresolved transaction rules and limited time to prepare infrastructure supported postponing the tax.

“Standards for different transaction types have not yet been finalized, and time is running short for practical preparations on the infrastructure side,” an exchange official told Yonhap. “There is a shared view in favor of postponing the start of taxation.”

On Friday, Democratic Party of Korea lawmaker Park Min-gyu introduced a bill seeking to postpone the tax until Jan. 1 of the second year after South Korea begins sharing data under OECD’s Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework (CARF). With the first exchange expected in 2027, taxation would begin in 2029.

JPMorgan is taking its bank-issued deposit token onto public Ethereum, an expansion that puts an established Wall Street payments product on infrastructure traditionally associated with crypto-native finance.

TL;DR: JPMorgan is expanding access to JPM Coin on Ethereum for institutional users. The token represents bank deposits rather than an independently issued stablecoin, and participation remains restricted.

The significance is in who is allowed to move the money, and where. JPM Coin gives eligible customers a tokenized claim on dollars deposited with JPMorgan. Its move onto Ethereum creates a way for institutions to send funds and settle transactions around the clock while still operating inside the bank’s permissioning framework.

That distinction separates deposit tokens from the conventional stablecoin model. A holder of a dollar stablecoin generally has a claim governed by the issuer’s redemption arrangements and reserve assets. JPM Coin is bank money represented in token form. It is not being offered as a freely transferable dollar for ordinary Ethereum users.

JPMorgan previously introduced the deposit token on Base, and Ethereum provides another venue where financial institutions and tokenization platforms can coordinate payments. Potential uses include moving collateral and settling transactions against tokenized assets, where a conventional banking cut-off can create delay between the asset leg and the cash leg.

A public blockchain does not automatically make the system open to everyone. The bank continues to control institutional access and compliance. The development is better understood as traditional finance adopting a public settlement network without abandoning its existing customer controls.

For Ethereum, that may be the bigger story: a major bank choosing its infrastructure for business that depends on predictable dollar settlement, rather than simply issuing another experiment.

#198. Banks Hold a Lever Over Stablecoin Adoption, BIS Economists Say

Banks Hold a Lever Over Stablecoin Adoption, BIS Economists Say

Banks worried about losing customers to stablecoins may already have a counterweight: the interest rate on a savings account.

That’s the takeaway from a new working paper published by the Bank for International Settlements, the Basel-based bank for central banks. Using weekly U.S. data from January 2019 through June 2025, BIS economist Iñaki Aldasoro and Rashad Ahmed of the Andersen Institute for Finance and Economics found that stablecoin growth slows when banks raise deposit rates.

Stablecoin market capitalization grew by about 15% over a typical 10-week span in the sample used by the researchers. A one-basis-point bump in deposit rates, a sizable weekly move for slow-moving savings rates, cut that to roughly 12% under the authors’ baseline estimate. Under a second method designed to isolate cause and effect, it fell to about 6%. Stablecoins kept growing, just more slowly.

To separate cause from coincidence, the authors relied on a quirk in bank behavior. Lenders barely raise savings rates until the federal funds rate passes about 3%, and then they reprice much faster.

The link was stronger for Circle’s USDC than for Tether’s USDT, which the authors attribute to USDC’s closer ties to U.S. users. The paper concludes that banks “retain some influence over the pace of that adoption through deposit pricing.”

The findings come with caveats. Working papers reflect the authors’ views, not necessarily the BIS’s, and the sample spans a single high-rate cycle in which stablecoins paid holders no interest.

The authors said regulators should weigh whether stablecoin issuers may pay holders yield, along with the trade-offs of requiring issuers to keep part of their reserves in bank deposits.

That debate is live in Washington. Banks have lobbied to keep stablecoin yield off the table, a fight that loomed over the Clarity Act’s failed Senate vote. Meanwhile, the OCC, FDIC, and Treasury are writing rules to implement the GENIUS Act, which takes effect in January. The GENIUS Act, signed into law by President Donald Trump in July of last year, essentially legalized stablecoins in the United States and set rules of the road for their issuance, use, and custody.

The BIS has long scrutinized stablecoins and the cryptocurrency space more broadly. In 2021, it argued the rise of blockchain-based digital dollars made central bank digital currencies more urgent, and a 2023 BIS survey warned they could threaten financial stability if widely adopted.

XRP holders should exercise maximum caution: the integration of the XRP Ledger into the banking sector, the launch of the RLUSD stablecoin, and Evernorth treasury transfers have had an unexpected side effect. While Ripple cements its institutional recognition, scammers have begun mass-stealing the names of well-known financial institutions, turning real corporate news into a tool for stealing assets.

This week, an XRPL Foundation contributor under the handle '@Vet_X0' warned investors about a new scheme. Scammers generate "beautiful" wallet addresses (vanity addresses) and issue dummy tokens that imitate brands from recent announcements.

This signals a change in tactics: the focus has shifted from hunting for bugs in code to social engineering. Previous technical incidents, from the summer Rippling-drainer botnet and fake NFTs to the September hack of the Bitget exchange (103 million XRP) and the compromise of XRPH Wallet ($452,000), have given way to pure psychology.

The main trigger for the deception was the legitimate news backdrop: Cross River Bank's tests of the RLUSD stablecoin and the deployment of the 473 million XRP Evernorth fund through major exchanges. As soon as a brand announces its entry into the XRPL, the scammers' software creates a similar wallet address within seconds (for example, rBankxxx) and issues a fake token such as $BANKxxx.

Then, through phishing sites, users are prompted to "verify" their wallets or exchange real XRP for new "bank" coins. To an inattentive investor, an entry in a blockchain explorer looks like a guarantee of authenticity.

This is the paradox: the openness of the blockchain has started working against security. A token's appearance on XRP Scan proves only its technical existence. Anyone can issue a coin with any name on the XRPL.

Institutional players operate at the level of internal gateways. Large banks do not require retail holders to sign transactions or redeem their assets. "Just sit on your hands and do nothing," concludes Vet_X0. The only confirmation that a real bank stands behind a project remains a publication on the corporation's own official press site. Any other offer is a guaranteed loss of capital.

Ripple CEO Brad Garlinghouse has admitted that the collapse of the CLARITY Act hurt. He also says XRP no longer needs Congress to settle the question that hung over it for years.

Speaking during celebrations for Evernorth’s Nasdaq listing, Garlinghouse said the bill’s failure “definitely stung.” He added that he had personally put a lot of energy into getting the crypto market structure bill through Congress.

Garlinghouse said XRP holders are in a stronger position than the failed vote suggests. He pointed to the outcome of Ripple’s long court battle with the SEC, saying the federal judge wrote in her opinion that “XRP is not a security.”

That ruling came from Judge Analisa Torres in July 2023. She found that XRP is not a security by itself and that Ripple’s sales of XRP on public exchanges were not securities offerings. She also ruled, however, that Ripple’s direct sales of XRP to institutional investors did count as unregistered securities sales.

The CLARITY Act failed a Senate cloture vote 49 to 50 on September 15. Garlinghouse said the SEC and CFTC have stepped into rulemaking to cover what the bill was meant to do. He said there are also lessons to learn from what went wrong in Congress.

Garlinghouse acknowledged that a future SEC or CFTC chair could take a harsher stance on crypto. He said that is possible, but argued that years of progress cannot simply be rolled back.

When the interviewer described it as being unable to “put the genie back in the bottle,” Garlinghouse agreed.

Without a law from Congress, crypto’s rules now come mostly from regulators and courts. Rules made by agencies can be changed by future leadership more easily than an act of Congress. For XRP specifically, Garlinghouse is relying on the 2023 court ruling as the foundation for its legal status.

#201. Qubic freezes chain after attacker drains 1.4K wallets with weak seeds

Qubic says 87.1% of the stolen funds remain onchain and the rest were frozen at crypto exchange MEXC, as network validators prepare to vote on a recovery plan.

Layer-1 blockchain network Qubic halted operations Sunday after an attacker reportedly exploited weakly generated wallet seeds to drain approximately $1.4 million from more than 1,400 accounts, according to the project.

In a statement on X, Qubic said the network was halted at tick 85,371,949, where it remains paused at the time of writing. Qubic said the vulnerability affected wallet seeds generated using any browser on an iPhone or iPad, Safari on a Mac until Oct. 18, 2026, or the Qubic iOS app before July 2025, leading to 2.94 trillion Qubit (QU) stolen.

“87.1% of the drained funds never left the Qubic network and remain frozen in place,” said Qubic. “The remaining 12.9% was sent to MEXC, whose team froze the receiving account within about an hour.”

The Qubic theft is the latest in a series of attacks tied to weak wallet seeds. In July, Coldcard disclosed that attackers had stolen funds from wallets whose seeds were weakened by a firmware bug. Similar flaws affected Trust Wallet’s browser extension and the Libbitcoin Explorer tool in 2023.

Related: Bitget’s $388M hack pushes Q3 crypto security losses past $1B

Qubic said it has fixed the seed-generation flaw in the latest version of its web wallet.

A GitHub commit for version 4.26.4 shows that Qubic replaced JavaScript’s Math.random() function, which is not suitable for generating cryptographic secrets, with the cryptographically secure crypto.getRandomValues() function when creating wallet seeds.

Qubic said its core team is identifying affected wallets and preparing recovery options for a vote by the network’s Computors, which will decide what happens to the frozen funds. The team said it would publish a full technical report after a recovery plan is settled. It has not announced when the network will restart.

Qubic did not immediately respond to Cointelegraph’s request for comment.

Qubic is a layer-1 blockchain that supports transactions and smart contracts without fees. It is built on Useful Proof of Work (UPoW) – a consensus mechanism that repurposes mining energy to train artificial intelligence. Qubic’s token had a market capitalization of about $62.6 million at the time of writing, according to CoinGecko.

In the third quarter, hacks and exploits accounted for 19% of crypto crime cases but 40% of reported losses, according to AMLBot’s 2026 investigations report, which looked at 250 investigations it opened since the start of the year.

#203. Binance And Coinbase Join West Africa Scam Crackdown As 28 Arrested

The arrest count is striking, but the scale of the online infrastructure removed may be the bigger story. An international effort against West African scam networks has resulted in 28 arrests, while technology companies say they removed more than 3.7 million accounts, pages and groups linked to fraudulent activity.

TL;DR: The US Justice Department says its October crackdown led to 28 arrests in Ghana and Nigeria. Binance and Coinbase were among the industry participants, and partners identified more than $11 million in potentially freezable funds, not confirmed recoveries.

The operation, called Joint Disruption Week, brought investigators together at the UK’s National Crime Agency in London during the week beginning October 6. Authorities targeted networks accused of investment fraud, impersonation and other online schemes that reach victims well beyond West Africa.

According to the Justice Department’s October 13 announcement, Ghanaian authorities arrested 19 people and seized 303 electronic devices in an operation near Accra. Nine more arrests were reported in Nigeria. Investigators also identified 117 trafficking victims in Ghana, a reminder that scam-centre operations can involve people held against their will as well as the victims losing money online.

Binance and Coinbase joined companies including Chainalysis, Elliptic, Meta, Google and Microsoft in sharing intelligence or disrupting the infrastructure used by scammers. That collaboration can help investigators connect social-media accounts, payments and wallet activity, but it should not be confused with proof that every suspect used cryptocurrency.

There is also an important distinction in the money figure. Officials said private-sector partners identified more than $11 million in funds that could potentially be frozen. They did not say that $11 million had been seized or returned to victims.

The real test now is how much of the identified money authorities can actually secure and how many disrupted operations stay offline.
