#205. Cardano Eyes Insanely Bullish Cup-And-Handle Breakout As Hoskinson Teases New Programming Language For ADA

Cardano (ADA) could be gearing up for an explosive comeback as a potentially bullish cup-and-handle pattern takes shape on its price chart, just as founder Charles Hoskinson stirs fresh excitement with hints of a new programming language that could reshape the blockchain’s future.

Cardano is carving out a textbook cup-and-handle on the weekly chart — the same bullish continuation pattern that preceded some of ADA’s parabolic rallies.

After bottoming in the $0.14- $0.16 zone, ADA has formed a perfect rounded bottom. Crypto analyst Giannis Andreou says the trigger is clear: a weekly close above $0.278.

Break that, and the math turns explosive. The measured cup-depth target sits at $0.416 — a 74% move from the $0.239 base. Above that, the chart opens to $0.5116, $0.8059, and $0.9601, with a long-term projection as high as $1.3291.

The line in the sand? Lose the rising support, and the setup weakens. Drop below $0.16, and the setup is invalidated. Until then, every ADA trader is watching $0.278.

However, ADA’s bullish setup faces an immediate hurdle as fresh selling pressure threatens to erase its recent gains. According to CoinGecko, the token is changing hands at $0.2158, down 2.6% in the past 24 hours and 13% over the last seven days.

At that price, ADA remains roughly 28.8% below Andreou’s crucial $0.278 breakout level, meaning it would need to rally by that percentage to reach the threshold. A weekly close above $0.278, followed by a successful retest, could strengthen the case for a sustained bullish breakout. Until then, the chart pattern remains unconfirmed, and its upside targets are far from guaranteed.

Meanwhile, Cardano founder Charles Hoskinson has unveiled another ambitious project that could expand the blockchain’s capabilities.

The crypto entrepreneur said he is personally developing a new programming language to bring advanced cryptographic functionality to Cardano. According to Hoskinson, the language will combine intent-based programming with proof-carrying data (PCD) and use Groth16 zero-knowledge proofs to enable new ways to build and verify blockchain applications. He described the project as the first of its kind, though that claim has not yet been independently verified.

“I’m actually personally developing a programming language for Cardano. It’s the first of its kind enabling intents + PCD via Groth16 proofs,” Hoskinson revealed in an X post.

Hoskinson shared the news in response to a community member who asked what sets Cardano apart as a decentralized foundation for blockchain applications. However, he kept the finer details under wraps, offering no name, technical specifications, or launch timeline for the proposed language.

The revelation follows another intriguing tease earlier this week, when Hoskinson hinted at a potentially groundbreaking use case for Midnight, Cardano’s privacy-focused partner blockchain.

#206. Wall Street freaked out Friday, but VIX and bitcoin trades say the fear may fade Monday.

Wall Street's fear gauge, the VIX index, ripped higher on Friday as stocks tanked on AI and geopolitical worries. Bitcoin BTC$82,836.58 traded in a choppy manner as well.

Traders are betting the fear gauge keeps climbing.

However, if VIX history and bitcoin’s steady weekend price action are any guide, the panic could subside just as quickly on Monday.

First, a quick primer. Cboe’s VIX measures how much traders expect the S&P 500, the blue-chip stock index, to swing over the next four weeks. It's derived from options prices. When people get nervous, they buy options, which are contracts used to hedge against price swings. That pushes the VIX up.

Bitcoin BTC$82,836.58, meanwhile, is the only macro asset thats trades over the weekend. As such, swings in bitcoin over the weekend are often seen as lead indicators of how traditional markets may open on Monday.

On Friday, the VIX jumped 21.5% to 19.99 as the S&P 500 fell by 1.09%.

That's VIX’s biggest one-day rise since June 5, when the S&P 500 suffered its worst day in months, according to data source TradingView.

Traders are betting the VIX stays high through November. CNBC reports that traders bought 9,200 of the Nov. 18, 20-strike calls for $1.7 million. Traders also bought 12,500 of the Nov. 18, 23-strike calls for $1.1 million. The bet is that the VIX closes above 23 by the third week of November.

That sentiment is consistent with the present macro developments. AI stocks have been hit hard in the week gone by. The cost of default insurance on AI-related firms has hit record highs. Geopolitics is pushing oil higher too. On Saturday, Iran's Revolutionary Guards said two oil tankers caught fire after hitting mines in the Strait of Hormuz. The Russia-Ukraine front looks like it's heating up as well.

Big Friday jumps in the VIX usually don't last, according to historical data.

CoinDesk's analysis of the data finds the VIX has jumped 20% or more on a Friday 32 times since January 1990, not counting the latest one. The next Monday, it fell 25 times and rose just seven.

In other words, investors slept over the Friday panic over the weekend and things normalized on Monday. The typical Monday move was a drop of 4.5%. A month later, the VIX was lower in 25 of the 32 cases, and the median drop was 16%.

Seasonality also favors the VIX bears, and by extension stock market stability.

The VIX has declined in November in 25 of the last 36 years, with a median drop of 7.2%. From October end to the end of the year, VIX has fallen in 22 of 36 years, with a median decline of 9.4%.

Bitcoin isn’t flinching. It continues to trade above $80,000, comfortably within its recent choppy range, suggesting Friday’s risk aversion and VIX rise may not carry into Monday.

The bitcoin market has been more active over the weekend this year, especially on Sunday, as geopolitical flareups that began in early March keep investors on edge. That activity highlights bitcoin’s role as a always-on macro asset: When traditional markets are shut, traders use bitcoin to express their early read on global risk appetite.

Volmex's BVIV, the bitcoin volatility index, or the bitcoin VIX, slipped 1% on Friday to just under 40% and has barely moved since. BVIV shows the 30-day implied or expected volatility in bitcoin.

Bettors on the decentralized platform Polymarket aren't panicking either. They see just an 9% chance the AI bubble bursts this year as of this writing.

None of the above guarantees a stable Monday. Moreover, in seven of the 32 cases, the VIX kept climbing sharply on Monday, including in August 2015, February 2018 and August 2024.

Going purely by the VIX levels, there's room for the index to run.

Even after Friday’s spike, the VIX is still under 20, a mark it has topped on more than a third of days since 1990. It has closed above 30 on just 8% of days. So, if fear grips the market further on Monday morning, the VIX can climb.

Crypto’s biggest political spender is turning up the pressure on one of the industry’s fiercest critics. Fairshake has reported fresh spending to defeat Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown in Ohio, pushing its total outlay against the former Senate Banking Committee chairman well past the $40 million mark.

A filing with the Federal Election Commission, signed Oct. 15, shows Defend American Jobs, the Fairshake affiliate that spends in Republican-friendly races, disclosed a $5.2 million media buy opposing Brown, followed by another roughly $1.95 million buy days later, plus media-production costs.

The filing lists Brown’s calendar-year-to-date total at about $46.66 million, cementing the Ohio contest as the most expensive target of the crypto industry’s 2026 campaign. The same filing showed parallel spending supporting Brown’s Republican opponent, Jon Husted, who inherited the seat after being appointed last year.

The sums dwarf what Fairshake is deploying elsewhere, underscoring how personal the Ohio race has become for the industry. The PAC earlier signaled plans to spend at least $30 million against Brown, a figure this filing shows it has already blown past.

Brown’s return to the Senate would hand crypto skeptics a powerful voice on the Banking Committee, the same perch from which he stalled market-structure legislation before losing his seat in 2024, a defeat Fairshake spent roughly $40 million to help engineer.

The renewed Senate blitz comes days after Fairshake broadened its map to the House. On Oct. 5, the PAC network announced it would back 32 House incumbents, 19 Republicans and 13 Democrats, framing itself as an issue-focused group that supports “pro-crypto candidates who support American innovation in both parties.”

It committed an initial $6 million, or $1 million each, to six of them: Republicans French Hill, Bill Huizenga and Bryan Steil, and Democrats Janelle Bynum, Steven Horsford and Derek Tran. All 32 voted to advance the Clarity Act when it passed the House in July 2025.

Fairshake, funded largely by Coinbase, Ripple, and Andreessen Horowitz, entered September with roughly $120 million in cash and is expected to spend more than $100 million across House and Senate races this cycle. Its push runs alongside the Coinbase-backed advocacy group Stand With Crypto, which has rolled out its own slate of midterm endorsements.

The spending reflects the industry’s hardened resolve after the Clarity Act stalled in the Senate, channeling its considerable war chest into reshaping the Congress that will decide crypto’s rules.

Headline coverage surrounding Arbitrum DAO’s active snapshot voting cycle centers on a high-profile proposal to drive adoption of the Global Dollar Network's USDG stablecoin using 100 million ARB in incentives.

However, four additional temperature check votes close concurrently on Thursday, October 22, 2026.

Chief among these voting initiatives is a constitutional Improvement Proposal (AIP) designed to resolve an existential operational vulnerability: establishing an on-chain fallback mechanism if Arbitrum’s Layer-2 governance machinery stalls or fails completely.

Proposed on the Arbitrum Governance Forum, the L1 Voting Recovery System serves as a constitutional fail-safe for protocol administration.

Under standard operations, Arbitrum DAO executes proposals natively on Layer 2. However, if L2 transaction execution freezes, L2 proposal creation contracts break, or cross-chain message passing experiences systemic disruption, the DAO's governance capacity becomes locked. While the Security Council holds emergency multi-sig powers to intervene during acute protocol crises, it operates as an operational guardian rather than a permanent administrative engine.

The proposed L1 Voting Recovery System constructs a parallel, emergency governance path deployed directly on Ethereum Layer 1. In the event that L2 governance becomes unresponsive or inaccessible, delegates can initiate, vote on, queue, and execute Arbitrum DAO proposals directly on L1 base-layer smart contracts.

By establishing this base-layer fallback, the DAO decouples its long-term administrative survival from L2 sequencer uptime or L2 smart contract execution state. The emergency path preserves the Security Council's authority without forcing the protocol to rely indefinitely on multi-sig intervention during prolonged L2 governance disruptions.

If delegates reject the L1 Voting Recovery System, Arbitrum DAO leaves its governance architecture exposed to single-point-of-failure risks.

Without an operational L1 recovery track, any software defect, state progression freeze, or prolonged outage impacting L2 governance contracts would paralyze the DAO. The community would possess no constitutional or technical mechanism to submit on-chain votes, reconfigure network parameters, or deploy treasury reserves until L2 functionality was manually restored, forcing total dependence on emergency Security Council multi-sig powers.

#211. GENIUS Act Stablecoin Regulation: Why the OCC’s Final Rule Is Critical

The U.S. Department of Treasury’s NPRM on payment stablecoin issuance, offer, and sale (RIN 1505-AC95) closed its public comment window today, October 19, 2026. The 87 questions Treasury asked the industry to weigh in on span issuer licensing, foreign stablecoin access, reserve composition, and exchange due diligence requirements. What closes today is the comment window, not the gap. The binding rulebook does not exist yet.

President Trump signed the Guiding and Establishing National Innovation for U.S. Stablecoins Act (GENIUS Act) on July 18, 2025. The Act required regulators to finalize implementing rules by July 18, 2026, around 12 months after enactment. That deadline passed with zero final rules in place across Treasury, OCC, FDIC, and the Federal Reserve.

The statutory effective date is the earlier of January 18, 2027, 18 months after enactment or 120 days after primary federal regulators issue final rules. Because the July 2026 rulemaking deadline was missed, the January 18, 2027 backstop is now the operative date. As of today, the OCC has not published a final rule. The 120-day clock has not started.

The Comptroller of the Currency stated publicly on August 19, 2026, that the OCC expects to publish its final stablecoin rule by November 2026. If that timeline holds, the 120-day clock starts in November and the effective date slides to approximately March 2027, after the January 18 statutory backstop. The January 18 backstop is no longer the latest possible date. It is the base case.

The NPRM establishes a new regulatory code under 12 CFR Part 1523. It defines who may legally issue, offer, sell, or make available payment stablecoins in the United States. The Act creates two qualifying categories: Permitted Payment Stablecoin Issuers (PPSIs) and Foreign Payment Stablecoin Issuers (FPSIs) that meet Section 18 requirements.

The $10 billion market cap threshold is a structural cut point. Issuers below $10 billion may operate under qualifying state regimes. Issuers above $10 billion must mandatorily transition to the federal OCC regime within 360 days of the effective date, or request a formal exemption. Both USDT (at approximately $180 billion in global market cap) and USDC (at approximately $72 billion) are above this threshold.

The NPRM asked 87 specific questions covering implementation, regulatory scope, foreign issuer treatment, and compliance mechanics. The volume of questions indicates that Treasury has made structural choices without settling all operational details. The comment period that closes today was designed to produce answers to those 87 open questions before the final rule is drafted.

Section 3(b)(2) of the GENIUS Act prohibits offering, selling, or making a foreign-issued stablecoin available to US persons unless the issuer can and will comply with lawful orders. This provision takes effect January 18, 2027. The burden falls on digital asset service providers (DASPs), exchanges, platforms, on-ramps, not the issuer directly.

Treasury explicitly acknowledged in the NPRM that a DASP may lack full insight into a foreign issuer’s technological capability to freeze funds on a US lawful order and cannot know with certainty whether the issuer will comply in the future. Treasury declined to impose a strict interpretation that would effectively foreclose platforms from offering any FPSI-issued stablecoin entirely. Instead it proposed a due diligence standard where the platform must have a reasonable basis to believe the foreign issuer can comply.

The Freshfields analysis published September 25 described the gap between the January 18, 2027 date for Section 3(b)(2), the due diligence requirement on exchanges and the July 18, 2028 date for Section 3(b)(1), the full prohibition on selling non-qualifying foreign-issued stablecoins to US persons, as the principal area the comment period would focus on. That gap is now the regulator’s problem to resolve in final rules.

USDC is issued by Circle, a US-domiciled company that already publishes monthly reserve attestations. Circle has filed an application with the OCC for a trust bank license under the federal PPSI pathway. USDC’s existing reserve composition, consisting of short-duration US Treasuries and cash equivalents, matches the GENIUS Act’s reserve requirements without structural modification.

USDT is issued by Tether Limited, incorporated in El Salvador. Tether is a foreign issuer under the GENIUS Act by definition. The Act bars foreign issuers from offering or selling stablecoins to US persons unless Treasury certifies that their home jurisdiction maintains comparable regulatory standards. As of October 19, 2026, no foreign jurisdiction, including El Salvador, has received a Treasury comparability determination.

Tether’s structural response to this constraint was the January 27, 2026 launch of USAT (USA Tether), a separate stablecoin issued by Anchorage Digital Bank, N.A., the only federally chartered crypto bank in the US, and custodied by Cantor Fitzgerald. USAT is Tether’s US-qualified instrument. USDT’s pathway into the US market after January 18, 2027 is a pending OCC comparability determination for El Salvador, for which no timeline has been stated.

USDT has until July 18, 2028 to fully comply under Section 3(b)(1). But the intermediate obligation, Section 3(b)(2), requiring exchanges to verify that Tether can respond to lawful US orders, takes effect January 18, 2027, 91 days from today. Platforms currently listing USDT need a written compliance rationale for that listing by January 18, or face potential liability under the GENIUS Act’s enforcement provision: up to $1 million per knowing violation and up to five years’ imprisonment.

The Treasury NPRM (RIN 1505-AC95) that closed today is one of four regulatory documents being produced in parallel. FinCEN and OFAC issued proposed AML and sanctions rules on April 8, 2026, with a comment period that closed June 9. Customer identification rules closed August 21. The Treasury NPRM on issuance, offer, and sale closes today. The OCC’s primary implementation rule, the single most consequential document for issuer licensing, targets a November 2026 final publication.

The OCC’s February 25, 2026 proposed rule (12 CFR Part 15) attracted 47 formal comments including Visa, JPMorgan, Coinbase, and three European central banks as informal observers by its May 1 close date. The final rule will establish the Federal Qualified Payment Stablecoin Issuer (FQPSI) designation, define capital requirements for federally supervised issuers, and set redemption and disclosure standards. Everything the GENIUS Act required on reserves and auditing will become operational through this document.

The Fed’s proposed capital and redemption requirements for stablecoin issuers within its supervisory perimeter, bank holding companies and state member banks, have not yet been finalised. If the Fed’s rule publishes after the OCC’s November target, entities under Federal Reserve supervision will have less time to reach compliance than those under OCC or FDIC jurisdiction. That regulatory gap between supervised entities is the unresolved structural asymmetry in the current GENIUS Act implementation.

The January 18, 2027 backstop activates a tiered set of obligations. Section 3(b)(2), the DASP due diligence requirement for foreign-issued stablecoins, takes effect on this date. Platforms currently listing USDT must have a documented basis to believe Tether can freeze funds on US lawful orders. A comparability determination from Treasury for El Salvador would resolve this. None exists and none has been scheduled.

Section 4(e)(3) of the GENIUS Act separately prohibits marketing a product in the US as a payment stablecoin unless it is issued in compliance with the Act. The fine is up to $500,000 per knowing and wilful violation. Section 3’s issuer prohibition carries penalties of up to $1 million per violation and up to five years’ imprisonment.

The EU’s MiCA enforcement deadline for non-compliant stablecoin removal from exchanges runs on a parallel January 2027 schedule. Both regulatory regimes reach their hard enforcement dates within weeks of each other. The stablecoin issuers and platforms operating globally in January 2027 will face simultaneous US GENIUS Act and EU MiCA compliance obligations for the first time.

1/ Comments close today on Treasury's proposal defining who issues a payment stablecoin "in the United States".The OCC says its final GENIUS rule is due "in the very near term". The Act takes effect in 91 days either way.Regulatory radar, week of 19 October: pic.twitter.com/Ht73De9wiT

The comment window closed today. The OCC final rule has not published. No comparability determination for any foreign jurisdiction exists. The GENIUS Act’s January 18, 2027 effective date is 91 days away. The 120-day rule clock, which would add four months from whenever the OCC publishes, has not started. Every stablecoin issuer, platform, and exchange operating in the US market is currently complying with a law whose final operational rules do not yet exist.

For USDT, the operational question is binary: either the OCC publishes a final rule before January 18, the 120-day clock starts, and the effective date slides to approximately March 2027,  giving Tether additional time to pursue comparability,  or the January 18 backstop activates with no comparability determination in place, and US platforms must decide independently whether they have a sufficient legal basis to continue listing USDT from that date.

For USDC and USAT, January 18 is the compliance deadline they are structurally positioned to meet. Circle has filed its OCC application. USAT operates under a federally chartered issuer already. The binding rulebook, when it arrives, confirms a competitive position they built in advance of today.

The HEX market cap fell from $561 million to $315 million this week after founder Richard Schueler — better known to the crypto community as Richard Heart — was detained by authorities in Istanbul on October 14.

Police seized $7.15 million in cash along with firearms and ammunition during an early morning raid in Istanbul’s Beşiktaş district, alongside searches of 15 related addresses according to Turkish Justice Minister Akın Gürlek.

Police impounded nine luxury vehicles registered to Schueler’s wife according to news agency Anadolu. The haul reportedly included 28 watches, 300 bags and 19 graphics cards.

Interpol issued a “Red Notice” for Schueler’s two years ago over allegations of tax fraud and assault, after Finnish authorities sought his arrest.

A spokesperson for Finland’s National Bureau of Investigations declined to comment on the matter.

Turkish media refer to Schueler as “Whale James” and have linked him to a $1 billion unregistered securities offering in the US. However that case was dismissed by a US judge in February 2025.

Images circulating in Turkish media appear to show a surprised Heart with no trousers on, and the bottom half of his body blurred out, provoking much merriment on social media. Vocal Hex critic Eric Wall, who has debated Schueler on video and social media, said he initially thought the image was AI generated but now believes it is real. (Cointelegraph can only verify the image is circulating not that it has not been altered.)

Hex supporters claim that authorities are yet to confirm if Schueler has been formally arrested or charged.

Ledger unveiled a new device on Thursday with stronger protections against tampering, days after confirming that wallets sold through a reseller in Asia contained malicious implants.

The French hardware wallet maker introduced Atom, an $849 device that combines a crypto wallet with everyday apps through a smartphone-like design. Atom separates Android apps from sensitive wallet operations and includes protections Ledger says would block the implants used in the recent Asia incident. It claims to detect tampering even when switched off.

Expected to become available in summer 2027, Atom will also support AI agent approvals, encrypted messaging and post-quantum cryptography.Meanwhile a war of words has broken out between former Mt Gox CEO Mark Karpeles, and Ledger CEO Pascal Gauthier. Google has demonstrated a new process called “magic state cultivation” on its Willow quantum processor that reduces errors 40-fold. The technique achieved a record 99.99% accuracy rate for a specialized quantum state required to perform advanced calculations.

Meanwhile Theta Labs has posted three news quantum circuits that could reduce the number of qubits required to break elliptic curve cryptography by 28% from Google’s current estimate of 1,175 logical qubits.

With fears that AI is now getting so good at math that it may be able to break elliptic curve cryptography even before QDay arrives, Starknet has opened a vote to transform itself from an Ethereum L2 into a post quantum L1. StarkWare CEO Eli Ben-Sasson says that Ethereum’s post quantum roadmap may be too slow to meet the challenge from AI, meaning that Starknet needed to consider becoming a fully post quantum L1.

“Quantum-proofing crypto is urgent, so we must move at lightning speed,” he told Cointelegraph. More than 99% of votes cast to date are in favor of the move. Starknet’s token has lost almost 50% in value this week, after a big surge last week.

Binance.US reportedly seeks to raise up to $100 million in a funding round that could value the cryptocurrency exchange at $1 billion.

According to a Thursday Bloomberg report, the US-based crypto exchange is pursuing private investment as it looks to expand its business. The potential $1 billion valuation would be well below the $4.5 billion pre-money valuation it secured in 2022, when it raised $200 million in seed funding.

“Page after page after page, it’s all the same: The most recent part of the chart is turning sharply upwards,” Hougan wrote. “That’s exactly what you want to see if you’re looking for the start of a crypto spring.”

#213. Crypto Hacks Cost $1.18 Billion In Q3 As Smart Contract Exploits Surge

Crypto’s third-quarter security bill came to $1.18 billion, but the headline total is only part of Hacken’s latest warning. The firm recorded 107 incidents between July and September, with smart-contract exploits taking a much larger share of losses than they did three months earlier.

TL;DR: Hacken reported $1.18 billion stolen across 107 incidents in Q3 2026, up 55% from Q2. Smart-contract exploits accounted for 48% of losses, compared with 12% in the previous quarter. Access-control and operational failures made up 40%.

According to Hacken’s Q3 2026 Security and Compliance Report, the pattern behind attacks changed sharply. In Q2, access-control and operational failures had accounted for 88% of losses. That share fell to 40% in Q3, even as total damage rose. Smart-contract losses moved in the other direction, rising from 12% to 48%.

That doesn’t mean wallet keys, infrastructure and vendors stopped being dangerous. Hacken says the largest individual losses were linked to supply-chain attacks, compromised keys, and weaknesses in signer and withdrawal systems. Meanwhile, smart-contract and protocol-code vulnerabilities continued to account for a large number of incidents.

Those distinctions matter when projects point to completed code audits as proof that funds are safe. A contract review can catch defects in one component, but it cannot by itself secure the signing processes, deployment infrastructure and third-party software that surround it.

The report also highlights recurring attack techniques and cases where fixes were already public before exploits happened. That is a less comforting picture for teams relying on one-off reviews rather than continuous checks.

For users and investors, the takeaway is practical: a security audit is worth reading, but its scope, date and follow-through matter as much as the badge on a website.

#214. France Crypto Tax Plan Returns to Assembly Debate

France crypto tax proposal would tax some MiCA stablecoin swaps, but passage remains uncertain after a finance committee setback in Paris.

The France crypto tax debate has a new flashpoint. On 7 October, the finance committee of France’s National Assembly approved a plan to apply the 31.4% capital-gains rate to certain cryptocurrency-to-stablecoin swaps from 1 January 2027.

Chainalysis France head Francois Volpoet warned that the step could push traders toward offshore platforms or less monitored routes. The proposal is still under discussion and has not become law.

The distinction matters for regulated crypto infrastructure developing under European rules: tax treatment could shape whether traders use those compliant channels, not just how much tax they owe.

BREAKING: 🇫🇷 France is planning a 31.4% tax on profits when converting crypto into stablecoins from January 2027.

— Ash Crypto (@AshCrypto) October 14, 2026

The amendment forms part of France’s proposed 2027 budget, which the National Assembly began debating the week before the report’s publication on Oct. 14. The finance committee later rejected the budget’s revenue section by 31 votes to three, requiring the crypto amendments to be resubmitted for consideration by the full Assembly.

Lawmakers were scheduled to vote on the revenue section on Oct. 20. Even if the stablecoin provision returns to the debate, its proposed Jan. 1, 2027 start date depends on enactment; none of the measures in the package had become law as of Oct. 14.

The wider package includes separate proposals to require disclosure of self-hosted wallets holding at least €100,000 in assets, with fines of up to about $11,600 for noncompliance.

Other measures would extend the exit tax to crypto holdings worth roughly $900,000 and let investors carry forward crypto losses for up to 10 years.

Those proposals are distinct from the stablecoin-swap amendment.

While there are record numbers of crypto-related kidnappings, wrench attacks and home invasions in France 🇫🇷, caused in many cases by tax officials who sold confidential personal information, they now want to:

1) Require self-custody crypto holders… https://t.co/9fvBzVLS1o

Market Intelligence: Crypto Security Analyst Recommends Best Anonymous Crypto Exchanges

Volpoet warned that taxing regulated stablecoin conversions could undermine efforts to bring more activity into supervised markets. He said authorities can more readily monitor transactions in regulated stablecoins than activity routed through decentralized finance (DeFi) or self-hosted wallets.

If converting to a MiCA-regulated token incurs tax while alternatives do not, traders may prefer non-MiCA assets, DeFi, or offshore trading.  That is an incentive analysis, not evidence of a confirmed response. Stablecoin routing across wallets and networks also gives traders multiple transaction paths, making the scope of the taxable event consequential.

That is the central stablecoin regulation tension: a policy intended to tax gains could shift activity away from channels authorities can monitor. Volpoet’s warning points to a potential trade-off between collecting tax on a defined transaction and keeping activity within regulated venues.

France’s proposal also sits within a diverging European tax landscape. Greece is preparing a proposed 10% crypto capital-gains tax, while France, Germany and Italy are setting or planning rates above 25%.

The French Assembly’s scheduled Oct. 20 vote is the next stated step for the budget revenue section; the stablecoin measure’s status remains a proposal.

#216. Latvia eyes crypto tax payments in 2027 as parliament overhauls crypto taxation

Latvia could allow residents to pay personal taxes with cryptocurrency as early as next year, as part of a push to attract crypto firms and investors.

The country’s Finance Ministry has agreed to the plan, though technical work with a payment provider remains, said Didzis Dejus, an adviser to the prime minister on strategic planning and the new economy.

Asked whether Latvians would be able to pay taxes in crypto during the prime minister’s term, Dejus told CoinDesk at the UN:BLOCK Fintech conference in Riga that “I believe that will take place next year.”

CoinDesk has reached out to Latvia’s Finance Ministry for comment but hasn’t heard back at the time of writing.

The move would give crypto holders a way to use their assets to meet tax bills. It also builds on plans announced in May 2025 to enable crypto tax payments and the tokenization of other assets like real estate.

“We are not afraid to be the fastest country,” Dejus said, describing efforts to attract crypto business beyond licensing.

The proposal comes as Latvia changes how it taxes crypto investments. On Oct. 15, the country’s parliament passed legislation to tax withdrawals from crypto investment accounts once they exceed the amount deposited, rather than taxing each trade.

The law also introduces a one-time declaration process. Holders can settle past tax obligations by paying 10% of their declared assets’ market value at the end of 2026. Declarations can be filed from April 1 to May 31, 2027, with the tax due by July 23.

Dejus said the measure would help people who bought crypto years ago but lack records to prove what they paid.

The payment plan’s timing could depend on the next government. Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs’ United List won the Oct. 3 parliamentary election, and is expected to be renominated, but still needs coalition partners.

Latvia would not be the first government to accept crypto for taxes. Colorado started allowing crypto tax payments through PayPal in 2022, with funds converted into dollars.

Dejus did not name Latvia’s payment provider or say which cryptocurrencies would qualify to pay taxes.

#219. Crypto Firms Launch Quantum Alliance as 6 Million Bitcoin Sit Exposed

Crypto Firms Launch Quantum Alliance as 6 Million Bitcoin Sit Exposed

A group of crypto companies is trying to settle one of the industry’s murkiest questions: what it actually means for a blockchain network to be safe from quantum computers.

Executives from nine organizations launched the Quantum Alliance on Thursday, an open standards body that will set criteria for judging quantum-resistance claims and create compatibility rules for networks as they migrate to new cryptography.

The founding contributors span base-layer protocols, privacy networks, rollups, hardware wallets and security auditing, including Quantus, Postquant Labs, Midnight Foundation, Keystone, Abelian and security firm Hacken.

Modeled on the Internet Engineering Task Force, the Alliance said proposals will advance on public evidence and working implementations rather than corporate size or token holdings, and everything it produces will be published openly.

Its work will run in four groups: blockchain migration, post-quantum zero-knowledge systems, wallet security and cross-chain compatibility. “In the future, ‘post-quantum cryptography’ will just be called ‘cryptography’ and everything else will be in a museum,” said Quantus founder and CEO Christopher Smith.

The problem it’s tackling is that there’s no agreed definition of “quantum-ready,” and no standard way to test one. A network can call itself quantum-resistant today with no shared understanding of what the claim covers or what evidence should back it, a gap the Alliance was formed to close.

The stakes are familiar to anyone following the beat. Nearly every major blockchain secures accounts with elliptic-curve signatures, and once an account’s public key is exposed on the ledger, a sufficiently powerful quantum computer running Shor’s algorithm could theoretically reverse-engineer the private key and seize the funds.

The same cryptography guards stablecoin minting keys, bridges, oracles, and governance contracts, meaning one cracked privileged key could cascade across platforms. By the Alliance’s count, roughly 6.04 million BTC, about 30% of supply, sit quantum-exposed at rest.

The timelines keep tightening. The Quantum Alliance cites a cluster of recent forecasts pointing toward the late 2020s, including a model co-built by two Alliance contributors that flags March 2028 as an early window, and a Google Quantum AI study that slashed the estimated qubits needed to break Bitcoin’s cryptography to under 500,000.

No machine can do it yet. Google has also chipped away at key quantum bottlenecks, while figures like famed investor Kevin O’Leary have flagged the quantum threat as a catch hanging over Bitcoin’s long-term case.

The newly formed Quantum Alliance joins a widening industry scramble to address the risk. Coinbase recently urged Bitcoin developers to start the quantum migration now, suggesting preparations could take years. Meanwhile, a consortium backed by BlackRock, Strategy, and Coinbase has committed $15 million to the problem.

#220. Staggered Agency Filings Squeeze Stablecoin Issuers as Fed Misses Statutory Rulemaking Target

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

The statutory deadline for federal regulators to issue final payment stablecoin implementing rules passed on July 18, 2026, one year after the GENIUS Act’s enactment, with no primary regulator having finalized them.

The Federal Reserve did not publish its core issuer proposal until September 29, leaving the least runway before the Act’s January 18, 2027 outer date.

By waiting until late September to issue its Notices of Proposed Rulemaking, the Fed compressed the remaining timeline for final rule implementation. With no final rules issued in time, the January 18, 2027 date now governs by default.

Under Section 108 of the Guiding and Establishing National Innovation for U.S. Stablecoins (GENIUS) Act, the law takes effect on the earlier of January 18, 2027, or 120 days after final regulations are published by primary federal payment stablecoin regulators. With public comment windows for late-filing agencies remaining open well into the fourth quarter of 2026, regulators face a tight timeframe to review public feedback, coordinate interagency harmonization, and publish final rules before the statutory outer boundary arrives in 91 days.

As of publication, no primary regulator has issued a final rule across the execution timeline:

Because the Federal Reserve's public comment window under FR Doc. 2026-21104 remains open through November 30, 2026, the central bank cannot legally publish a finalized rule until December 2026 at the earliest.

Under the statutory 120-day transition clause in Section 108, any final rule published after September 20, 2026, fails to trigger an accelerated effective date ahead of January 18, 2027. Consequently, the default January 18 outer limit now serves as the primary target.

However, if the Fed and FDIC require additional weeks in December and January to reconcile public comments against OCC and Treasury frameworks, market participants will face a narrow window between final rule publication and mandatory compliance.

With the Treasury’s main issuance comment period closing today, October 19, attention shifts to the OCC’s imminent final rule release.

If the OCC publishes its final standards this month while the Fed continues accepting comments through late November, national banks and non-bank stablecoin issuers will navigate a staggered compliance environment. Issuers must monitor official Federal Register notices over the next 60 days to determine whether regulators achieve interagency alignment before the statutory deadline arrives.

#223. Ledger Reseller Attack Raises Questions About Hardware Wallet Supply Chains

A hardware wallet’s strongest cryptography offers little protection when an attacker can interfere with the device before its owner even switches it on. That is the uncomfortable lesson from the CryptoBilis case now facing Ledger customers in Southeast Asia.

TL;DR: Investigators have linked roughly $90 million or more in reported crypto losses to tampered wallet devices sold through a reseller channel. Ledger says its own systems were not compromised and has warned affected customers to move to newly generated recovery phrases.

The incident involves physical modifications rather than an ordinary phishing message. Reports describe implants that could capture a recovery phrase during device setup and transmit information to attackers. Once someone else possesses that phrase, they may be able to recreate the wallet without needing physical access to the device.

Ledger said confirmed cases involved wallets sold through CryptoBilis, a reseller listed in parts of Southeast Asia. It asked the reseller to stop sales and shipments while investigations continued. Customers who received affected devices were advised not to initialize them, and those already in use were told to secure funds with new credentials using trusted equipment.

The precise loss figure is still an estimate, and investigators have not publicly established a complete count of affected units. A device successfully passing an ordinary software or chip authenticity check should not automatically be interpreted as proof that no unauthorized physical component has been added elsewhere.

This attack is especially troubling because hardware wallets are bought to reduce dependence on third parties. Here, the supply chain itself became the point of exposure. For anyone buying a security device, provenance and physical integrity now deserve attention alongside firmware version and backup discipline.

#225. The Math Behind the $210 XRP Price Target

Ahmed Barakat is a journalist and copywriter based in Georgia with a growing focus on blockchain technology, DeFi, AI, privacy, digital assets, and fintech innovation.

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Using approximately 63.13 billion circulating XRP, multiplying the supply by a $210 price produces a value of about $13.26 trillion. A trader is turning a viral year-end call into a valuation claim on a scale rarely seen in any asset. With XRP trading under $1.35, the arithmetic-not Ripple’s expanding business alone-is the test the prediction has to pass.

Crypto Captain posted that XRP would reach $210 before the end of 2026. The claim drew pushback from XRP supporters, while the token was trading around $1.31, down from approximately $1.50 on October 6, a decline of roughly 13%.

BOOM💥💥 #XRP going to hit 210$ before end of year pic.twitter.com/9Zdgy8vWxs

The basic calculation is price multiplied by token supply. Using approximately 63.13 billion circulating XRP, $210 produces an implied XRP market cap of about $13.26 trillion; applying the same price to the full 100 billion maximum supply yields a fully diluted valuation of $21 trillion.

At roughly $1.31, the circulating-supply calculation implies a market value near $82.9 billion. Reaching $210 would require the token price to rise about 160-fold from that level, or 15,900%; this is not a routine extension of a bullish chart target but a claim that XRP would command a multi-trillion-dollar valuation.

Market capitalization is the circulating token count multiplied by the proposed price, not a forecast of how much capital would need to flow into XRP. But a target of that scale still requires a credible account of why buyers would value the outstanding supply at $210 per token.

The prediction arrived amid five Ripple-related institutional developments announced between October 6 and October 15. They covered brokerage, custody, tokenization, stablecoin settlement, and derivatives access-business lines that broaden Ripple’s institutional footprint.

Ripple Prime announced brokerage, clearing, and financing services for funds managed by Brevan Howard, an investment group with approximately $35 billion under management. But that figure describes the group’s assets, not capital committed to XRP.

Standard Chartered launched institutional custody for RLUSD issued on the XRP Ledger, while DriveWealth announced plans to integrate RLUSD on the ledger for settlement in Europe before a planned U.S. expansion. Meritz Securities partnered with Ripple to explore custody and tokenization, and Ripple Prime also launched institutional access to perpetual swaps across more than 100 reference markets.

Those developments matter to Ripple’s commercial reach, but their connection to XRP varies. Custody and planned settlement focused on RLUSD, while brokerage and financing arrangements do not establish how much XRP institutions need to hold or trade.

Even activity on the XRP Ledger does not translate one-for-one into XRP buying. The report cites a standard transaction fee of 0.00001 XRP, a small amount that means greater stablecoin use can generate ledger activity without requiring institutions to accumulate a comparable value of the native token.

The central investment question is whether Ripple’s business growth creates sustained demand for XRP itself. That depends on the role the token plays in institutional activity, not simply the number of partnerships or services associated with Ripple.

RLUSD custody gives institutions a way to hold Ripple’s stablecoin, and the stablecoin may also serve as collateral in institutional trading. These uses can expand Ripple’s financial infrastructure while leaving clients without a need to hold significant XRP balances.

A more direct demand channel would emerge if institutions used XRP to transfer value between currencies or provide trading liquidity. The scale of that activity-and the XRP balances participants retain to support it-would matter more to token valuation than the headline count of Ripple announcements.

The $210 call is a social-media assertion, while its implied valuation is clear: approximately $13.26 trillion on circulating supply and $21 trillion on the maximum supply. Those figures put the burden on the prediction to explain the demand and value capture that could support such a price.

The Web3 gaming industry is on the verge of a trading card game (TCG) boom that will attract venture funds and specialized ETFs in the coming years. This was stated by Kaj Leroy, known by the nickname Brad Punkhouse, a key developer of the XRP Ledger ecosystem and creator of the first major NFT collection built on XRP (XPUNKs).

In his assessment, the sector is shifting toward hybrid products at the intersection of the real world and blockchain, while the rest of the market is missing the trend.

"Trading cards have been around for over a century, so none of this is new. What's new is crypto catching on," the developer notes. In his view, the mass market needs tangible assets, because "normies want something easy to understand that they can hold in their hands."

Physical cards and the opening of real booster packs ensure long-term user engagement, building much stronger social bonds within communities than passively watching the price chart of PFP collections.

Kaj emphasizes that the complexity of developing a blockchain TCG acts as a natural defense against quick speculative projects: "The hardest part isn't the art or the hype. It's building a game that's actually fun and actually works." Balancing game mathematics requires significant resources, since a deck of 150 cards can generate more combinations than there are atoms in the observable universe.

Projects that started development early gain a strategic advantage in logistics and production, because "physical products take way more time than anything onchain."

As evidence of the trend, the creator of XPUNKs cites the figures of his own hybrid project, Fuzzycards, on the XRP Ledger, with an issuance of about 100,000 booster packs, where NFT holders burned them to have physical cards delivered. The process is already extending beyond the XRP ecosystem: the launch by Yuga Labs of Mudwater cards on the Solana blockchain, where each real pack in storage is tied to an NFT, confirms the institutionalization of the mechanic.

In the developer's estimate, the current situation in the sector is comparable to the rise of the Pokémon franchise in the 1990s. He predicts that the hype will inevitably spread to other major brands (Mario, Harry Potter, Tolkien's Middle-earth), which will move their TCGs onto onchain rails to control the secondary market.

Summing up the prospects of a sector hidden from most before the arrival of institutional capital, Kaj added: "Next comes TCG ETFs, hedge funds, VCs and much more. The market is about to get a lot bigger. We're early."

#228. The October 2025 Crypto ETF Wave Split: Commodity S-1s Advance, Staking Funds Stall

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

A full year after asset managers submitted a cluster of Form S-1 registration statements for non-traditional digital asset funds, the fate of the October 2025 filing surge has diverged into active commodity trusts, dormant applications, and targeted withdrawals.

Rather than signaling a complete collapse of institutional crypto product pipelines, SEC EDGAR database records point to an asset-class boundary. While plain spot commodity trusts, such as Canary’s XRP filing, remain in registration review, yield-bearing and liquid-staking products face direct operational hurdles.

This review examines four representative S-1 filings from the October 2025 wave. They show where those filings stand today but do not measure the full wave

Searching EDGAR records for crypto-related S-1 filings submitted during October 2025 reveals distinct legal statuses across key Central Index Key (CIK) entries:

Among the four filings above, two have filed S-1/A amendments (Canary on October 24, 2025, and T. Rowe Price on March 16, 2026), one has been withdrawn through Form RW, and one has posted no prospectus updates on its staking-enabled filings. Four filings cannot size the wider October 2025 wave.

The official Form RW submitted by VanEck on October 14, 2026, formally ended the only standalone liquid-staking trust sitting on the SEC docket. Signed by Vice President Matthew A. Babinsky, the filing confirmed that the trust never reached effective status, distributed no preliminary prospectuses, and sold zero shares.

The withdrawal underscores the ongoing friction between liquid staking protocols and regulated trust structures. Unlike spot Ethereum funds that hold native ETH directly, the VanEck fund sought to track Lido’s stETH token. This model exposed the trust to dual-layer fee structures, combining Lido's protocol fees with standard management expenses and added smart contract risks associated with derivative staking wrappers.

While plain spot funds eliminate derivative layers, liquid-staking trusts require additional custodial indemnification and liquidity management for unbonding periods. When combined with low retail demand for fee-heavy derivatives, these friction points make pure-play stETH wrappers economically unviable for major issuers.

Comparing VanEck’s Form RW against active altcoin filings suggests a market divide. Among the filings detailed above, Canary’s spot XRP trust and T. Rowe Price’s multi-asset trust have each filed S-1/A amendments, and REX’s plain commodity applications remain pending.

In contrast, funds attempting to pass on-chain yield to shareholders, such as Lido stETH or REX’s staking-enabled single-asset filings, have either stalled completely or withdrawn from EDGAR review. Until regulators establish a clear accounting framework for protocol-level staking rewards within public trusts, asset managers are prioritizing straightforward commodity exposure over complex yield-generating wrappers.

For institutional market participants, inspecting EDGAR full-text CIK records provides an unfiltered view of which product structures are moving forward.

#229. Cysic crypto bridge halted after unauthorized mint of 10M CYS

Cysic said the incident was limited to bridge message processing and minting and did not affect the mainnet or other operational systems.

Cysic Foundation is investigating an unauthorized issuance on BNB Smart Chain and said the mint size alone does not establish the incident’s dollar impact.

The foundation said in a Sunday X incident report that its cross-chain bridge was suspended after an attacker exploited a processing flaw to mint 10 million CYS on BNB Smart Chain on Saturday, with preliminary findings pointing to unauthorized access to a database supporting the bridge.

The mint occurred at 12:31:38 UTC on Oct. 17, and Cysic added the recipient address to the token contract’s blacklist at 13:47:52 UTC. About 2.8 million CYS remained at that address, with transfers restricted. There are roughly 160.8 million tokens in circulation, according to CoinMarketCap data.

CYS coordinates incentives for users, compute providers, governance participants and contributors in Cysic’s network, according to the project’s tokenomics documentation.

Cysic said the incident was limited to bridge message processing and minting and did not affect the mainnet or other operational systems. “The incident did not result in the theft or unauthorized transfer of existing CYS or other assets held in user wallets,” it said.

The post said the number minted does not establish the final dollar loss; token transfers, swaps and actual losses remain under review. Cysic has hired an unnamed security firm and plans to publish a follow-up report after the current investigation phase.

#230. MARA-Linked Wallets Send 1,000 Bitcoin To Exchanges, But A Sale Is Unconfirmed

Addresses associated by on-chain analysts with miner MARA Holdings have sent approximately 1,000 BTC to Binance and Gate over five days, putting the company’s treasury movements back in focus.

TL;DR: Lookonchain-linked analysis values the transfers at about $82.8 million. Exchange deposits can precede selling, but the transfers do not establish that MARA sold the coins.

The timing comes during a difficult period for mining economics, with companies balancing Bitcoin holdings against operating costs and competing investment demands. MARA has previously been watched closely because of the size of its Bitcoin treasury and its willingness to use holdings as part of a broader financing strategy.

There is a common trap in interpreting these blockchain alerts. An analytics label may link an address to a corporation or mining operation, but an exchange-bound transaction is not the same as an executed spot sale. Coins can also be transferred for custody, collateral, trading inventory or other operational reasons. Determining the actual transaction purpose requires more than knowing the destination wallet.

The reported 1,000 BTC arrived at the exchanges over several days rather than through one single transfer on Monday morning. Treating the full amount as an immediate market sell order would therefore exaggerate both timing and certainty.

What matters next is whether MARA provides a treasury update, or whether more detailed on-chain evidence clarifies how the funds were used. Until then, the movement is significant enough to monitor but insufficient to conclude that another liquidation has taken place.

In a market quick to trade on wallet labels, that distinction is worth keeping.

#231. Chinese Startup StepFun Launches a Phone Built Around an AI Agent, Not Apps

Chinese Startup StepFun Launches a Phone Built Around an AI Agent, Not Apps

StepFun, a Chinese AI startup backed by Tencent, launched the STEPX Neo, a phone whose AI agent is built into the operating system itself instead of sitting in an app.

The operating system is the core software that runs a phone, like iOS or Android. Pre-orders opened that evening at 3,999 yuan, about $560, with a first sales event on Oct. 16.

Instead of opening a ride-hailing app, typing an address and picking a car, you tell the phone where you want to go, and its agent—software that takes a goal and carries it out on its own—handles the remaining steps.

StepFun told the launch audience that in the agent era AI is no longer an add-on to a smartphone but the product itself.

StepFun first showed the agent, the operating system, and the STEPX brand in Shanghai on July 13, without a price or sales date. The company said at the time that conventional smartphone software was never built for autonomous task execution.

Siri and Gemini are assistants that live inside iOS and Android. StepFun says its Step AOS 1.0 was instead built from scratch for the agent, with long-term memory, task scheduling, and security controls in the base layer. The company describes the system as a mix of Android, Linux, and real-time operating system components.

Step AOS breaks phone functions such as messaging, apps, files and settings into small blocks the agent can call directly, using Model Context Protocol, or MCP, a shared standard that lets AI programs plug into other software. Users get two entrances: the familiar app grid and a separate space for the agent.

The agent, called Amoo, keeps one memory for the user's facts, habits, and preferences and another for what it has learned about carrying out tasks. Simple commands like setting an alarm run on a small model inside the phone, some of them offline, while harder requests that span several apps go to a larger model in the cloud. A second MiniLED screen on the back shows what Amoo is doing.

Nearly 100 companies and products, including Alipay, Tencent, Ctrip, Didi and Meituan, have signed on to Amoo, and payments, travel bookings and content creation are still completed by their own platforms. That is StepFun's alternative to the screen-reading and simulated-click approach Doubao used.

StepFun, founded in 2023 by former Microsoft vice president Jiang Daxin, builds its own large language model, or LLM, the kind of AI system behind ChatGPT. Its flagship, Step 5 Preview, arrived in September with 600 billion parameters, the internal numbers a model adjusts while training, of which 27 billion are active at a time.

Step 5 Preview can take in up to 1 million tokens, the chunks of text AI services count and bill by, at once. The smaller Step 3.5 Flash, released earlier this year, is open-source under an Apache 2.0 license.

The 3,999-yuan price includes 12 months of the STEPX Token Plan, which provides 100 billion tokens a month, and StepFun has not said what the AI costs after the first year.

#233. Stablecoin supply stalls, but payments jump 45% as Visa, Mastercard and Stripe connect crypto to cash

Stablecoin supply has barely budged this year, but the digital dollars already in circulation are doing more work in payments, according to a fresh report from blockchain analytics firm Allium.

Stablecoin payments are growing at a rapid pace, reaching $482 billion in the first nine months of 2026, up 45% from a year earlier, the report found.

That growth contrasts with the broader stablecoin market. The total value of stablecoins — cryptocurrencies tied to fiat currencies such as the U.S. dollar — in circulation stood at about $305 billion at the end of September, up a meager 0.4% since the start of the year, according to the report.

The number of payments grew even more, jumping 71% to over 1 billion, the report said, suggesting that stablecoins are changing hands more often without much new supply entering the market.

Stablecoin-linked cards showed some of the fastest growth. Spending measured by Allium reached $3.9 billion through September, ten times the amount a year earlier. Small purchases — under $50 — accounted for 84% of the increase in card transactions.

Three announcements earlier this week offered a glimpse of how stablecoins are becoming increasingly part of global payments.

Mastercard (MA) introduced Thursday its Global Money Platform with BVNK, the stablecoin infrastructure firm it acquired in August. The service combines traditional currency accounts, stablecoin balances, conversions, card spending and bank payouts through one connection.

Banks and fintechs can use the platform to offer accounts that hold both fiat currencies and stablecoins, the firm said. Payments firms Nuvei and Marqeta are among the first customers integrating that service.

Stripe, meanwhile, is working with Plasma XPL$0.07801, a blockchain-based financial services firm, on cards that support balances in dollars, euros, Brazilian reais, Mexican pesos and Colombian pesos, alongside eligible stablecoins.

The companies said they plan to let customers spend from the balance that matches their purchase, cutting unnecessary currency conversions. Stripe's expanded card infrastructure covers more than 30 countries, with plans to reach over 100 by next year.

Read more: Stripe to expand stablecoin cards to over 100 countries by the end of the year

And Visa (V) said it is bringing stablecoins into the funding side of international payments.

The company said Inyo Global, a payment orchestration firm for fintech, money transmitter, banks, became the first provider to put Visa Direct's stablecoin prefunding service into commercial use. Payment firms can use Circle's (CRCL) dollar stablecoin USDC USDC$1.0002 to fund cross-border payouts in nearly real-time instead of waiting for traditional banking windows, while recipients can still receive money through conventional payment channels.

That rapid growth of stablecoin payments comes with some caveats. Of $97.9 trillion in raw stablecoin transfers through September, Allium classified just $2.4 trillion, or 2.5%, as end-user activity after filtering out exchange, decentralized finance and automated transactions. Its $482 billion payments estimate comes from that smaller pool, the report said.

Stablecoin cards also remain a tiny fraction of conventional payments. Allium estimated that second-quarter spending through those cards amounted to just 0.03% of Visa's $4 trillion in payment volume.

For payment companies, that leaves a large market to pursue. Nuvei CEO Phil Fayer, whose company is among the first to integrate Mastercard's new platform, said stablecoins are becoming part of how businesses move money across borders and currencies.

"The future of global commerce depends on money moving as freely as the businesses and consumers it serves, across borders, currencies and increasingly, between traditional and digital forms of money," Fayer said.

The recent efforts by Mastercard, Stripe and Visa to incorporate stablecoins on blockchain rails reinforce that trend. Companies increasingly want stablecoins integrated into their existing financial operations, instead of running separate systems for digital assets, according to Patrick Mollard, co-founder and CEO of Paris-based Fipto, a stablecoin-powered business payments firm.

“The distinction between 'traditional' and 'digital' money is less important than giving businesses the ability to use whichever rail makes most sense for a particular payment or treasury operation,” he said in a note shared with CoinDesk.

“Businesses don't want separate crypto infrastructure sitting alongside their existing financial operations,” Mollard said. “They want to move between fiat and stablecoins within the same payments and treasury environment.”

#234. Cardano Is One Upgrade Away From Being Fully Complete, Hoskinson Declares — Will It Be Enough To Ignite ADA’s Price?

Cardano could be on the brink of a major milestone, with founder Charles Hoskinson declaring that the blockchain is just one upgrade away from being “finished” in the sense of being fully built — a bold claim that raises a tantalizing question for ADA investors: could this final push finally unlock the price momentum they have been waiting for?

IOG Co-Founder and CEO Charles Hoskinson has weighed in on whether the blockchain is fully developed. During an exchange on X, a user asked whether Cardano was fully developed overall. Hoskinson’s response pointed to one key milestone still ahead before the network can be considered complete: the upcoming Leios upgrade.

“After Leios, yes. It has everything I wanted to do,” Hoskinson replied. He went on to highlight Cardano’s core features, including decentralized consensus, on-chain governance, the extended UTXO (eUTXO) model, Plutus smart contracts, scalability, security, formal verification, and support for multiple independent node implementations. He also pointed to the network’s capacity for continued improvement and its millions of ADA holders as part of his vision.

Leios is designed to significantly improve Cardano’s transaction capacity and processing speed while preserving its decentralization and security. The upgrade aims to raise throughput from an estimated 5–10 transactions per second (TPS) to around 100 TPS, with a longer-term goal of reaching 1,000 TPS or more. However, achieving those figures will depend on further testing, validation, and network parameter settings.

That said, Leios is far more than a routine network upgrade. It calls for a major overhaul of Cardano’s existing architecture, a complex undertaking that could fundamentally change how the blockchain handles transactions and pave the way for a dramatic leap in performance.

Hoskinson also hinted at an ambitious new initiative involving Midnight, Cardano’s privacy-focused partner blockchain designed to help decentralized applications protect sensitive data while meeting regulatory compliance requirements.

According to the Cardano creator, he is close to completing the conceptual design of an innovation he believes could tackle some of the crypto industry’s biggest challenges. He even described the still-unrevealed concept as the “magnum opus” of his career, hinting at what he considers his most significant achievement yet.

For ADA, Leios and Midnight could prove to be a powerful combination. Faster transactions paired with privacy-focused infrastructure could draw more developers, projects, and users into Cardano’s ecosystem, potentially giving ADA’s long-term growth story fresh momentum. But the real test is whether these upgrades translate into meaningful adoption and stronger demand for the token. Without that, even major technical breakthroughs may struggle to deliver a lasting price rally for the 15th largest cryptocurrency.

#236. Hedera's SEC Comment: Codify March Asset Types in Rule 400

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

The Securities and Exchange Commission’s public comment window for Proposed Regulation Crypto Assets (File No. S7-2026-27) closes on October 20, 2026.

Published in the Federal Register as Document 2026-17183 (91 FR 54510) and issued under SEC Release No. 33-11434, the 146-page regulatory framework establishes conditional registration exemptions and a safe harbor for digital asset offerings.

Rather than debating generic timelines, public comment letters filed on the official SEC comment docket for S7-2026-27 focus on specific operational mechanics, contrasting exemption caps against asset definitions.

In a comment letter dated October 7, 2026, Hedera Hashgraph, LLC (signed by Chief Policy Officer Nilmini Rubin and General Counsel Gregory Schneider) pressed the Commission on a central omission in proposed Rule 400. Hedera argued that while Regulation Crypto Assets attempts to codify when a token dissociates from an investment contract, the proposal fails to explicitly incorporate the asset-type distinctions established in the SEC’s March 2026 Interpretation.

Specifically, Hedera urged regulators to formally adopt clear boundaries between digital commodities and other asset classes within Rule 400. Without explicitly codifying these asset types, Hedera warned that projects clearing essential managerial milestones under the Rule 400(a) safe harbor could still face regulatory ambiguity regarding secondary market transactions.

To replace conceptual flowcharts, the regulatory framework divides token lifecycle exemptions into three specific statutory pathways:

A second major point of friction across recent filings centers on the transactional limits governing proposed registration exemptions.

Under proposed Rule 200, the $5 million startup exemption limit counts all token distributions, including developer grants, community airdrops, and liquidity incentives. Comment letters on the docket argue that a cumulative $5 million ceiling over four years imposes severe operational constraints on early-stage protocol development.

Conversely, while Tier 2 of the fundraising exemption provides a $75 million ceiling, the associated compliance costs mirror those of traditional public offerings. Other letters contend that this leaves a gap between small developer grants and large-scale token distributions, urging the Commission to raise the startup threshold or allow recurrent annual raises.

Not every letter supports the framework. Comment letters filed in October 2026 challenge the legal foundation of proposed Rule 400, arguing that the SEC lacks statutory authority under Section 2(a)(1) of the Securities Act to grant a conditional safe harbor that unilaterally terminates an asset’s status as part of an investment contract

Other letters contend that existing frameworks, namely Regulation D and Regulation A, already provide lawful pathways for capital formation, rendering a bespoke Regulation Crypto Assets unnecessary.

These arguments are summarized from the docket. The individual letters, linked on the docket page, give the filers’ identities and exact wording.

As the SEC evaluates public submissions across its 154 specific inquiries, the docket highlights a divide between letters like Hedera’s, which ask for explicit asset classification, and letters that ask the SEC to drop the safe harbor.

Market participants tracking ongoing administrative law and digital asset policy can view the updates and stay informed. Whether the agency adjusts proposed Rule 400 thresholds or maintains the $5 million cap, the official filings under SEC File No. S7-2026-27 establish the foundation for US crypto capital formation.

#237. Chinese suspect in $75M international crime network arrested in Bangkok

Police alleged the suspect was involved in cryptocurrency and foreign-currency exchanges for criminal groups across more than 133 accounts.

Thai police arrested a 37-year-old Chinese man wanted by authorities in China for alleged involvement in an international crime network and money laundering.

Investigators said the network handled more than 500 million yuan ($75 million) in transactions, Thai media Khaosod English reported in a post on X on Saturday.

Police alleged the suspect was involved in cryptocurrency and foreign-currency exchanges for criminal groups across more than 133 accounts.

They also claimed that he was involved in arranging visas for members of international crime groups linked to other money-laundering cases.

Investigators said he attempted to evade arrest by using forged documents to report his residence and changing vehicle registration plates before police found him in a luxury house in Bangkok.

His Thai visa had expired more than three years ago, so he will face legal proceedings before authorities coordinate his return to China to face the outstanding warrant.

#240. Claude Traces NIST Cryptography Seeds To An Old Random-Number Generator

An unusual piece of cryptography history has gained an answer. Anthropic says Claude reconstructed how the original seed values behind several widely used NIST elliptic curves were generated, resolving a question that had attracted suspicion for more than two decades.

TL;DR: Claude identified a process involving the C library’s lrand48 generator and Unix timestamps. Anthropic stresses that the research does not reveal an attack on P-256 or other affected curves.

The seeds have mattered because the standards published their values without a convincing public account of how the numbers were chosen. The U.S. National Security Agency had supplied them, leaving generations of researchers to ask whether a secret selection method could hide some mathematical advantage.

Anthropic reports that a model worked backward from the published values and found an ordinary pseudorandom generation procedure. In the case of P-256, it took 1,842 iterations through candidate outputs to reproduce the standardized seed. The work also examined P-192, P-224, P-384 and P-521.

This is interesting to crypto users because elliptic-curve signatures underpin many kinds of account security, including passkeys and hardware-backed authentication. Explaining the provenance of parameters can improve confidence in the standards without changing the mathematics used by existing products.

There is a crucial limit to the story: recovering the seed-generation history is not the same as breaking a private key, proving the curve has a vulnerability or establishing that every implementation is safe. Anthropic itself says there is no urgent corrective action to take.

The headline is less about AI defeating encryption than AI helping researchers reconstruct a forgotten design decision. In cryptography, knowing why numbers look the way they do can be almost as valuable as knowing that the calculations work.

Written by the News Desk and edited by Samuel Rae.

#242. Bitcoin’s $100,000 year-end hope divides analysts as inflation clouds outlook

Bitcoin BTC$82,836.58 could reclaim $100,000 before year-end as institutional adoption and demand for hard assets overcome near-term economic uncertainty, according to crypto asset manager Bitwise, offering a more bullish outlook than traders who expect inflation and elevated interest rates to constrain gains.

The forecasts highlight a divide over timing. Analysts see longer-term support from institutional investment, regulatory progress and concerns about government debt, but disagree on whether those forces can drive a breakout before the end of 2026.

Ryan Rasmussen, head of research at Bitwise, expects bitcoin to emerge from the coming weeks’ uncertainty at a higher valuation.

“We believe bitcoin ends the year higher, potentially above $100,000,” Rasmussen told CoinDesk.

He identified three longer-term drivers: institutional buying through exchange-traded funds (ETFs) and corporate purchases; demand for hard assets amid inflation, rising debt and currency debasement; and clearer regulation that reduces the perceived risk of owning crypto.

“In our view, these tailwinds significantly outweigh the potential headwinds,” he said.

Rasmussen nevertheless expects volatility around a possible late-October Federal Reserve rate increase and November’s U.S. midterm elections. A breakout would be difficult in that environment, he said, although the uncertainty could create an opportunity for investors to build positions.

Adam Morgan McCarthy, head of research at LO:TECH, a London-based crypto trading and market data firm, is more cautious. His base case is an $85,000–$95,000 trading range into year-end.

“Macro has gone against Bitcoin all year, with the Fed hiking in September and a December hike priced at roughly 75%,” McCarthy said. “This will continue to weigh on bitcoin.”

The Fed raised its benchmark rate by a quarter percentage point in September. Inflation figures released Oct. 14 complicated the outlook: consumer prices rose 0.6% from the previous month, while core prices increased 0.3%. Gasoline accounted for more than half of the headline increase.

McCarthy said a return above $100,000 would require expectations for a December hike to give way to a pause, supported by easing oil prices and inflation.

James Butterfill, head of research at CoinShares, sees a similar tension between persistent inflation and weakening employment. Cooling prices would give the Fed more room to respond to labor-market weakness; further inflation pressure could keep policy restrictive and weigh on bitcoin.

The world’s largest cryptocurrency was trading around $81,500 at publication time.

Luca Invernizzi, senior derivatives trader at Laser Digital, Nomura’s crypto subsidiary, expects bitcoin to remain largely a macro trade into year-end, taking its direction from longer-dated Treasury yields.

He described the rebound from summer lows as unconvincing, citing thin volumes, fading ETF inflows and slowing corporate buying.

Positioning offers more encouragement. Leverage has largely been flushed out of bitcoin, with much of the speculative excess moving into altcoins, Invernizzi said.

McCarthy also sees fewer crowded bullish positions that could unravel. Funding rates, payments between perpetual futures traders, are at or below zero, while August’s rally was driven by traders closing bearish bets rather than adding new bullish positions.

That reduces the fuel for forced selling and leaves room for another squeeze higher.

“A clean break above $90K for BTC could trigger another round of short covering,” Invernizzi said.

With implied volatility back near its lows and options pricing still tilted toward downside protection, he sees upside calls as an attractive way to position for a rally without chasing bitcoin in the spot market.

The broader industry’s recovery provides another source of optimism.

In a research note to clients earlier this week authored by Peter Christiansen, Citi (C) said total crypto market capitalization rose from roughly $2.1 trillion to nearly $3 trillion during the third quarter. Institutional ETF flows turned positive, while activity across exchanges, stablecoins and digital asset infrastructure improved.

The bank also sees investors increasingly looking beyond crypto prices toward businesses supporting tokenization, custody, stablecoins and settlement. Regulatory progress continues despite the Clarity Act’s failure to advance, Citi said.

Butterfill cautioned that investment-product flows have since slowed following $11.1 billion of inflows since mid-July. He views that as uncertainty rather than deteriorating bitcoin fundamentals, but said sustained gains require renewed buying.

Like Rasmussen, he sees concerns about government finances as a potential longer-term source of demand. Higher Treasury yields typically hurt bitcoin by tightening financial conditions, but that relationship could shift if investors increasingly interpret those yields as compensation for fiscal risk.

“Our bias is towards higher prices over the medium term, but we would want to see the fiscal argument translate into sustained allocations before expecting a decisive breakout,” Butterfill said.

Rasmussen is more confident those forces will translate into gains sooner.

“Once the market churns through this period, we expect bitcoin to rerate significantly higher,” he said.
