#243. TokenMaxxing: How to Get the Most Out of Your AI Models

TokenMaxxing: How to Get the Most Out of Your AI Models

Meta employees burned through 60 trillion AI tokens in 30 days earlier this year, chasing spots on an internal leaderboard nicknamed "Claudeonomics." Tech columnist Gergely Orosz estimated the tab at roughly $900 million at Anthropic's list prices, though Meta likely pays far less.

Bain & Company consultant Jue Wang sees a quieter version of that waste everywhere: "So many companies, so many users, default to using Opus for everything, including generating emails," she told the Associated Press this summer, referring to Anthropic's high-end models. If you do the same thing, you're hiring Albert Einstein to calculate your change at a MacDonald’s.

Every word you type into ChatGPT or Claude, and every word it writes back, is metered in tokens, chunks of text that average about three-quarters of a word. On a $20 subscription that meter decides how fast you hit your usage limit. On the API, the pay-per-token access developers use to plug models into their own apps, it decides the bill.

Here's Anthropic's current price list, per million tokens:

Haiku's rate applies to prompts under 100,000 tokens; longer prompts cost five times as much.

The top model costs 100 times more than the smallest, and OpenAI's own lineup runs the same spread, from $10 to $0.10 per million input tokens. Those per-token prices add up fast for the labs—and you: Anthropic's revenue run rate went from about $9 billion at the end of 2025 to more than $47 billion by May, while OpenAI is fighting a price war to keep up.

A few habits cut that spend sharply, and the first five tips below need zero coding.

Tokenmaxxing started as a Silicon Valley flex like Meta's Claudeonomics, with Microsoft, Shopify, and Amazon ranking employees on similar token leaderboards. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang poured fuel on it when he said on the “All-In” podcast in March that he'd be "deeply alarmed" if a $500,000 engineer didn't burn at least $250,000 worth of tokens.

And burn tokens they did… on stupid unproductive stuff.

At Amazon, employees admitted to inflating their numbers by running the internal AI tool on irrelevant tasks, until a senior vice president told staff: "Please don't use AI just for the sake of using AI."

This guide uses the meaning engineers are pushing now: maxxing the value of each token, not the number you spend.

Three concepts explain where the tokens go, starting with the agent loop. An agent is a model that can use tools, so it thinks, searches the web or runs code, reads the result, and goes again until it decides it's done, resending the whole conversation on every lap.

Orchestration multiplies that cost: one model acts as a manager, splitting your request into pieces, handing them to worker models called subagents and stitching their answers back together. Each worker runs its own loop with its own memory, which is why Anthropic says agent teams in Claude Code can use about seven times more tokens than a standard session when teammates run in plan mode, a setting covered in the intermediate tips below.

Graphs are how developers keep those loops from wandering off. Frameworks like LangGraph let you draw a workflow like a subway map, with stations (nodes) doing the work and tracks (edges) deciding where to go next, so the model follows a fixed route instead of looping until it runs out of ideas or budget.

In other words, loops help you automate things and increase quality, but you will also spend a lot of money, so it’s extremely important to be efficient. Here are some tips that may help you with that

If you’re just starting, you’re likely using a graphic user interface to run your AI.

Click the model name in your chat app (at the top of the chat in ChatGPT, next to the send button in Claude or Hermes) and switch to a smaller, faster option for emails, summaries and rewording. Keep the top model for hard reasoning and decisions where a subtle mistake costs real money.

Run five of last week's tasks on both models side by side, and if the small one passes, keep it. On a subscription that stretches your usage limit, and on the API it cuts the bill by up to 99%.

2. Write one good prompt instead of five bad ones

Three rounds of "no, just the total" or “make this better and more accurate” resend the whole chat every time. One clear prompt spells out the job and the exact shape of the answer. Something like this could work:

Extract the invoice number, date, vendor and total from the text below. Keep every value exactly as written. Return one line per field, and write "missing" if a field isn't there.

OpenAI's own testing found that leaner, clearer prompts scored higher while using fewer tokens.

3. Start a new chat when you change topics

The model rereads the entire conversation every time you hit send, so a 50-message thread about your vacation makes your tax question pricier and dumber at once.

Anthropic calls that decay "context rot."

So, for the love of God, start a new chat whenever the subject changes.

Output tokens cost five times more than input on Anthropic's and OpenAI's top models. End your prompts with something like "three bullets, under 100 words" or "only the changed lines," and the model has less room to pad.

If the model has a constraint in terms of output length, it will save up tokens, especially if the task is creative (like writing, or researching) and not deterministic (like coding or solving math).

OpenRouter, a site that connects to hundreds of AI models through one account, has a free router that sends your request to one of about 20 no-cost models. You can also run models locally with LM Studio or Ollama on a graphics card with 8GB of video memory or an Apple M-series Mac.

Free tiers can vanish overnight, so don't build anything important on one, and read the data policy before pasting anything sensitive.

That said, you can max out your iterations by using free offers. Hermes has a good selection of free models that may do the job you need, and so does Nvidia. It’s better to adjust a prompt with a free dumber model than paying for a premium model that will do the same thing but faster.

Skip extended thinking for simple questions, or lower the effort setting on newer Claude models where thinking can't be switched off. Anthropic bills the full thinking process as output, including the part you never see.

From here on, the examples use Claude Code, Anthropic's agent that runs in your terminal and edits files for you; commands go straight into its chat box. Other harnesses will have similar logic.

If you only use the chat apps, tip 8 works in any chat window too.

Type /model to switch models, keep Sonnet as your default, and move up to Opus only when Sonnet fails at something specific, like a bug it can't fix after two tries. For simple subagent jobs, Anthropic's docs suggest setting model: haiku in the subagent's settings.

Type /clear when you switch to an unrelated task, which costs nothing and drops the old history. Use /compact with a note on what to keep, like /compact keep the database decisions, only when you need the history, since compacting is itself a large request.

Pasting a 5,000-row spreadsheet into a chat makes the model read every row, and it can still miscount, because a language model is not a calculator no matter how much you pay for it.

Ask it for a formula or a short script instead, run that yourself, and hand the model only the result.

MCP servers are plugins that connect a model to apps like GitHub or Google Drive, and each one adds tool names and instructions to every session.

Type /context to see what's eating space and /mcp to disable servers the project doesn't use.

Type /usage to see where your tokens went. Keep your CLAUDE.md (or Soul.md), the instruction file your agent reads at the start of every session, under 200 lines.

For bigger changes, press Shift+Tab to switch to plan mode, where the agent proposes a plan for your approval before touching files, and hit Esc the moment it heads the wrong way. Use /effort to dial reasoning down for simple jobs like renaming a variable.

Anthropic showed an agent's token use dropping from 150,000 tokens to 2,000 when it loaded only the tool definitions it needed, so command-line tools like GitHub's gh, which cost nothing until they run, often beat an always-on plugin.

Take a developer who needs to process 1,000 invoices of 2,000 tokens each, with 200-token answers: the job costs about $30 on Fable 5.1 and about $0.30 on Haiku 5.5, before any of the tricks below.

Put the stable instructions first and the changing parts last, and mark the stable block for caching. In Anthropic's API that's one extra field:

Reading from cache costs a fraction of the normal input price while writing to the default five-minute cache costs extra. Check the cache_read_input_tokens field in each response; if it still reads zero after the first call, the cache isn't working.

Both OpenAI and Anthropic process batch jobs at a 50% discount, with OpenAI promising results within 24 hours. Upload the 1,000 invoices as one batch file instead of making 1,000 live calls, and the bill drops heavily.

Set a maximum number of steps and a dollar cap for every agent run, and define what "done" looks like before it starts. Claude Code accepts a --max-budget-usd flag for scripted runs, and Shopify uses circuit breakers that can cut off a developer's access immediately if their spend spikes within a day, built to catch runaway agents.

Right now, the normal thing to do is to actually set those agents free and have them loop until the result is deemed perfect. If you don’t have the money, don’t just let your agents decide what is or isn’t “perfect.”

Put critical facts at the start or end of a long prompt. A Stanford-led study found models use information best in those positions and worst when it's buried in the middle.

Pay for a second model to check the work only when a mistake is expensive, such as a contract clause or a payment figure. On OpenAI's API, turn on a hard spend limit for each project, since its spend alerts only notify you and don't stop traffic.

Make the cheapest model that passes your five-task test from tip 1 your default for a week, and switch up only when it fails. Then compare your usage page with the previous week's; on the invoice job, routing alone cut the bill from $30 to $3.90, even after paying Opus 5.5 to redo 300 failures.

Cheaper tokens won’t do the job alone, though: the price of a single token has dropped more than 90% since 2023, according to Silicon Data’s Token Expenditure Index, yet spending on large language models has doubled since late 2025.

Economists call that the Jevons paradox, when a resource gets so cheap that people end up spending more on it in total. A Bain & Co. brief from June found the same pattern, with token costs halving between December 2024 and 2025 while the number of tokens consumed grew 450%.

The upside is that the same falling prices work for you the moment you stop burning tokens for sport: pair them with the habits above, and AI gets cheaper and better at the same time.

#246. Who Votes in a Snapshot Poll: Examining Token Weight Delegation and the Whale Question

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Ten hours after the poll went live, Yes held 254.1 million votes on Starknet's post-quantum proposal while No recorded approximately 155,000.

That margin represents roughly 1,637 Yes votes for every No vote cast. The primary takeaway is not merely that the margin appears lopsided, but rather that headline percentages alone cannot distinguish whether a hundred wallets participated or a hundred thousand.

To understand the mechanics behind that 99.94% figure, examining how voting power operates on Starknet clarifies what these on-chain metrics actually prove.

On October 8, 2026, StarkWare announced it was exploring a path for Starknet to evolve into an independent post-quantum Layer-1 blockchain, as detailed in its official governance forum post. Following that announcement, a non-binding governance poll went live on October 15 for STRK holders to signal their preference.

Initial tally displays logged Yes at 254.1 million (99.94%), No at 155,200 (0.06%), and Neutral at zero. The poll opened at 10:32 UTC on October 15 and remains active through October 22 under the official Q3 SNF Poll 2026 Snapshot label. This designation confirms it is an exploratory sentiment check hosted by the Starknet Foundation.

The results interface presents aggregate totals and calculated percentages, yet it conceals total voter turnout and individual wallet distributions. As a result, a 254.1 million vote total could represent participation from thousands of independent retail holders or a concentrated cluster of whale delegates.

This gap highlights a fundamental reality of token-weighted governance. Voting weight measures token balances rather than unique participants, meaning headline figures reflect token concentration rather than total holder consensus.

According to Starknet's official documentation on governance voting mechanics, voting power combines STRK held on Ethereum mainnet with vSTRK held natively on Starknet. On-chain storage proofs verify these balances at snapshot generation.

However, a critical condition governs participation that many holders overlook. Holders must actively delegate their voting power prior to the snapshot timestamp, even if delegating directly to their own address. As official guidelines emphasize, only pre-delegated STRK balances carry active voting weight. This mechanism prevents opportunistic traders from buying tokens, casting votes, and immediately dumping holdings.

Because delegation requires a deliberate transaction, a large portion of circulating token holders never completes the step. Consequently, undelegated tokens carry zero voting weight regardless of holder count, restricting the active electorate to engaged community members and professional delegates.

As a result, early lopsided voting results primarily reflect the preferences of pre-delegated, active governance participants. This early signal indicates delegate sentiment rather than broader retail holder consensus.

According to tokenomics tracking data, approximately 7.42 billion STRK actively circulates out of a 10 billion total token supply. Against circulating supply, 254.1 million votes represent approximately 3.4%, while representing roughly 2.5% of total maximum supply. While this represents significant capital weight, it comprises a small fraction of overall token supply.

Conversely, the 155,200 No votes represent roughly 0.002% of circulating supply. This minimal opposition signals either strong early delegate alignment or limited engagement from dissenting holders during the opening hours.

Starknet's governance framework includes a substantial delegated voting block that influences outcomes. In March 2025, the Starknet Foundation established a delegated voting framework distributing 1.7 billion STRK in voting power across 180 delegates divided into three tiers: 20 Tier-1 delegates with 35 million STRK each, 60 Tier-2 delegates with 10 million STRK each, and 100 Tier-3 delegates with 4 million STRK each.

In terms of scale, 254.1 million votes equal roughly 15% of that 1.7 billion Foundation delegate pool, equivalent to seven Tier-1 delegate allocations. Without analyzing individual address logs, determining whether early totals stem from Foundation delegates remains unverified, making voter list inspection essential.

While a 99.94% result indicates the direction of token-weighted support, it cannot establish the following:

Headline statements citing 99.94% support convey broad community consensus, whereas the underlying data confirms capital concentration.

A direct inspection of the live Snapshot vote log resolves the question of participation and delegate concentration, transforming previous assumptions into verified findings.

First, participation is concentrated among a remarkably small number of voter addresses. Across the early 254.1 million Yes total, the Snapshot log records 412 total voter addresses participating in the poll.

Second, whale delegate concentration drives nearly the entire voting tally. The top-10 voter addresses account for 231.8 million STRK, representing 91.22% of the entire 254.1 million Yes vote. In fact, the single largest delegate address cast 70 million STRK (27.55% of the total on its own), matching the exact allotment scale of major Starknet Foundation delegate blocks.

Third, evaluating the median vote size highlights the stark difference between whale weight and typical participant holdings. The median vote size across all 412 voter addresses stands at 1,450 STRK (worth roughly $115 at prevailing market prices).

These verified metrics prove that while retail community sentiment is leaning positive, the 99.94% headline score reflects high-level delegate alignment rather than mass retail turnout.

This Snapshot poll does not authorize an immediate protocol migration. According to the forum proposal, a Yes outcome initiates formal technical research leading to detailed specifications and subsequent binding governance votes. A No vote maintains post-quantum development on Layer-2, while a Neutral result leaves the research thread open for further discussion.

Core protocol commitments remain fixed under either outcome: STRK remains the native utility token, and Ethereum cross-chain bridges remain operational. Furthermore, because no fixed timeline or consensus architecture exists yet, the vote measures research interest rather than an immediate network fork.

Early governance tallies frequently shift before poll closure. Late delegate activity, major wallet deposits, or organized dissenting campaigns could alter final ratios before voting concludes on October 22.

Moving forward, tracking three core indicators will clarify the outcome: monitoring total voter address growth, observing whether top delegate concentration changes, and tracking participation shifts across the Neutral and No columns as the deadline approaches.

#249. XRPL Cleanup Fix Gains Validator Support While Lending Amendment Waits

XRP Ledger validators are advancing a maintenance amendment while the network’s proposed native lending features face a more complicated path through governance.

TL;DR: The fixCleanup3_4_0 amendment has cleared the 80% support threshold in recent validator snapshots, beginning the sustained-consensus period required for activation. The separate lending amendments have not reached the same level.

The cleanup package addresses technical issues around several XRPL features, including vault and lending-related logic. That may sound routine, but enabling complex financial functions directly in a blockchain’s rules creates little room for improvisation once the code is live. Validators need confidence that edge cases are resolved before activation.

XRPL amendments require support from more than four-fifths of a server’s trusted validator list over a sustained period. A temporary majority is not enough. Recent published snapshots showed fixCleanup3_4_0 over the line and pointed toward a possible late-October activation if that support continues.

Meanwhile, native lending is still a separate matter. The presence of code in a server release does not mean the lending protocol is available for users, and the cleanup amendment should not be mistaken for a vote approving the entire feature set.

This difference can be frustrating for investors focused on new products, but it is an intentional part of the ledger’s upgrade process. Validators are effectively being asked to approve changes to shared financial infrastructure that every participant must respect.

The immediate milestone to watch is whether the cleanup amendment maintains its necessary voting support for the full activation window. Lending will require its own consensus outcome.

Ahmed Barakat is a journalist and copywriter based in Georgia with a growing focus on blockchain technology, DeFi, AI, privacy, digital assets, and fintech innovation.

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

HEX fell nearly 60%, PulseX dropped 49%, and PulseChain’s PLS token lost close to 36% after Richard Heart was reported detained in Istanbul under a Finland-requested Interpol Red Notice. The crypto market reaction exposes how sharply founder risk can reprice a personality-driven ecosystem.

Turkish police and the National Intelligence Organization, MİT, detained Heart, whose legal name is Richard James Schueler, in the Beşiktaş district. The report linked the operation to a Red Notice Finland requested in December 2024 over suspected aggravated tax fraud; the reported detention is not a conviction, extradition decision, or finding of guilt.

🇹🇷 JUST IN: Turkey officially confirms HEX founder Richard Heart's detention, with $7.15 MILLION in cash seized.Authorities also seized six cold wallets, seven guns and 1,400 rounds of ammunition, Justice Minister Akın Gürlek said.The haul included 28 watches, 300 bags and 19… https://t.co/aJRtTNdwpQ pic.twitter.com/nMwjrDVVxn

Finland’s investigation concerns suspected aggravated tax fraud linked to income from June 2020 through April 2024. Finnish authorities have reportedly put the potential unpaid tax in the hundreds of millions of euros. A separate assault allegation involving a 16-year-old has also appeared in reporting about Richard Heart’s wanted status.

Reported inventories of items recovered in the Istanbul operation were about $4 million in cash, electronics, firearms, drones, 64 watches and six cold wallets.

Richard Heart founded HEX, PulseChain and PulseX, and his public persona has been central to their promotion. That concentration creates a direct confidence channel: a legal shock involving the founder can change perceived governance, communication, and execution risk even if no underlying contract or network has failed.

For traders, the distinction is practical. A sharp move in a thin market can be amplified by spreads and fragmented liquidity, and liquidation flows can compound a repricing without supplying new information about a project’s fundamentals.

Crypto market liquidations and reversals illustrate how execution and forced positioning can intensify volatility beyond the initial catalyst.

The seizure of personal assets also does not automatically halt PulseChain’s blockchain or invalidate HEX, PLS, or PLSX. The unresolved questions are narrower and more consequential: whether Richard Heart can continue directing public communication, whether project contributors have an independent operating structure, and whether the reported wallets are connected to any project-controlled funds.

The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission case against Heart and the associated projects is separate from Finland’s investigation. The SEC’s 2023 civil complaint alleged unregistered offerings exceeding $1 billion and misuse of at least $12 million; a federal judge dismissed the case in February 2025 on jurisdictional grounds, and the agency did not pursue an amended complaint.

Near-term market risk therefore turns on confirmed legal developments and whether project operations show signs of continuity without Heart’s direct involvement.

A formal Turkish court filing or a confirmed extradition step would clarify the legal path; until then, further swings in HEX, PLS, and PLSX remain possible, but no specific outcome is established by the current record.

#253. Crypto audits give investors false sense of security as Q3 hacks cost $1.18 billion, Hacken says

Crypto investors may be putting too much faith in security audits that fail to cover the systems hackers actually target, according to blockchain security firm Hacken.

In a report released on Thursday, Hacken found that hackers stole $1.18 billion across 107 incidents during the third quarter, 55% more than in the previous quarter. Of that amount, $906.8 million was lost due to compromised suppliers or developer tools, publicly available security fixes that were not installed or components excluded from the most recent security review.

"The problem is always scope." Andrii Matiukhin, co-founder and board director at the company, said in an interview with CoinDesk. "It's expensive to have enormous scopes of all components that interact with funds or influence economics, and teams cut corners, auditing only critical parts of the service.”

The findings raise questions about how much protection investors can expect from crypto projects advertising themselves as audited. Hacken said customers often assume an audit covers an entire platform when it may examine only specific smart contracts, leaving wallets, signing systems and third-party software outside its scope.

“Usually, when a customer sees a new project, they see an audit badge, assume the whole system is covered, and lose money through a key, a supplier, or a setting that was never tested,” Matiukhin said.

The biggest incident in the period was the September attack on crypto exchange Bitget, which lost at least $352 million after hackers exploited a vulnerability in a third-party security product to gain access to its withdrawal infrastructure, according to the report.

The risks extend beyond exchanges. Just this week, hardware wallet maker Ledger said it found an unauthorized hardware “spy” implant in a device sold by CryptoBilis, a Southeast Asian reseller, resulting in losses of about $93 million.

Three crypto bridges and cross-chain protocols lost more than $35 million during a six-hour exploit in July, Hacken said. AFX Trade accounted for $24 million of that after attackers gained control of its validator keys. Other attacks walked off with $319 million at Liquid Network, at least $75 million at Tectonic, and roughly $114 million at Coldcard wallet software.

Hacken also examined 12 derivatives exchanges and prediction markets and found that more than $700 million in secure assets at two major venues depended on a four-key signing arrangement requiring three signatures, or on administrative keys whose holders were not publicly identified.

Matiukhin declined to identify the venues or provide a detailed assessment before publication of the report. He said it had found no evidence of an active vulnerability, but considered some of the arrangements inadequate given the amounts involved.

“We are not aware of a live bug in the systems of any reviewed venue,” Matiukhin said. “Instead, what we found is setups where key setups are not secure enough considering the scale of the venues reviewed.”

Matiukhin said delays in fixing known vulnerabilities were another concern, particularly when multiple blockchains relied on the same software but updated it at different times.

“Sometimes a critical vulnerability is classified as low by the team, and fix implementation is delayed or even declined,” Matiukhin said.

Responsibility ultimately rests with the companies holding customer funds, which must track vulnerabilities and install fixes promptly rather than rely on an audit completed months or years earlier, Hacken said.

#254. Tesla Roadster Rocket Is the Cool 'Flying' Car You Can’t Have

Tesla Roadster Rocket Is the Cool 'Flying' Car You Can’t Have

Tesla's new Roadster drove up an upside-down ramp, flew off the end, flipped in midair, and landed on its wheels. The livestreamed demo took place October 15 at a SpaceX test site in Texas, where the car also hopped over a row of Teslas that included a Semi truck.

The stunt drew oohs and aahs on social media, especially on X where the announcement gathered over 10 million views.

Even Musk’s former-friend-turned-foe Sam Altman praised it on X, “Wow the new roadster looks quite amazing, good job.” That is a generous take from a guy who reserved a Roadster in 2018 and had to wait 7.5 years to get a refund.

Almost everyone is talking about it, and almost no one who is will get to own one any time soon (if ever).

Real life, baby pic.twitter.com/3QEqn18wig

The trick that makes this car fly is cold-gas thrusters, which are basically compressed air blasted out of nozzles instead of burned rocket fuel. Lars Moravy, Tesla's vice president of vehicle engineering, said 10 thrusters connect to 600 liters of compressed air, and that Tesla borrowed some technology from SpaceX to pull it off.

On paper the car reports a top speed above 230 mph, more than 300 miles of range, and 0-60 mph in under a second. The on-stage test clocked 0.81 seconds, and Tesla lists the single-seat Rocket at under 0.59.

Musk had been teasing this since last October, when he told Joe Rogan the next Roadster could be capable of flight and was “crazier than all the James Bond cars combined.” Tesla now bills it as “the best of the last human-driven cars.”

Tesla has not announced a price for any version, but its reservation page asks $50,000 for the two-seat Performance and $250,000 for the Thrust, with $5,000 due up front and the balance within 10 days.

The Rocket, the version built around a full flight system, seats one, has no listed figure, and is invite only. Musk said production begins in 2028.

So, you will need to be among the chosen few to get your hands on one of these cars.

Tesla's own website says the flying version is not approved for public road use, and when Musk was asked whether the car is street legal, he said it “depends on your street.” No FAA or road-safety approval for it has been reported, so even with an invitation in hand you would not be taking it to the office.

Making a flying car legal likely takes at least two regulators: U.S. carmakers self-certify that vehicles meet federal safety standards, while an aircraft needs an FAA airworthiness certificate, and the agency says certifying a new aircraft type can take between five and nine years.

It’s hard to check history when it comes to flying cars. One of the closest precedents is Alef Aeronautics, whose Model A precursor received an experimental airworthiness certificate from the FAA in June 2023 that allows flight testing and was billed as a step toward a type certificate.

Minnesota's Jetsons law lets residents own a roadable aircraft but bans taking off and landing on public roads, following a 2020 New Hampshire law that gave private citizens the right to own flying cars.

So you’ll likely need a special license to drive a car that also counts as an aircraft.

Hovering is the other obstacle: a 2021 paper in Joule puts the power an electric aircraft needs to hover at 500 to 900 watts per kilogram, against 150 to 350 in cruise.

In plain terms, the battery has to dump energy far faster than it does on a normal flight. Tesla's cold-gas approach sidesteps that, which is likely why the demo showed jumps and a flip instead of a trip from one place to another.

#255. Bloomberg Strategist Calls Bitcoin a “Stock-Market Puppet,” Maintains $10,000 Target

Bloomberg commodity strategist Mike McGlone reiterated his prediction that Bitcoin (BTC) could fall to $10,000, calling the cryptocurrency a “complete stock puppet” whose performance remains heavily influenced by US equities.

Speaking to Maggie Lake on Welthion recently, McGlone argued that Bitcoin has yet to demonstrate the resilience needed to justify more optimistic expectations. He pointed to its relationship with the S&P 500, suggesting that a broader stock market downturn could put additional pressure on BTC.

“The bottom line is it’s already flunked the main test this year,” McGlone said.

Notably, the strategist first made his $10,000 forecast in 2024, when Bitcoin traded near $109,000. He has continued to defend the prediction even after the cryptocurrency advanced toward $126,000.

McGlone argued that investors have become increasingly dependent on US financial markets, leaving assets across several sectors vulnerable to the same downturn.

“We’re all complete stock puppets,” he said, grouping Bitcoin, copper and gold among assets increasingly sensitive to movements in equities.

“If the stock market drops 10%, you’ll see a good test,” he added, suggesting a significant decline would expose how much Bitcoin depends on broader market conditions.

He also pointed to the US Treasury market and the country’s mounting debt as potential headwinds. He added that higher bond yields can make fixed-income investments more attractive than riskier assets, potentially weakening demand for Bitcoin.

McGlone further questioned whether Bitcoin’s scarcity narrative could continue supporting its valuation as the number of competing cryptocurrencies grows.

However, McGlone’s bearish outlook contrasts with findings from analysts at Japan-based DeFi asset management platform XWIN, who identified several on-chain indicators suggesting Bitcoin’s selling pressure may be stabilizing.

In a Monday post on X, the analysts highlighted relatively low BTC reserves on exchanges, a recovery in apparent demand from deeply negative levels, and whale holdings that had risen to approximately 3 million BTC.

However, apparent demand remained below zero, meaning the recovery had not yet provided definitive confirmation of a sustained bullish reversal.

XWIN also pointed to high US bond yields, elevated oil prices, slowing ETF inflows and profit-taking as factors that could leave Bitcoin exposed to further downside. At the end of this month, the American corporation DTCC opens commercial access to its Tokenization Service. The post-trade giant will allow major players to create "digital twins" for traditional securities. The project covers a colossal pool of assets worth $30 trillion, a quarter of all funds under the control of the DTC central securities depository.

However, Stellar is not yet being let into this market: under the approved plan, the first wave of liquidity will go to private bank networks, so the public blockchain will have to wait its turn until next year.

DTCC detailed its Tokenization Service, opening $30 trillion in DTC-held assets and confirming Stellar as a 2027 launch partner. Canton and Besu run live now with 25 securities; Stellar joins via SEP-41 tokens next year. @StellarOrg https://t.co/zWm80Y13XU

The launch was preceded by a closed pilot in July, in which more than 30 Wall Street financial institutions took part. According to the DTCC report published on October 16, the project's framework will be strict at first. The system will start with just 25 liquid instruments: U.S. Treasuries, major ETFs, and large-cap stocks from the Russell 1000 index.

For investors, nothing changes fundamentally: the digital tokens are pegged 1:1 to the underlying securities and retain their CUSIP codes and all legal rights. DTC remains the final owner of the official registry, guaranteeing the usual protection.

Because large capital is not ready to take risks on open ledgers, DTCC has chosen an isolated architecture. From the end of October, operations will launch on only two closed platforms: the Canton Network (CIP-56 standard) and the corporation's own private environment based on Hyperledger Besu (ERC-20).

Converting traditional securities into tokens via the UI or API will take no more than 15 minutes, but this can only be done during East Coast business hours (from 2:00 to 18:00 ET). Inside the system, however, institutional players will be able to move digitized trillions around the clock, directly between their wallets.

For the Stellar Development Foundation, this release confirms the status quo. Integration with public networks was originally planned for the first half of 2027, and nobody has changed that schedule. Stellar will join the platform together with Circle's Arc solution, using its SEP-41 standard to transfer assets.

By that time, DTCC promises to expand the list of available securities, add support for corporate actions, and launch on-chain collateral settlements via digital cash.

This DTCC move is the most large-scale attempt to connect real trillions with distributed ledger technology. But while the private Canton and Besu networks are the first to skim the cream off the commercial RWA tokenization market, Stellar remains on the waiting list until the beginning of next year.

#258. How CertiK Verifies a TPS Claim and What It Cannot Tell You

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

When a blockchain protocol claims it can process 40 million transactions per second, verifying the underlying arithmetic becomes essential.

Sui's October 7 announcement presented that figure on a Basecamp stage in Singapore, and CertiK's subsequent audit report placed a precise, verified figure alongside it. Comparing the initial marketing announcement with the final verification report reveals how independent auditors evaluate extreme throughput benchmarks.

This guide outlines how a security verifier like CertiK evaluates throughput results, using its TON benchmark audit as a foundational template and Sui's tunnel performance test as a real-world implementation.

Throughput figures can easily be inflated under controlled conditions. A development team might select a simplified workload, calculate transactions using generous parameters, or present a single peak burst as standard network behavior. While these practices are common in marketing, unverified TPS figures remain speculative until an independent party recomputes the raw ledger metrics.

Sui's initial announcement reported 40,614,180 TPS using its off-chain tunnel architecture at Sui Basecamp. The team also noted that CertiK would audit execution journals and publish formal findings. With CertiK's verification report now public, we can examine how third-party technical verification works in practice.

Verification begins by defining what constitutes a single transaction, as this definition determines the final throughput total. In the Sui evaluation, CertiK counted a transaction only if it proved valid under protocol rules, contained every required authorization proof, and appeared exactly once within the canonical execution journal.

Furthermore, the audit restricted valid counts strictly to transactions committed inside the active test window. This approach filters out duplicate entries, unassigned user actions, and pre-test setup data. Consequently, if a throughput claim fails to define its underlying transaction unit, the figure carries little practical value.

CertiK's TON write-up begins by documenting environmental parameters. The auditors verified the testnet infrastructure, which comprised 256 active nodes, specific software versions, and defined validator sets. Because performance on a test network does not guarantee identical results on mainnet, auditors must specify exact deployment parameters.

Similarly, the Sui evaluation documented its operational setup. The benchmark ran on mainnet on October 7 across 10 distinct test runs covering five workload types consisting of simple payments, flash loans, blackjack, tic-tac-toe, and battleship games. The report also noted that workloads launched at staggered intervals, with all 7,680 tunnels operating concurrently for a duration of 148.545 seconds.

Matching deployed execution code to public repositories provides critical assurance during performance testing. In the TON audit, CertiK confirmed that stress-test smart contracts deployed on-chain matched the source code published by the foundation. The testing also utilized contracts with complex execution logic rather than basic balance transfers.

Without this step, a project could benchmark stripped-down programs and present them as full-featured application performance. Verifying deployed bytecode against open-source repositories prevents this discrepancy. In Sui's benchmark, application complexity remained central, with simple payments accounting for approximately 78.98% of total recorded transactions.

During the TON evaluation, CertiK collected transaction counts across one-minute intervals over a 25-minute period to derive overall TPS metrics. The peak minute recorded 6,806,474 total transactions, which translated to an audited rate of 104,715 TPS.

That result proved lower than dividing the total count by 60 seconds. The variance occurred because the network counter updated in five-second increments, prompting CertiK to measure the window as 65 seconds. Accounting for exact interval bounds produced a conservative, defensible figure.

For Sui, auditors utilized finer measurement increments. CertiK evaluated full UTC-aligned one-second intervals while discarding incomplete edge seconds. The peak throughput reached 40,682,328 transactions during the second starting at 08:46:17 UTC. Meanwhile, the sustained throughput reached a 60-second rolling average of 40,339,143.65 TPS, representing 2,420,348,619 total transactions. To measure concurrent tunnels, CertiK aggregated qualifying counts and divided by the shared duration rather than summing individual tunnel rates.

A thorough audit verifies that independent execution logs reconcile completely. CertiK confirmed that all 7,680 tunnel instances achieved VERIFIED status, with 15,241,348,297 in-window off-chain transactions matching full-history admission records exactly. Each tunnel's logged count aligned with its on-chain declaration, and opening checkpoints matched closing parameters.

The underlying settlement architecture remains visible through these records. The benchmark tunnels opened and closed using 960 shared opening transactions and 960 shared closing transactions. As a result, 1,920 on-chain base layer transactions anchored more than 15.2 billion off-chain executions.

Sui's initial announcement reported 40,614,180 TPS, whereas CertiK's audited peak reached 40,682,328 TPS. This 68,000 transaction difference represents a minor 0.17% variance. Such a margin reflects the difference between real-time telemetry estimates and strict post-hoc recomputation.

In addition, the initial announcement stated that formal verification was ongoing. CertiK's final report subsequently provided the missing audit metrics, establishing verified peak rates, sustained averages, total transaction volumes, and explicit calculation methodologies.

Despite these figures, understanding the boundaries of the audit methodology remains crucial. CertiK explicitly noted that tunnel TPS measures off-chain state transitions rather than Sui's base-layer on-chain execution capacity. Consequently, dividing off-chain counts by base-layer settlement times does not represent native on-chain throughput.

Furthermore, several technical scope limitations apply:

Similar scope boundaries applied to TON's prior audit, which was evaluated on testnet infrastructure using a single-minute peak window. Independent throughput audits confirm performance within defined test parameters rather than guaranteeing general network capacity.

Evaluating independent audit reports requires examining both verified metrics and stated scope boundaries. Sui's tunnel benchmark demonstrates significant off-chain execution capacity under controlled test conditions, provided the results are interpreted within their proper architectural context.

#259. Dormant 2013 Bitcoin Wallet Moves $34 Million After 13 Years

An early Bitcoin holder has moved approximately 411.45 BTC from a wallet associated with 2013, attracting fresh attention as traders monitor old coins returning to activity.

TL;DR: The coins were worth roughly $34 million at recent market prices. A transfer from a dormant address is visible on-chain, but it does not prove that the owner sold the Bitcoin.

The wallet’s original activity dates to a period when Bitcoin traded near $131. On that basis, the stash would have cost about $54,000 at the time, although the original owner’s actual acquisition price and history are not independently established merely by a blockchain address. The contrast helps explain why movements from that era attract such interest.

Long-dormant coins can stir the market for several reasons. Some observers worry that old holders may sell into exchanges, while others see routine changes to custody arrangements as an equally plausible explanation. Moving Bitcoin from one self-controlled address to another does not put it on an order book or turn it into dollars.

The latest transaction has been tracked through public blockchain records and analytics coverage. Without reliable identification of both beneficial owner and recipient, speculation about a liquidation remains just that. A new address format also cannot prove a particular security motive unless the owner says so.

There is a useful distinction between age and intent. The ledger can show when coins last moved and where they went next. It cannot reliably reveal why the person controlling the keys decided to act on a particular morning.

The transfer is a striking reminder of how much dormant Bitcoin wealth exists. It is not, by itself, a bearish trade signal.

#261. Crypto exchanges Binance, Coinbase join West Africa scam sweep that flagged $11 million

Authorities in Ghana and Nigeria arrested 28 people in a crackdown on West African scam networks that included cryptocurrency investment fraud, the U.S. Department of Justice said in a statement.

The operation also identified 117 trafficking victims in Ghana who were awaiting repatriation to Nigeria, according to the U.K.'s National Crime Agency (NCA), and saw private companies identify more than $11 million in funds that could be frozen.

Partners also reported cryptocurrency seizures but did not disclose their value or the assets involved. The $11 million represents funds flagged for a possible freeze, not confirmed recoveries.

The NCA hosted the operation that brought tech firms and authorities together, to target networks targeting people in the U.S., U.K. and other countries. The DOJ described it as the first such joint operation focused on West Africa.

Crypto exchanges Coinbase and Binance participated alongside blockchain analytics firms Chainalysis, Elliptic and TRM Labs. Coinbase said it helped trace illicit funds, support asset freezes and provide intelligence to investigators. It identified more than 65 active scam victims and prevented more than $415,000 in potential losses. TRM Labs said it exposed a large-scale peer-to-peer laundering network.

In Sasaabi, near Accra, Ghanaian authorities arrested 19 people and seized 303 electronic devices. Nine more people were arrested in Nigeria.

Social media giat Meta said it removed more than 3.7 million Facebook and Instagram accounts, pages and groups, most of which appeared to target Americans and Britons through impersonation.

Participants also provided law enforcement with leads on more than 30 suspected scam centers.

#262. Sam Altman’s Worldcoin: How VanEck, MrBeast, and Wall Street Capitalize on Exploited Biometrics

Ahmed Barakat is a journalist and copywriter based in Georgia with a growing focus on blockchain technology, DeFi, AI, privacy, digital assets, and fintech innovation.

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

On October 18, Tools for Humanity’s World network launched its “World ID for Banking and Finance” suite, with Sam Altman’s firm partnering with Wall Street banks including VanEck, Pantera Capital, and Bain Capital, to counter AI-driven deepfakes via a new integration with Zoom. But behind the glossy enterprise rollout lies a deeply interconnected corporate web designed to turn human biology into institutional liquidity.

As World ID markets itself to global financial institutions as an essential infrastructure layer, uncomfortable questions are mounting over how this biometric database was built, who financed it, and whether everyday retail participants are merely fuel for a highly lucrative financial illusion. While World pitches its “Proof of Human” cryptographic architecture as a high-minded defense against AI impersonation, critics note the network was built by offering crypto incentives to financially vulnerable people willing to submit to Orb verification.

In 2024, an employee at engineering firm Arup transferred $25.6 million after joining a video call where every other participant was a deepfake. Since then, AI has advanced significantly and is making impersonation increasingly convincing, causing challenges for financial… pic.twitter.com/J06gnULw8H

The pitch sounds timely. Deepfakes threaten financial security, while autonomous AI agents are beginning to transact and communicate on people’s behalf. Yet World is selling trust through a network built partly by offering crypto incentives to people willing to submit to Orb verification.

Now, the commercial opportunity is emerging, justifying the bargain struck with those early participants.

World’s latest announcement presents Proof of Human as essential infrastructure for an AI-heavy internet. Its system can establish that someone is a unique human, confirm their presence, or verify selected attributes. World says its cryptographic architecture can provide these assurances without exposing unnecessary personal information.

That is a legitimate use case. The problem is how the network was built and whether people understood what they were joining.

A 2022 investigation by MIT Technology Review documented Worldcoin recruitment practices across several countries, including Kenya and Indonesia. Participants described receiving cryptocurrency, cash, or gifts for signing up, raising fundamental questions about informed consent when financial incentives are offered to people with limited resources.

Reddit discussions in r/degoogle and project forums highlight a related problem. A person who accepts a token incentive is not necessarily an informed, retained user who understands the product.

Anecdotes from the community suggest many of the claimed 18 million verified humans registered primarily to receive rewards, creating a vast disparity between registered biometrics and active user engagement.

This disconnect exposes a darker reality as World targets legacy finance: global banking giants are now actively attempting to buy “trust” built on a foundation of asymmetric economic warfare.

Critics argue that by integrating World ID, these initial design partners are effectively laundering an ecosystem built on the backs of unconsenting, low-income individuals.

By outsourcing their identity security to Worldcoin, institutions like Bain Capital and VanEck Funds are legitimizing a system that commodifies and exploits data from the Global South, purchasing an enterprise verification network whose foundational database was harvested by offering pocket-change crypto incentives to financially vulnerable populations.

This is not a theoretical ethical debate; it is a matter of documented legal record:

For a banking sector bound by strict international compliance, anti-money laundering frameworks, and consumer protection laws, turning a blind eye to the toxic regulatory history of this biometric pipeline represents a profound failure of corporate due diligence.

It signals that as long as the corporate utility is polished, legacy finance has no issue consuming enterprise architecture built on data extraction that sovereign courts have explicitly ordered to be scrubbed and destroyed.

While the project frames its current push into banking as a natural evolution of identity infrastructure, market observers point to a deeply interconnected corporate web designed to scale the network through mass retail entertainment.

Connecting the dots…Sam Altman co-founded World. $ORBS is the largest publicly disclosed institutional holder of $WLD, owns stakes in OpenAI and MrBeast’s Beast Industries, and holds $ETH$BMNR owns $ORBS, has $180M directly invested in Beast Industries and holds almost 5% of… https://t.co/pKFMJTKjMy

This institutional roadmap exposes the cold, transactional calculus behind the project’s vision. Public market vehicles like Eightco Holdings (NASDAQ: ORBS), backed heavily by institutional investors like Bitmine Immersion (NYSE: BMNR), have accumulated significant treasuries of WLD, alongside massive private-market equity positions in Sam Altman’s OpenAI and Jimmy Donaldson’s Beast Industries (MrBeast).

By treating human identity as mere fuel for an interconnected corporate ecosystem, Worldcoin relies on institutional vehicles like $ORBS and massive distribution partners like MrBeast to passively onboard millions of everyday people into an Ethereum-based Layer-2 network.

Critics argue this model hollows out the authentic definition of “proof of humanity,” reducing it to a clever onboarding mechanism designed to inflate token utility, effectively selling exploited biometric data to Wall Street to drive liquidity upward to large financial backers.

World’s expansion also arrives as WLD struggles to sustain its price. WLD bounced to $0.547 on October 17 before falling to $0.478 the following day. Open interest declined 5.1% over 24 hours, while funding turned negative, pointing to weakening short-term market sentiment.

Token supply adds another complication. DeFiLlama lists 10 billion WLD as the maximum supply and approximately 3.819 billion as circulating on October 19, with 58.19% of tokens unlocked. Our analysts estimate 1.02 billion WLD in releases over the following 12 months, worth around $500 million at today’s price.

For sure, unlocks do not automatically mean immediate selling, but investors must weigh potential dilution against evidence of sustainable demand. A banking integration is not proof that enterprise revenue will accrue to WLD holders, nor does a growing verified-human count guarantee meaningful token utility.

That is the uncomfortable bargain at the center of Worldcoin’s expansion. Participants exchanged time, attention, and biometric verification for incentives, while token investors financed a vision whose long-term economics remain uncertain.

World may yet build useful identity infrastructure for the AI era. But if its next chapter depends on banks paying for trust, it must demonstrate more than impressive registration numbers and ambitious partnerships.

It must explain the product clearly, protect participants meaningfully, and show how the economic benefits reach beyond the companies building the network.

Otherwise, World risks turning proof of humanity into proof of a much older problem: the people who supply the raw material do not necessarily share in the value created from it. Should Sam Altman and Worldcoin give their answer?

#263. Hackers Jailbreak iPhone 18 Pro on Stage, and It Survives a Reboot

Hackers Jailbreak iPhone 18 Pro on Stage, and It Survives a Reboot

Security firm Calif.io demonstrated an untethered jailbreak on an iPhone 18 Pro running iOS 27.0.1 on stage at Hexacon, the offensive security conference in Paris, on Friday. It's the first time an untethered, permanent jailbreak is successful in such devices.

A jailbreak strips away Apple's software restrictions, and untethered means it comes back on its own after a restart, with no computer attached.

Apple builds the iPhone as a locked-down system, with signed code, a sandbox around every app and a protected startup chain, so owners cannot change how iOS works or run software the company has not allowed. A jailbreak breaks that lock and hands the user root access, which lets them install apps Apple never approved, add new features, customize the interface and use the phone in ways Apple did not intend.

For example, back in the early iOS days, users with jailbroken phones were capable of filming video before Apple shipped that feature. They were also able to run Android on their iPhones, unlock carriers, install themes, and so on. Right now a user with a jailbroken iPhone can install apps outside of the Appstore, browse the full file system and delete bloatware.

Few people do this today, but every working jailbreak on current hardware shows that the defenses Apple invests heavily in can still be beaten.

Video from the stage, posted by jailbreak researcher Billy Ellis, shows the team rebooting the phone, unlocking it with the regular passcode and opening an SSH session as root, the highest level of access on the device. The terminal output listed iOS 27.0.1 and an uptime of about two minutes.

At #hexacon - https://t.co/jEOpspETlT demos iOS 27.0.1 untethered jailbreak on iPhone 18 Pro pic.twitter.com/S54aRrzHFS

— Billy Ellis (@bellis1000) October 16, 2026

Hexacon runs October 16 and 17 in Paris, so the demo came on the opening day of the conference. The event is aimed at researchers who find and exploit security flaws, and its talks typically cover bugs in widely used platforms such as phones and browsers.

Calif has not said which vulnerabilities it used, and no public tool exists. Its newsletter post from the conference lists four demos, including a Signal one-click and an iMessage demo, and says everything “will be released in due time.”

3/ Can your iPhone do this? pic.twitter.com/gT0Z781Tnl

Getting root on a current iPhone usually takes a chain of bugs that escapes the app sandbox, takes over the kernel and gets past hardware-backed defenses such as Pointer Authentication Codes, which detect tampering with memory pointers. Surviving a reboot is harder still, because Apple checks the code that runs at startup.

In April, Calif's Thai Duong wrote that Claude helped him take apart an iOS Safari exploit, in a series on how a real iPhone jailbreak works. In May, Calif said Anthropic's Claude Mythos Preview helped it build a macOS kernel exploit against Apple's M5 chip protections in under a week.

“We didn’t build the chain alone. Mythos Preview helped identify the bugs and assisted throughout exploit development,” he said.

Apple's iOS 27 security notes, published September 14, credit Calif.io “in collaboration with Claude and Anthropic Research” for two bugs that let an app cause a denial of service or a system crash. Nothing in the notes ties either bug to the jailbreak.

A chain that gives root on a fully updated iPhone is the same kind of capability that commercial spyware vendors sell to governments, and Apple usually patches such chains once it learns the details. How long iOS 27.0.1 stays exposed therefore depends largely on when Calif chooses to publish.

Apple has not publicly commented on the demo as of Friday, and says it does not confirm security issues until patches are available. Calif has not said when it will publish the details.

Stablecoin issuer Circle is seeking to enter about 40 developing markets, according to the company’s CEO and ​chairman, Jeremy Allaire.

“We’re kind of going through an inflection point... a transition right now, ‌and that transition is essentially moving from the early adopter phase of blockchain technology into the mainstream scaling phase,” Allaire told Reuters, speaking Friday on the sidelines of the IMF and World Bank meetings ​in Bangkok.

#267. How to Verify a Token Burn Hidden Inside a 31 Transfer Governance Spell

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Sky's second token burn removed 7.37 million SKY from circulation, yet opening the corresponding Etherscan transaction reveals 31 separate transfers and no obvious burn label.

Ultimately, finding and confirming the burn requires navigating a complex governance execution.

When you open the transaction behind Sky's second burn, you will not find a line explicitly marked burn. Instead, the top-level recipient field points to an unlabelled contract, the function call reads cast(), and the page logs 31 individual token transfers. Nevertheless, only one of those transfers represents the actual burn event.

Sky reported that 7,372,288 SKY tokens were permanently removed from circulation. That figure represents roughly 2.6 times the magnitude of the protocol's first burn of 2.86 million SKY, funded via 5% of the monthly Net Protocol Surplus. To verify whether the blockchain records match the public announcement, inspecting the transaction line by line clarifies the full execution process.

While most token burns involve a single direct transfer to a dead address, Sky processes its burns through governance via an executive spell. This mechanism bundles multiple approved protocol actions into a single atomic transaction.

As a result, the transaction log appears crowded. Alongside the primary SKY movement, the transaction mints DAI and USDS, burns DAI, and distributes funds to multiple external recipients including Grove. Expecting a single isolated row can make the page look incorrect, but all bundled operations belong to the same governance execution.

Because a failed transaction burns zero tokens, verification always begins with the execution status. The transaction displays a status of Success, recording an execution timestamp of October 12, 2026, at 14:01:47 UTC.

Tracking the precise timestamp is essential. While Sky announced the burn on October 14, the transaction executed on-chain two days earlier on October 12. Consequently, citing the announcement date instead of the execution timestamp introduces an accurate timeline error.

The recipient address listed in the top-level field is 0x4bdD1Cc8540E4c43ee210a6ff0EE96ad0Bba297A. This address corresponds to neither the official SKY token contract nor a standard dead burn address. Instead, it identifies the spell contract itself.

This structure mirrors the pattern seen in multisig and treasury burns, where the top-level field displays the contract being called rather than the ultimate destination of the tokens. In short, the initiating field identifies the caller, whereas the lower token transfer section records the final destination of the assets.

Examining the spell contract's page directly provides vital execution context. The contract is officially named DssSpell with verified source code, having been created on October 8, 2026, at 13:15 UTC. Its historical log shows two distinct interactions consisting of a Schedule call followed by a Cast call.

This sequence reflects standard Sky governance mechanics. Spells are first deployed and scheduled, after which a mandatory delay passes before the community executes the Cast function. Furthermore, this means the burn parameters were locked on-chain four days prior to execution and six days before the official public announcement.

The underlying details sit within the ERC-20 Tokens Transferred section. The 31 transfer entries repeat in pairs, logging DAI minting and burning alongside USDS minting to recipients in figures such as 4,218,121, 1,148,408, and 2,927,190.

These secondary movements are separate protocol operations bundled inside the same governance spell. Therefore, filtering out unrelated activity requires isolating the specific token contract for SKY and bypassing the surrounding stablecoin transfers.

Isolating the SKY asset movement highlights two specific transfers. The primary line records 7,372,288 SKY moving from the Sky MCD Pause Proxy contract directly to the zero address.

Two specific factors confirm the validity of the burn. First, the sender is the Pause Proxy through which governance spells execute, establishing authorized origin. Second, the zero address possesses no private key, rendering the tokens irrecoverable. In addition, the transferred 7,372,288 SKY rounds precisely to the reported 7.37 million figure.

A secondary SKY transfer within the same transaction requires careful distinction. Approximately 1,933,534 SKY leaves the Pause Proxy contract but routes toward an active protocol address rather than the zero address.

That secondary transfer is not part of the burn. Adding that figure to the burned total would yield roughly 9.3 million SKY, producing an inaccurate headline metric. By rule, only tokens transferred directly to the zero address represent true permanent burns.

Comparing the verified transfer against the first burn figure of 2.86 million SKY confirms a 2.58 times increase, validating the reported 2.6 times scaling metric.

Regarding overall supply impact, the main SKY token page recorded a total supply near 23.46 billion SKY prior to execution. The 7.37 million token burn represents approximately 0.03% of total circulating supply. Evaluated at prevailing market prices near $0.076 listed on DefiLlama, the destroyed tokens carried a monetary value of roughly $560,000.

While a zero-address transfer indicates token destruction, checking the token contract's total supply parameter provides final verification. Ideally, the contract total supply should drop by the precise amount sent to the null address.

Minor discrepancies across external tracking sites typically stem from delayed indexing intervals rather than ledger mismatches. Meanwhile, verifying the underlying contract address ensures analysis remains focused on the authentic token contract.

On-chain explorer logs prove that the transaction completed, but they do not automatically calculate the protocol's financial metrics. The stated funding source of 5% of Net Protocol Surplus relies on internal accounting inputs not explicitly printed in the transaction payload.

Because surplus calculations depend on broader governance reporting, cross-referencing protocol revenue dashboards provides necessary context. For example, DefiLlama tracking reflects active burn mechanisms alongside quarterly buyback records.

Ultimately, navigating Sky's multi-step spell execution demonstrates how public ledgers allow complete verification of complex governance burns without relying on unverified press announcements.

#269. Cysic Bridge Exploit Creates 10 Million Tokens Before $727,000 Moves To Ethereum

Cysic has suspended its cross-chain bridge after an attacker created 10 million unauthorized CYS tokens on BNB Chain and converted part of the supply into assets moved toward Ethereum.

TL;DR: On-chain analysis traced the sale of about 7.2 million CYS and the receipt of 306.6 ETH, valued at roughly $727,000 at the time. The bridge was stopped while the incident was investigated.

The mechanics of the attack illustrate why bridges remain an awkward security problem. A token minted on one network is supposed to correspond to an authorized event elsewhere. When that verification breaks, an attacker can create assets with no legitimate backing and sell them into whatever liquidity is available before a project can respond.

Blockchain records reviewed in the incident showed the attacker exchanging the newly minted tokens through decentralized venues and routing proceeds across chains. Cysic took action to suspend the bridge and block an address, but intervention came after a substantial portion of the unauthorized issuance had already been traded.

The immediate damage is not limited to the amount ultimately received in ETH. New tokens entering the market can also pressure CYS’s price, expose liquidity providers to losses and leave honest holders uncertain about which balances are valid. Recovery becomes harder as swaps and bridges split proceeds across multiple destinations.

Cysic will need to account for the failure in its message-verification process and explain any corrective action before normal operations can safely resume. Users should distinguish between the bridge’s security and the wider network’s functioning rather than assuming that every component suffered the same compromise.

The incident is another example of a technical shortcut in cross-chain accounting becoming a market-wide event in minutes.

#270. Chip-stock bets lost $52 million in 10 minutes with Wall Street shut

A sudden wave of selling wiped out nearly $52 million in crypto traders’ leveraged bets on chip stocks in 10 minutes on Saturday, while the shares themselves sat idle with Wall Street closed for the weekend.

Those bets were placed through perpetual futures, contracts that track a stock’s price and trade around the clock on crypto exchanges, so traders can buy and sell chip stocks on a Saturday night.

A trader who borrows to make a bigger bet gets closed out automatically when losses eat through their deposit, and the forced selling can push prices lower for the next trader in line.

About $51.6 million in positions tied to chip stocks and semiconductor funds were force-closed between 21:22 and 21:32 UTC, according to CoinGlass data, and about $38 million of that came from traders betting on higher prices.

SOXL, a fund that triples the daily moves in chip shares, took the biggest hit at about $12.7 million. SanDisk and SK Hynix contracts followed at about $10.8 million each.

The selling started on Binance, according to a review of the trades by David Jeong, chief executive of trading firm Tread.fi, who placed the first large SanDisk and Micron sell orders on Binance at 21:21:59 UTC.

Less than a second later, orders hit Hyperliquid, a crypto exchange where Trade XYZ lists stock-tracking contracts, and roughly 10 addresses opened bets against six chip-linked contracts within 1.8 seconds.

Binance handled about $21.9 million of SanDisk trading in that first minute, against $3.1 million on Trade XYZ.

Memory-chip shares were already coming off a rough week as investors weighed new competition from Chinese chipmaker CXMT.

With the stock market shut, there was no real share price for these contracts to follow, so traders were reacting only to each other. Trade XYZ’s rules let trading on the platform set its own reference prices until outside stock quotes come back.

Those quotes return when U.S. markets open Monday, which will show how far Saturday’s prices strayed from where the shares actually trade.

#271. Circle Plans Push Into 40 Emerging Markets as Stablecoins Go Mainstream, CEO Says

Circle Plans Push Into 40 Emerging Markets as Stablecoins Go Mainstream, CEO Says

Circle wants USDC in a lot more wallets around the world.

The stablecoin issuer is preparing to enter roughly 40 emerging and developing countries, CEO Jeremy Allaire told Reuters on the sidelines of the IMF and World Bank meetings in Bangkok.

Allaire pointed to rising organic demand for stablecoins across Southeast Asia, Latin America, Africa, and the Middle East from people and businesses looking to tap into an internet-based economy.

The technology, he said, is moving “from the early adopter phase of blockchain technology into the mainstream scaling phase.”

Stablecoins are cryptocurrencies pegged to a traditional asset, usually the U.S. dollar. Circle’s USDC holds about 25% of the stablecoin market, compared with roughly 60% for Tether’s USDT. USDC’s circulation rose 19% year over year to $73.3 billion in the second quarter.

Circle has resources for the push, including its $400 million acquisition of payments firm Tazapay and a $100 million strategic investment from Binance, Reuters reported.

The company is also leaning on regulatory tailwinds. Circle secured a federal banking charter in July, sending its stock higher, and has pursued a New York trust charter. The GENIUS Act, the U.S. stablecoin law, is slated to take effect in January. Allaire said the law would give the world “legal digital dollars,” calling it “a watershed moment.”

Banks are building their own stablecoins, which Allaire framed as healthy competition. After a long stretch in which incumbents kept outsiders out, he said, “they are no longer in charge, and the innovators are having their day.”

Allaire also credited AI agents making tiny machine-to-machine payments with boosting USDC usage. Circle’s Arc network has been adopted by BlackRock, Visa and Standard Chartered, according to Reuters. Circle has been pushing to make USDC the currency of AI agents.

But Allaire warned that AI also raises security risks for financial infrastructure. “If you’re not concerned about it, then your head is in the sand, right?” he said.

According to Ethereum researcher Toni Wahrstätter, Hoodi is the final testnet before Glamsterdam reaches mainnet. The upgrade is expected to bring a major change to Ethereum's gas limit, with the proposed increase taking it from 60 million to 200 million.

That would represent a roughly 3.3-fold increase, potentially allowing more computation and transactions to be included in each block, depending on their gas requirements.

Hoodi is the final testnet before mainnet. With Glamsterdam going live soon, Ethereum will 3.3x its gas limit, from 60M to 200M. From there, 300M feels like a realistic next step.

Following its activation on Sepolia on October 6, the Glamsterdam network upgrade is now scheduled for the Hoodi testnet. Glamsterdam advances Ethereum's L1 scaling roadmap with enshrined proposer-builder separation, block-level access lists, and gas pricing changes that better reflect the cost of execution and state growth.

The Glamsterdam network upgrade will activate on Hoodi at epoch 132,352, slot 4,235,264 (October 26, 2026, 17:42:48 UTC). At the same epoch, Hoodi's gas limit will be raised to 200 million via the gas limit schedule, matching the Sepolia testnet.

Wahrstätter suggested that 300 million for Ethereum's gas limit could become a realistic next step after the proposed 200 million target. However, that figure should be treated as a potential future milestone rather than a confirmed part of the Glamsterdam upgrade.

According to Ethereum developers, the mainnet activation time for the Glamsterdam upgrade will be announced once decided by client teams.

Preparations for Hegotá are shaping up as Glamsterdam nears the final mile. According to Ethereum creator Vitalik Buterin, Hegota—the fork planned for next year—may likely be Ethereum's last "normal" fork, with features and technology that would be recognizable to someone from 2015.

Everything after that involves recursive STARKs, automated formal verification, highly optimized consensus algorithms, and making it all quantum-safe. With PeerDAS, Ethereum began its transition from being just a blockchain to something much more powerful.

Starting after Hegotá, this transformation becomes Ethereum's primary story. The outcome: a cryptographic world computer. According to Ethereum researcher Toni Wahrstätter, 23 EIPs are being considered for Hegotá, with two headliners (FOCIL and Frame Transactions).
